items.title: Home
items.text:
Where:

  • \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{u}\) are the optimization variables corresponding to the system state and controls,
  • \(H\) is the optimization horizon,
  • \(\ell_k(\cdot) \in \mathcal{R}\) is the cost function for optimization stage \(k\),
  • \(\boldsymbol{f}_k(\cdot) \in \mathcal{R}^{n_x}\) is the dynamics function for optimization stage \(k\), and
  • \(\boldsymbol{c}_k(\cdot) \in \mathcal{R}^{n_c}\) is the constraints function for optimization stage \(k\).

This problem formulation splits the OCP into multiple stages up to a desired time horizon and allows the user to assign costs and constraints for each of those stages.

\(\boldsymbol{x}\) is not required to be a flat Euclidean vector: SSQP works natively on manifolds, so a state can include components like a floating-base orientation (an \(SO(3)\)/\(SE(3)\) element) alongside ordinary vector components, with linearization and integration carried out through the correct tangent-space operators throughout. See Manifold-valued states for details.

At each iteration, SSQP quadratizes the cost and linearizes the dynamics/constraints around the current guess to build a Quadratic Program (QP), exploits the stagewise (banded) structure of that QP to solve it efficiently, and uses the QP solution as an update step, governed by a line search. See The SSQP Solver for details.

items.title: Home
items.text:
SSQP is an implementation of a Structure-exploiting Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP) Non-Linear Problem (NLP) solver that works natively on manifolds, specifically tailored to Optimal Control Problems (OCPs) of the following form:

\[ \begin{split} \min_{\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}} \sum_{k=0}^{H-1} \ell_k(\boldsymbol{x}_k, \boldsymbol{u}_k) + \ell_H(\boldsymbol{x}_H) &\\ \text{subject to} \\ \boldsymbol{x}_{k + 1} = \boldsymbol{f}_k(\boldsymbol{x}_k, \boldsymbol{u}_k)&, 0 \leq k < H \\ \boldsymbol{c}_k(\boldsymbol{x}_k, \boldsymbol{u}_k) \geq \boldsymbol{0}&, 0 \leq k < H \\ \boldsymbol{c}_H(\boldsymbol{x}_H) \geq \boldsymbol{0} & \end{split} \]

items.title: Repository layout
items.text:
• examples/: examples using SSQP to construct and solve OCPs for robotics tasks: offline trajectory generation, and real-time Model Predictive Control (MPC) both in simulation and on real systems.
  • include/ and src/: the C++ header and source directories for the library.
  • python/: the library's Python binding code (the ssqpy module), built using nanobind.
  • tests/: unit tests for library functionality.
  • external/: external dependencies of the library.

items.title: Solver Mode Benchmarks
items.text:
benchmarks/solver_modes/ compares SSQP's own solver modes against each other, rather than against other solvers: for a given problem, how does formulating the dynamics equality constraint as ForwardDynamics (torque controls), InverseDynamics (acceleration controls), or ReducedInverseDynamics (acceleration controls, unactuated DOFs propagated implicitly) affect convergence?

This page covers the trajgen/ half of that directory, which benchmarks offline trajectory generation. For each model, many randomly generated problems (different targets, same cost/constraint structure) are solved once per applicable dynamics mode, all the way to --horizon/max-iteration limits rather than stopping at the first converged solve, so that the full convergence trace is available for every problem.

items.title: Reading the plots
items.text:
Each plot aggregates every problem generated for that model, one line per solver mode, against SQP iteration on the x-axis:

  • Problems Solved: the cumulative percentage of problems that have converged by a given iteration. A failed problem still counts toward the total, so it pulls the curve down rather than being excluded.
  • Cost: the per-problem worst per-stage cost, log-scaled. The solid line is the median across problems, the band the 25th-75th percentile range.
  • Constraint Violation: the per-problem worst per-stage violation (position/velocity/torque/friction bounds and the dynamics-transition defect), log-scaled, against the shared solver tolerance. Median line and interquartile band, as above.

All three plots below use the HPIPM QP backend.

items.title: Running the benchmarks yourself
items.text:
See the solver_modes/ README for full setup. Once set up, from the trajgen/ directory:

python run_benchmark.py [pendubot|panda|go2] -q hpipm

--modes restricts which dynamics modes are run (all applicable modes by default), and -n/--n-problems changes how many problems are generated (50 by default; the Pendubot, Panda, and Go2 plots below were generated with -n 500). Results land in trajgen/data/results; plot.py then renders one model's results into the plots shown below:

python plot.py pendubot -q hpipm

items.title: Pendubot
items.text: The same Pendubot Swing-Up problem as in the solver benchmarks, run here with a randomized target configuration per problem, comparing ForwardDynamics against InverseDynamics.

items.title: Panda
items.text: The Franka Panda reaching random targets within its feasible region, comparing ForwardDynamics against InverseDynamics.

items.title: Go2
items.text: The Go2 quadruped walking to a randomized target pose, comparing all three dynamics modes: ForwardDynamics, InverseDynamics, and ReducedInverseDynamics (which propagates the unactuated floating base implicitly instead of constraining it explicitly).

items.title: Go2 Multi Jump
items.text:
The Go2 performing five jumps in place, landing on a different combination of feet in each gap between jumps (see Go2 Multi-Jump). Unlike the models above, this problem keeps the same fixed choreography across runs rather than randomizing targets, so only a single generated problem is benchmarked per mode; there's no convergence trace to aggregate into a plot, just that one run's runtime, iteration count, final cost, and constraint violation, using HPIPM. Constraint violation is the same worst per-stage quantity described above (bounds and dynamics-transition defect), against the shared tolerance of 1e-2.

Dynamics Mode Runtime Iterations Final Cost Constraint Violation ForwardDynamics 9.1 s 64 0.0507 0.219 InverseDynamics 25.6 s 282 0.0748 0.121 ReducedInverseDynamics 3.4 s 30 0.0527 0.124

items.title: G1 Jump
items.text:
The Unitree G1 humanoid jumping vertically in place (see G1 Jump). Same single fixed-choreography problem setup as Go2 Multi Jump, benchmarked with HPIPM.

Dynamics Mode Runtime Iterations Final Cost Constraint Violation ForwardDynamics 59.0 s 218 0.7534 0.173 InverseDynamics 338.2 s 1000* 0.8314 26.814 ReducedInverseDynamics 8.0 s 38 0.7539 0.097

* Hit the 1000-iteration cap without meeting the solver's convergence criterion.

items.title: Solver Benchmarks
items.text:
benchmarks/solver/ compares SSQP against a handful of other OCP solvers on the same set of problems. Every solver formulates the identical problem through ProblemWrapper, an abstract interface (costs, constraints, finalize, solve, save) with one subclass per backend translating those calls into that backend's own API, so a given problem stays defined once while every solver attempts the same costs and constraints on it.

Seven solvers are compared:

  • ssqp-admm / ssqp-hpipm / ssqp-piqp: SSQP itself, using the three per-stage QP backends described in QP Solvers
  • fatrop / ipopt: formulated through CasADi's Opti stack, solved with the respective plugin
  • aligator: Aligator
  • mim_solvers: mim_solvers' CSQP, built on Crocoddyl

All seven are run to the same nominal tolerance (1e-2 by default, see benchmark_config.py), even though that tolerance bounds a different internal quantity for each (SSQP's per-stage KKT/constraint residual, Fatrop/Ipopt's scaled KKT error, Aligator's primal-dual residual, CSQP's convergence gap), since reimplementing every solver's own termination criterion for an exact match isn't practical.

On fairness

A fully fair, apples-to-apples comparison across seven independent solver codebases is close to impossible: each has its own convergence criterion, its own QP backend and warm-starting strategy, its own default tuning, and its own years of separate engineering investment behind it. These benchmarks are not a claim that SSQP is faster or higher-quality than any of the others. The goal is to give a rough sense of where SSQP sits relative to the state of the art on a shared set of problems, not to crown a winner.

Known gaps

  • On the Go2 problems, we were unable to get JIT compilation working in a timely fashion, so a fair benchmark for Fatrop and Ipopt (which rely on it) wasn't possible for those.
  • On the contact-switching problems (Go2 Jump, Go2 Wheelie, Go2 Frog), we excluded mim_solvers, since we were unable to get it to converge at all.
  • On Go2 Frog specifically, we were also unable to get Aligator to converge, leaving only the two SSQP solvers.
  • On Duffing Local, Fatrop is missing at m = 256 for the two largest horizons (N = 500 and N = 1000): JIT-compiling its formulation at that size requires more memory and time than a fair evaluation could accommodate, so those points were left out.
  • On Duffing Global, whose all-to-all coupling makes for a much denser formulation, both Fatrop and Ipopt are missing entirely at m = 256 (every horizon) for the same reason.

Using the selector below, you may change the tolerance to view the corresponding plots for each problem.

Tolerance: 1e-3 5e-3 1e-2 5e-2 1e-1

items.title: Problem sizes
items.text:
The problems range from Pendubot's long, low-dimensional swing-up to Go2 Frog's short but heavily constrained, contact-switching locomotion. Sizes below are per SSQP's own direct-transcription formulation (state = generalized position + velocity, control = generalized torque plus one force variable per active contact); a range means the value changes over the horizon with the contact schedule.

Problem Horizon State Dimension Control Dimension Constraints per Stage NLP size (vars / constraints) Pendubot 2500 / 2.5s 4 2 6 (terminal: 4) 15,004 / 15,004 Go2 Standing 100 / 1s 37 30 72 (terminal: 27) 6,737 / 7,227 Go2 Jump 150 / 1.5s 37 18–27* 51–78 (terminal: 42) 9,367 / 10,932 Go2 Wheelie 200 / 2s 37 24–30* 66–84 (terminal: 39) 12,957 / 15,405 Go2 Frog 300 / 3s 37 18–30* 48–84 (terminal: 30) 18,841 / 21,342 Panda Circle 400 / 4s 18 9 30 (terminal: 21) 10,818 / 12,021

* Varies with the number of feet in contact at each stage: every active contact adds a 3D force variable to that stage's control vector, so the dimension shrinks during flight phases and grows back during stance.

items.title: Reading the plots
items.text:
Each plot bars four quantities per solver, side by side:

  • Runtime, in milliseconds
  • Iterations, the outer solve loop's iteration count
  • Final objective, the converged cost
  • Constraint violation, summed over every stage of that stage's worst bound violation (position, velocity, torque, friction, and, for the direct-transcription solvers, the dynamics-transition defect), against a dashed line marking the shared tolerance

A fast, few-iteration solve is not a meaningful win if the trajectory it returns is infeasible, which is what the constraint violation panel is for. A solver that fails to converge for a given problem is labeled "failed".

Since it's summed across stages rather than reported per stage, the plotted constraint violation is not directly comparable to the problem tolerance, which bounds a per-stage quantity. On a long horizon, this sum can end up above the tolerance even for a solver that has actually converged, since it is adding up many small, individually in-tolerance violations rather than reporting a single one that exceeds it.

items.title: Running the benchmarks yourself
items.text:
See the solver/ README for the full setup (a Docker image is provided, since several of these solvers pull in their own heavy dependency chains). Once set up:

python run_benchmark.py [problem] -s [solver]

plot_benchmarks.py then renders one problem's data/<solver>/<problem>.json results into the plots shown below:

python plot_benchmarks.py pendubot

The Coupled Oscillators problems below are swept over problem size instead, via --duffing-m/--duffing-horizon (multiple values run a grid search), and rendered with plot_grid_search.py:

python run_benchmark.py duffing_local --all-solvers --duffing-m 2 4 16 64 256 --duffing-horizon 20 100 200 500 1000
python plot_grid_search.py duffing_local --duffing-m 2 4 16 64 256 --duffing-horizon 20 100 200 500 1000

items.title: Pendubot
items.text: The Pendubot Swing-Up problem: an underactuated double pendulum swinging from hanging to upright, actuated at the shoulder joint only.

items.title: Go2 Standing
items.text: The Go2 quadruped holding a fixed standing configuration, all four feet in contact throughout, with no other motion target. A short, contact-heavy but otherwise static regulation problem.

items.title: Go2 Jump
items.text: The Go2 Jump problem: stance, flight, stance, with all four feet leaving the ground for a scheduled window in the middle and landing back at a specified footprint. In this case, the front left foot has no contact and, therefore, should always remain in air.

items.title: Go2 Wheelie
items.text: The Go2 rearing up on its rear two feet: the rear feet stay in stance for the whole horizon, while the front two lift off for a window in the middle and come back down at the end. Unlike Go2 Jump, there's no target trajectory for the freed feet; the standing-configuration cost is what pulls them (and the rest of the robot) back down once the window closes.

items.title: Go2 Frog
items.text:
A longer, four-hop bounding motion 2 meters forward, with staggered per-leg liftoff/landing and brief full-flight windows between hops rather than Go2 Jump's single synchronized flight phase. The same motion also appears, run directly rather than through the benchmark harness, as Go2 Frog in the Gallery.

mim_solvers and Aligator both failed to converge on this problem (see "Known gaps" above), so only the two SSQP solvers are meaningfully compared below.

items.title: Panda Circle
items.text: The Franka Panda tracing the circular (green) end effector path in task space via frame-pose tracking costs, additionally constrained to the rectangular window (red) inscribed in that circle, same as Panda Circle (Trajectory Generation), reformulated here in ForwardDynamics mode (torque-actuated) so every backend solves an equivalent problem.

items.title: Coupled Oscillators
items.text:
A scalable benchmark instead of a fixed-size one: m weakly-coupled Duffing oscillators (state x = [q_1, ..., q_m, v_1, ..., v_m], one control force per oscillator), swept over both m and the horizon to see how each solver scales with problem size. Two coupling topologies are benchmarked: duffing_local, where oscillator i only interacts with its immediate neighbors (a discrete Laplacian), and duffing_global, where every oscillator interacts with every other one through a sinusoidal coupling term.

Each plot below lines runtime (left axis, solid) and iterations (right axis, dashed) per solver, faceted by the other swept variable; a missing point means that solver wasn't run at that grid point, while a point where the solver ran but didn't converge is marked with a red X.

items.title: Benchmarks
items.text:
benchmarks/ contains two independent sets of benchmarks, covering two different questions:

  • Solver: how does SSQP compare against other established OCP solvers (Fatrop, Ipopt, Aligator, mim_solvers/CSQP) on the same robotics problems, each one solved through a shared problem definition so every solver attempts the same costs and constraints?
  • Solver Modes: within SSQP itself, how does the choice of dynamics formulation (ForwardDynamics, InverseDynamics, ReducedInverseDynamics, see Model) affect convergence on a given problem?

items.title: Why we run these
items.text: Neither set of benchmarks exists to produce a single headline number. The Solver benchmarks exist to give a rough, honest sense of where SSQP sits relative to the state of the art on realistic robotics OCPs, rather than only ever being evaluated in isolation. The Solver Mode benchmarks exist for a more practical reason: SSQP supports several ways to formulate the same underlying problem, and picking well between them matters for how fast and how reliably a given problem actually solves, so we wanted data to back that choice rather than intuition alone.

items.title: General conclusions
items.text:
Across the Solver benchmarks, SSQP is competitive with the other solvers on this shared problem set; see the "On fairness" note on the Solver Benchmarks page for why that's phrased carefully rather than as a claim of being faster or higher-quality than any specific one of them.

Across the Solver Mode benchmarks, the clearest pattern is with floating-base, legged problems: ReducedInverseDynamics tends to converge in fewer iterations and less time than ForwardDynamics or InverseDynamics there (see the Go2 Multi Jump and G1 Jump tables). It also tends to produce solutions of higher quality. Both sets of plots go into the actual per-problem numbers; this page is only meant as a starting point before reading either in full.

  • Solver Benchmarks: SSQP vs. other OCP solvers, problem by problem
  • Solver Mode Benchmarks: SSQP's own dynamics modes, compared against each other

items.title: Examples
items.text:
The examples/ directory contains robotics-related OCPs built with SSQP, covering offline trajectory generation as well as real-time MPC in simulation and on real systems.

See the Gallery for videos of what SSQP produces →

Directory Contents trajgen/ Offline trajectory generation, in both Python and C++: SSQP generates a full trajectory from scratch given costs/constraints and little to no initialization. Includes di.py (the Quickstart double integrator), pendulums, the Panda and iiwa arms, and legged-robot examples (Go2, G1, A1, Talos). Most Python examples take command line parameters, and each one prints the final solver state and writes its result to a JSON file. mujoco_mpc/ MPC examples using MuJoCo as the simulated "real" system: MuJoCo provides state feedback, and SSQP's MPC helper solves and re-solves the OCP each control step. Covers the pendubot (with optional online model identification), the Panda and the Go2. The simulation is synced with the controller, so it does not run in real time. real_mpc/ MPC examples running against real hardware instead of a simulator: a double pendulum, a Franka Emika Panda and a Unitree Go2. Several of them use a server-client architecture, since the machine controlling the robot is not always the one running SSQP. visualizer/ visualize.py / visualize_srbd.py, using viser to visualize trajectories written by solver.write(...). models/ Custom SSQP StageDynamics/etc. models usable in place of XML files (the single rigid body model of a quadruped, and the planner that generates its contact schedules and references), plus related utilities. assets/ URDF/MJCF assets used by the examples. The URDFs of SSQP's built in model presets (Go2, A1, Panda, G1, Talos and the double pendulum) come from here, and are embedded into the library when it is built.

Each directory has its own README with the details of every example, including the parameters it takes.

Solver benchmarks, comparing SSQP against other OCP solvers on a shared set of problems, live separately in benchmarks/ rather than under examples/; see Benchmarks.

items.title: Walkthroughs
items.text:
A few examples are covered in detail:

  • Pendubot Swing-Up: trajgen, XML-based model, predefined costs, and a swing-up scheduling trick, ForwardDynamics mode
  • Panda Circle (Trajectory Generation): trajgen, frame-relative pose tracking, a real box constraint, InverseDynamics mode
  • Go2 Jump: trajgen, per-stage contact scheduling for a jump (stance → flight → stance), ReducedInverseDynamics mode
  • Panda Circle (MPC): mujoco_mpc, the same circle tracked in closed-loop MPC against a live MuJoCo simulation, with per-step target retargeting, ForwardDynamics mode by default (--inverse-mode switches to InverseDynamics)
  • Go2 Walking (MPC): mujoco_mpc, a gamepad-driven trot in closed-loop MPC against MuJoCo, with a gait schedule that retargets every cost and contact constraint each plan stage, and a jump, ReducedInverseDynamics mode

items.title: Running the Python examples
items.text:
The built ssqpy Python extension must be importable; see Using the Python bindings in Installation. Once built, source examples/setup_env.sh:

cd examples
source setup_env.sh
python trajgen/python/di.py

Then run any example script from its directory the same way (for example, cd trajgen/python/go2 and python go2_gaits.py --gait trot). The scripts take their settings as command line parameters, so --help lists them. Several example subdirectories (MuJoCo, real robot SDKs, the visualizer) use their own Python virtual environments for extra dependencies, so check for a *-venv/*venv directory or a README alongside the specific example before running it.

items.title: Running the C++ examples
items.text:
The C++ trajectory generation examples are only built when the library is configured with examples enabled:

cmake -S . -B build -DBUILD_EXAMPLES=ON
cmake --build build

Each one becomes an executable under build/bin, in the same subfolder as its source, and should be run from the repository root, since asset and output paths are relative to it (for example, ./build/bin/urdf/panda/panda_circle).

items.title: FAQ
items.text: Answers to common "how do I...?" questions, for getting things done quickly before diving into Concepts. Where the Python and C++ APIs differ, switch the tabs below to compare. If you haven't yet, read the Quickstart first; these answers assume you already have an importable ssqpy (Python) or a linked ssqp (C++, see Installation).

items.title: How do I define a custom cost, dynamics, or constraint?
items.text:
Subclass StageCost/StageDynamics/StageConstraints and override the abstract methods. Here's a minimal linear dynamics example; see Costs, Constraints & Dynamics for the full interface each one requires.

In Python, the input vectors (x, u and the multipliers) are read-only views of the solver's data that are only valid during the call, so copy them (x.copy()) if you need to modify or keep them.

PythonC++ 
import ssqpy
import numpy as np


class MyDynamics(ssqpy.model.dynamics.StageDynamics):
    def output_size(self):
        return 2

    def state_size(self):
        return 2

    def control_size(self):
        return 1

    def evaluate(self, x, u):
        return np.array([x[0] + x[1] * 0.1, x[1] + u[0] * 0.1])

    def gradient(self, x, u):
        dX = np.array([[1.0, 0.1], [0.0, 1.0]])
        dU = np.array([[0.0], [0.1]])
        return dX, dU

#include "model/stagewise/StageDynamics.hpp"

class MyDynamics : public ssqp::model::stagewise::StageDynamics
{
  public:
    uint state_size() const override { return 2; }
    uint control_size() const override { return 1; }
    uint output_size() const override { return 2; }

    void evaluate(ConstVecXRef x, ConstVecXRef u, VecX &out) const override
    {
        out.resize(2);
        out << x(0) + x(1) * 0.1, x(1) + u(0) * 0.1;
    }

    void gradient(ConstVecXRef x, ConstVecXRef u, MatX &dX, MatX &dU) const override
    {
        dX = (MatX(2, 2) << 1.0, 0.1, 0.0, 1.0).finished();
        dU = (MatX(2, 1) << 0.0, 0.1).finished();
    }

    // Linear dynamics: all Hessian-vector products are zero.
    void hessprod_xx(ConstVecXRef, ConstVecXRef, ConstVecXRef, MatX &Pxx) const override { Pxx.setZero(2, 2); }
    void hessprod_xu(ConstVecXRef, ConstVecXRef, ConstVecXRef, MatX &Pxu) const override { Pxu.setZero(2, 1); }
    void hessprod_uu(ConstVecXRef, ConstVecXRef, ConstVecXRef, MatX &Puu) const override { Puu.setZero(1, 1); }
};

items.title: How do I track a target pose vs. a target joint configuration?
items.text:
Two different predefined costs cover these, and picking between them depends on what you actually care about matching:

PythonC++ 
# Joint-space: match a specific set of joint angles
configuration_cost = ssqpy.model.costs.SquaredConfigurationErrorCost(model, desired_configuration, weight)
model.addCost(k, configuration_cost)

# Task-space: match a frame's position and orientation, regardless of joint angles
pose_cost = ssqpy.model.costs.FrameSquaredPoseErrorCost(
    model, "frame_name", desired_pose, translation_weight, rotation_weight
)
model.addCost(k, pose_cost)

#include "model/stagewise/predefined/Costs.hpp"

model.addCost<ssqp::model::stagewise::predefined::costs::SquaredConfigurationErrorCost>(
    k, model, desired_configuration, weight);

model.addCost<ssqp::model::stagewise::predefined::costs::FrameSquaredPoseErrorCost>(
    k, model, "frame_name", desired_pose, translation_weight, rotation_weight);

SquaredConfigurationErrorCost penalizes deviation from an exact set of joint angles; use it when the configuration itself is what matters, as in Pendubot's swing-up target. FrameSquaredPoseErrorCost penalizes deviation of a named frame's pose (position and/or orientation) in task space, ignoring which joint angles get there; use it for manipulation-style tasks specified by where something should end up, as in Panda Circle's end-effector circle.

The two aren't mutually exclusive: for a redundant arm (more joints than the 6 DOF a pose constrains), tracking pose alone leaves the extra joint-space freedom unconstrained, which can drift over a long closed-loop run. Panda Circle (MPC) adds a small SquaredConfigurationErrorCost toward a nominal configuration alongside the pose-tracking cost for exactly this reason.

items.title: How do I build a model from a URDF or MJCF file?
How do I choose a good initial guess?
items.text:
SSQP is a local solver: it improves on whatever guess it's given rather than searching globally, so the initial guess affects both how fast it converges and which local solution it lands on. init_states/init_controls passed to finalize do double duty: they fix \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) (which the solver cannot change) and seed the guess for every other stage before the solver improves on it.

PythonC++ 
model.finalize(init_states=[my_init_state], init_controls=[my_init_control])

config.init_states   = {my_init_state};
config.init_controls = {my_init_control};
model.finalize(config);

There's no single right way to build one; which approach fits depends on the problem:

  • No guess at all falls back to SSQP's own manifold-aware neutral configuration (e.g. angle \(0\) on a joint's tangent/circle manifold rather than literal zero, which wouldn't be a valid point on it), which is enough for straightforward problems; see Pendubot.
  • A single configuration already close to the expected solution, repeated across every stage, helps a lot when you have domain knowledge about roughly where the solution should be; see Panda Circle.
  • For contact-rich problems, the control guess matters as much as the state one: seeding contact forces at a static-equilibrium value (e.g. each foot supporting its share of the robot's weight) avoids wasting early iterations discovering that a standing robot needs to push against the ground; see Go2 Jump.

A guess that actively points the wrong way can be worse than no guess at all; see the swing-up scheduling trick in Pendubot for a case where the fix was designing the costs around this rather than picking a better guess directly.

See finalize arguments in Model for the full set of initial-guess-related options.

items.title: How do I solve a trajectory optimization problem?
How do I run MPC (real-time control)?
What happens if MPC fails to converge mid-run, and how do I detect it?
items.text:
mpc.step(...) always returns an (x, u) trajectory, even if that step's SSQP iterations didn't fully converge within the tight per-step budget (sqp_iters/qp_iters): it has to return something for the control loop to apply, so it doesn't raise or signal failure on its own. To actually check whether a given step converged, keep convergence data and inspect it after each step:

PythonC++ 
mpc = ssqpy.solvers.MPC(model, sqp_iters=5, qp_iters=50, keep_convergence_data=True)

while running:
    x, u = mpc.step(read_state())
    apply_controls(u.stage(0))

    data = mpc.getConvergenceData()[-1]
    if data.max_iter_reached and not data.loose_success:
        print("MPC step did not converge")

ssqp::solvers::MPC::Params mpc_params;
mpc_params.keep_convergence_data = true;
ssqp::solvers::MPC mpc(model, mpc_params);

while (running)
{
    auto [x, u] = mpc.step(read_state());
    apply_controls(u.stage(0));

    const auto &data = mpc.getConvergenceData().back();
    if (data.max_iter_reached && !data.loose_success)
        std::cout << "MPC step did not converge" << std::endl;
}

An occasional non-converged step is usually not fatal in a receding-horizon loop with good warm-starting (see Warm-starting in MPC): the next step re-solves with fresh state feedback rather than letting the error compound open-loop. A persistent run of failures is worth investigating the same way as an offline non-converging solve (see How do I inspect solver convergence?), and is often a sign that sqp_iters/qp_iters is too tight for how far the state has drifted from the warm start, or that the tracked target has left the problem's feasible region. Note this is a different failure mode from the per-step solve simply running too slowly to keep up with real time. In those cases, trying different solver parameters or attempting to simplify the model might instead be helpful. If that does not help or is not possible, the next solution would be to use SSQPy's MPC as a high level plan, generated at a lower frequency and followed using a low-level controller running at a higher frequency.

items.title: How do I correct the controls between MPC steps?
items.text:
When the control loop runs faster than MPC can solve, the first stage's controls go stale as the state moves away from the one they were solved for. mpc.feedbackGain(k) returns the feedback gain \(K_k\) of the last step at stage \(k\), which gives the change of the stage's controls for a change of its state. Apply it with the difference between the measured state and the planned one, taken in the tangent space of the dynamics:

PythonC++ 
x, u = mpc.step(read_state())
K = mpc.feedbackGain(0)
dynamics = model.getDynamics(0)

while not solved_again():
    dx = dynamics.state_right_minus(read_state(), x.stage(0))
    apply_controls(u.stage(0) + K @ dx)

auto [x, u] = mpc.step(read_state());
const MatX K  = mpc.feedbackGain(0);
const auto &dynamics = model.dynamics()[0];

VecX dx;
while (!solved_again())
{
    dynamics->state_right_minus(read_state(), x.stage(0), dx);
    apply_controls(u.stage(0) + K * dx);
}

The gain describes the last QP, so it only holds near the plan and for the plan's active constraints. With HPIPM it is the Riccati gain of the last interior point iteration, where the barrier stiffens the active constraints (a looser tolerance gives a smoother gain). With ADMM it is the gain of the final LQR, which penalizes inactive constraints as well, so it is stiffer. PIQP does not provide a feedback gain, so feedbackGain raises an error with it. The gains can be too aggressive to apply as they are when the loop adds delay, so scaling them down may be needed.

items.title: How do I switch between the ADMM, HPIPM and PIQP QP solvers?
items.text:
HPIPM requires building SSQP with -DWITH_HPIPM=ON and PIQP with -DSSQP_WITH_PIQP=ON (see Installation); both are enabled by default. For example, to use HPIPM:

PythonC++ 
solver = ssqpy.solvers.ssqp(
    model,
    qp_solver_type=ssqpy.solvers.HPIPM,
    hpipm_mode=ssqpy.solvers.HPIPMMode.Speed,
)

ssqp::solvers::ssqp::Params params;
params.qp_solver_type    = ssqp::solvers::ssqp::HPIPM;
params.hpipm_params.mode = ssqp::solvers::SPEED;

ssqp::solvers::ssqp solver(model, params);

PIQP is selected the same way, with qp_solver_type=ssqpy.solvers.PIQP and piqp_-prefixed keyword arguments in Python, or ssqp::solvers::ssqp::PIQP and params.piqp_params in C++.

See QP Solvers for the tunable parameters of each backend.

items.title: How do I add a contact constraint (e.g. for a robot foot)?
How do I schedule contacts over a trajectory (a gait, a jump, ...)?
items.text:
How do I add a contact constraint? covers a single contact at a single stage; a gait or a jump needs that decision to change per foot, per stage, over the whole horizon. There isn't a dedicated scheduling API for this: it's the same addContactConstraint/addConstraints calls as always, driven by a schedule you compute yourself and apply inside your own per-stage loop. Two ways to turn a contact on/off for a given stage:

PythonC++ 
for k in range(H):
    # Way 1: only add the constraints for the stages where the foot is grounded
    if in_stance(k, "foot_1"):
        model.addContactConstraint(k, "foot_1", mu=0.6, max_normal_force=200.0)

    # Way 2: add them at every stage, and disable them where the foot is airborne
    contact = model.addContactConstraint(k, "foot_2", mu=0.6, max_normal_force=200.0)
    if not in_stance(k, "foot_2"):
        contact.set_enabled(False)

namespace constraints = ssqp::model::stagewise::predefined::constraints;

for (uint k = 0; k < H; ++k)
{
    // Way 1: only add the constraints for the stages where the foot is grounded
    if (in_stance(k, "foot_1"))
    {
        model.addConstraints<constraints::ContactConstraint>(k, model, "foot_1", 0.6, 200.0);
    }

    // Way 2: add them at every stage, and disable them where the foot is airborne
    auto contact = model.addConstraints<constraints::ContactConstraint>(k, model, "foot_2", 0.6, 200.0);
    if (!in_stance(k, "foot_2"))
    {
        contact->set_enabled(false);
    }
}

The two approaches suit different situations: conditionally adding the contact constraint only inside the stages where a foot is grounded is simplest when the schedule is just a stage-index check. set_enabled is more convenient when a constraint's applicability depends on something more complex than that, or when you want to create the constraint object once upfront and reuse it. Neither approach requires all feet (or any other set of contacts) to share the same schedule; per-foot, per-stage toggling is exactly what makes asymmetric gaits representable with the same building blocks. Inside a fully airborne window, adding no contact constraints at all for any foot lets the dynamics reduce to free-fall, which is usually what you want for a flight phase. See Go2 Jump for a complete worked example, including both toggling styles side by side.

items.title: How do I choose a solver mode?
items.text:
ForwardDynamics, InverseDynamics, and ReducedInverseDynamics all solve the same underlying problem, just formulated differently (see Solver mode in Model for what each one actually changes); which one converges best depends on the problem:

  • ForwardDynamics (torque controls) is the most direct formulation and a reasonable default when there's no particular reason to prefer one of the others; see Pendubot.
  • InverseDynamics (acceleration controls) can ease convergence for fully-actuated systems: accelerations enter the dynamics linearly, so the QP built at each iteration is a better local approximation than it would be with torques, where that mapping is nonlinear in the configuration; see Panda Circle.
  • ReducedInverseDynamics (acceleration controls, unactuated DOFs propagated implicitly) is strictly an improvement over InverseDynamics for systems with manifold-valued states, and is used mainly for free-flyer systems, e.g. legged robots, where the base isn't directly actuated; the base's 6 degrees of freedom are enforced through the dynamics instead of being treated as free control inputs, which InverseDynamics alone wouldn't handle; see Go2 Jump.

If you're not sure and the problem is floating-base, ReducedInverseDynamics is worth trying first: across the Solver Mode benchmarks, it tends to converge in noticeably fewer iterations and less time than the alternatives on legged problems specifically (see the general conclusions on the Benchmarks page). For a fully-actuated system, comparing ForwardDynamics against InverseDynamics directly on your own problem is more reliable than assuming one is always better; see the "Things to try" section of Panda Circle for exactly this comparison.

See How do I change the solver mode or integration scheme? for the syntax to actually set it.

items.title: How do I change the solver mode or integration scheme?
How do I save a solved trajectory and load it back later?
How do I inspect solver convergence, or debug why it isn't converging?
How do I enable or disable a cost or constraint at runtime?
How do I control SSQP's logging output?
items.text:
SSQP's output is controlled by a single global mask of independent log levels, set with the functions below.

PythonC++ 
# No output at all
ssqpy.setSilentMode()

# Only warnings and errors: silence everything, then add those levels back
ssqpy.setSilentMode()
ssqpy.setLogLevel(ssqpy.Warning | ssqpy.Error)

# Or remove a single level from the current mask
ssqpy.unsetLogLevel(ssqpy.Info)

# Turn on the (very verbose) debug output
ssqpy.setLogLevel(ssqpy.Debug)

# Keep the iteration table, but with fewer columns
solver.setReducedOutput(True)

// No output at all
ssqp::set_silent_mode();

// Only warnings and errors: silence everything, then add those levels back
ssqp::set_silent_mode();
ssqp::set_log_level(ssqp::Warning | ssqp::Error);

// Or remove a single level from the current mask
ssqp::unset_log_level(ssqp::Info);

// Turn on the (very verbose) debug output
ssqp::set_log_level(ssqp::Debug);

// Keep the iteration table, but with fewer columns
solver.setReducedOutput(true);

setLogLevel adds levels to the mask; it doesn't replace it. Info, Warning and Error are on by default, so setLogLevel(Warning | Error) on its own changes nothing, which is why the "only warnings and errors" example silences everything first. Each level covers a different kind of output:

Level On by default What it prints Info yes The SSQP iteration table (iteration, step norms, constraint violation, and, unless the output is reduced, the first violated stage, QP iterations, QP runtime and step size) and the total solve time Warning yes Non-fatal problems: HPIPM returning a non-zero status, PIQP not reporting a solved QP, NaNs in the QP solution, one dynamics object shared by several stages, or asking an MPC for its convergence data when keep_convergence_data is off Error yes Line search failure with regularization disabled Debug no The initial guess, every iterate's states and controls, the QP matrices built for each stage, and HPIPM's and PIQP's status; this is a lot of output for anything beyond a tiny problem

setReducedOutput only trims the iteration table; it doesn't change which levels are on. The mask is global to the process, so it applies to every model and solver at once, and it only affects printing: the solve's convergence data is recorded either way. To remove the logging from the build altogether, configure with -DDISABLE_LOGGING=ON (see Installation).

items.title: How do I visualize a solved trajectory?
items.text:
The visualizer example renders a written-out trajectory JSON against its URDF using viser (Python only):

cd examples
source setup_env.sh
python visualizer/visualize.py -u path/to/robot.urdf -i path/to/trajectory.json

items.title: How do I use SSQP from C++ without the Python bindings at all?
items.text: Link the ssqp::ssqp CMake target from your own project, either from an installed package (find_package(ssqp)) or by adding SSQP with FetchContent/add_subdirectory, which leaves the Python bindings off by default. See Using the C++ library for both and C++ API Reference for the full class-by-class interface.

items.title: Gallery
items.text:
Trajectory generation Simulated MPC Real MPC

MPC running on real hardware, from the scripts under examples/real_mpc/. The state comes from the robot instead of a simulator, SSQP re-solves a short horizon at every control step, and the first control is sent back to the motors. The README there describes each example, the parameters it takes, and the precautions to take before running it on your own robot.

items.title: Pendubot Swing-Up
items.text: The pendubot, a double pendulum with only its shoulder joint actuated, swinging up and balancing on real hardware. Produced by pendubot.py, the MPC server, together with hardware.py, the client that reads the motors and applies the torques. The two exchange the state and the controls over a socket, which is how the MPC can run on a different machine from the one connected to the motors. This is the real counterpart of the simulated pendubot swing-up.

items.title: Acrobot Swing-Up
items.text: The acrobot, the same double pendulum with only its elbow joint actuated instead, swinging up and balancing. Produced by acrobot.py, run with the same hardware.py client. Having the actuator at the elbow makes swing-up harder than for the pendubot, and the cost also tracks the elbow's height to help it.

items.title: The Double Pendulum in the AI Olympics
items.text:
Our solver was also used in the 4th AI Olympics, held in Bremen in August 2026, where we took first place. The competition's double pendulum task was run on Chalmers University's cloud pendulum platform: a real double pendulum that participants control remotely, with their controllers running on the computing resources the platform provides, rather than on their own hardware.

Taking part meant adapting the same pendulum MPC code shown above to that setting. The platform's computing resources are more limited than those of the machine we use with our own pendulums, so the problem had to be formulated in an easier form that could still be solved in real time, and then retuned for the platform's pendulum. The code also had to be adapted to the platform's API in place of our own hardware client. Beyond that, the solver itself was the same, which made the competition a test of how well SSQP holds up on a real system it was not originally tuned for, with tighter computing limits. The code for our submission is available at upatras-lar/2026_ai_olympics_underactuated_dp.

items.title: Panda Reaching a Target
items.text:
A Franka Emika Panda moving its end effector to a target position, in two runs of the target task from models.py, served by controller_server.py to the robot's hardware.py client.

  • Unconstrained. The end effector goes to the target and holds it. When the robot is pushed, it recovers and returns to the target.
  • Constrained. The model bounds the end effector to a half space along one axis, and the target lies beyond that bound, so it cannot be reached. The end effector gets as close to the target as the constraint allows, and stays there. Pushes are recovered from as well, and this includes a push towards the target, into the disallowed region: once released, the end effector returns to the allowed side of the constraint.

The constraint is a plain bound added to the MPC problem, like the one in the simulated obstacle avoidance demo, so no part of the controller is specific to it. The robot tracks the MPC's joint references with a compliant joint-space controller.

items.title: Go2 Trot Across Terrain, in unitree_mujoco
items.text:
The Go2 trotting over bars, a step, stairs, a slope and rough terrain, with the gamepad commanding its velocity. This is not the real robot, but a simulation, shown here as the step between the simulated Go2 walk and the real one.

What makes it different from the simulated walk. The simulated walk is synchronous: MuJoCo only advances after the controller has produced its control, so a slow solve just makes the simulation run slower, and the controller never experiences a delay. Here the simulator is unitree_mujoco, which runs as its own process, in its own time, and exchanges the robot's low-level state and joint commands with the controller through the same Unitree SDK interface the real Go2 uses. The controller therefore lives with what it will meet on the robot: state messages that arrive on their own schedule, a solve that takes real time, and a plan that is only applied some milliseconds after the state it was solved from was measured.

As such, this uses the real controller. Specifically, it is go2_joystick.py, run with --simulation, which differs from a run on the robot mainly in the network interface it binds to and in the joint gains, set for the simulator. The whole-body walking MPC in dynamic_walk_model.py is unchanged, and so is everything around it that exists because of the real world:

  • The solver runs in its own thread at a fixed rate, and solves from a state predicted forward to when its plan will start, to make up for the latency.
  • The base position and velocity, which the robot does not measure, are estimated with a Kalman filter that fuses the accelerometer with the leg odometry of the stance feet.
  • The plan is played back between solves, with the joint torques recomputed from the measured state at every command.
  • Footholds and swing heights follow a terrain model, which is what lets the robot place its feet on the bars, up the step and the stairs, and across the slope and the rough patch, and keeps them away from edges. The terrain is mapped with the LIDAR, here a simulated one.
  • A fallback lowers the robot to the ground and damps the joints if the solver stalls, the state stops updating, or the joints stop following the plan.

Note that the map the simulated LIDAR produces is much better than what we get on the real robot: it is cleaner, more complete and free of the noise, gaps and pose errors of a real sensor. The terrain in this video is therefore easier for the controller than the real one will be, and the real map is the harder part of the sim to real gap that this demo leaves open.

Running the controller this way is the closest test possible without the robot: failures that depend on timing, such as a plan that arrives too late or a state estimate that drifts, show up here. It stays a simulation, though, so the actuators, the contacts and the sensors are still models of the real ones.

items.title: Go2 Trot
items.text:
From here on, the videos are of the real Go2, running the same controller as in the simulation above: the whole-body walking MPC of go2_joystick.py, driven with a gamepad. The robot trots and turns, with the sticks commanding the forward, sideways and yaw velocity. The base position and velocity it plans from are estimated on the robot from the leg odometry and the accelerometer, and the plan is re-solved at 50 Hz on a computer connected to the robot.

The video also includes changing the base height, as well as the leg swing height, during the trot.

items.title: Go2 Jump
items.text: A sequence of jumps in place in between trots. The jump is part of the same MPC problem as the walk: the base follows a crouch, push off, flight and landing reference, and all four contact constraints are dropped for the flight stages, as in Go2 Jump, but scheduled at run time from a button press on the gamepad. The robot then steps its feet back under the hips after the landing and goes on trotting.

items.title: Go2 Walk
items.text: A slower walking gait, which lifts one foot at a time instead of a diagonal pair, so that three feet are on the ground at all times. It is one of the gaits the gamepad switches between while the robot stands, along with the trot, and it moves at a lower top speed than the trot.

items.title: Push Recovery
items.text: The Go2 being pushed, while trotting and while standing. Nothing in the controller is specific to pushes: the MPC re-solves from the measured state at every step, so a push shows up as a state error that the next plan corrects, by shifting the contact forces and stepping where the feet need to land to catch the base. While standing, a push that moves the base fast enough starts the robot stepping, so that its feet can catch it.

items.title: Go2 Trotting onto a Platform
items.text:
The Go2 getting up on a platform and walking on it, in two runs. This is the real counterpart of the terrain in the unitree_mujoco video, and it is harder than it looks next to that video. On the real robot, the terrain comes from a LIDAR map that is noisier and less complete than the simulated one, and the base position estimate is not perfect, so the footholds and heights the robot plans for are less accurate than in simulation. Late or uneven touchdowns, which a simulation rarely produces, make this harder still. Because of these real world conditions, the platform is a much harder task for the robot than the same terrain in simulation.

A sample screenshot of what the real LIDAR's map looks like, after it is cleaned up to be used by the solver

This is roughly what the map from the real robot's LIDAR looks like once it has been cleaned up for the solver to use. The robot stands in the middle, and the heights around it are shaded from low (blue) to high (yellow). Even after the cleanup, the map is far from the clean terrain of the simulation, with jagged edges, tall spikes and patchy ground. The footholds, swing heights and base heights the robot plans for come from this map, which is a large part of why the real platform is harder than the simulated terrain.

items.title: Gallery
items.text:
Trajectory generation Simulated MPC Real MPC

Closed-loop MPC running in MuJoCo, from the scripts under examples/mujoco_mpc/. Unlike the trajectory generation results, nothing here is solved once and played back: the state comes from the simulator, SSQP re-solves a short horizon at every control step, and only the first control is applied.

items.title: Pendubot Swing-Up
items.text: The pendubot, a double pendulum with only its shoulder joint actuated, swinging up and balancing upright. Produced by pendubot.py, which builds its model from SSQP's double pendulum preset and tracks the tip position with a terminal cost on the upright configuration. The script also takes --noise to disturb the system with random torques, and --identification to estimate the second link's parameters online. The offline version of this problem is covered in Pendubot Swing-Up.

items.title: Panda Obstacle Avoidance
items.text: A Franka Panda reaching a new random goal every few seconds, drawn as a red sphere, while a random pillar placed between the end effector and the goal blocks the straight path. Produced by panda_move.py. A box-shaped bound is convex, so the pillar is not excluded directly: any stage the previous plan puts over the pillar has to stay above its top face, so the end effector passes over the pillar rather than around it. This is not a hard guarantee, since the solve has a limited iteration budget. The closely related Panda Circle (MPC) is covered in detail.

items.title: Go2 Standing on Three Legs
items.text: The Go2 standing on three legs, with a fourth foot lifted, while pushes of increasing force are applied to it in the viewer. The MPC holds the base over the support triangle with contact constraints on the three stance feet, and recovers after each push. Produced by go2_standing.py with --legs 3; --legs 4 and --legs 2 stand on four and two legs. If a push is hard enough to lift or slip a stance foot, the plan still assumes that contact, and the optimization soon fails.

items.title: Go2 Walking
items.text: A gamepad-driven trot, showing the walk itself, jumping in place, turning the base's orientation while the feet stay planted and while walking, and changes to the base height and the feet's swing height. Produced by go2_walking.py, covered in detail in Go2 Walking (MPC). All of these are changes to the references of a single MPC problem, solved once per 24 ms plan stage with the whole-body dynamics.

items.title: Gallery
items.text:
Trajectory generation Simulated MPC Real MPC

A few trajectories generated by scripts under examples/trajgen/python/, to give a feel for what SSQP actually produces before digging into the code that produces it. Every one of these is an offline trajectory-generation solve, not a live simulation: SSQP solves the whole horizon once, and the result is played back.

Solve times

Each solve time and iteration count below is from a single run of the linked script on this machine: an Intel Core i9-14900K (24 cores / 32 threads), 64 GB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04. Both are SSQP's own reported figures, not the script's total wall-clock time, so setup (URDF loading, model construction) isn't included. Each script was run with both of SSQP's per-stage QP backends (see QP Solvers), ADMM and HPIPM, and the faster of the two is shown, labeled accordingly. Treat these as a feel for solve difficulty rather than a rigorous benchmark, for which see Benchmarks.

items.title: Go2 Walk
items.text:
The Go2 quadruped walking 2 meters forward. Produced by go2_gaits.py, which builds its footstep and contact schedule with the GaitManager helper rather than hand-writing per-stage contact logic (compare to Go2 Jump, which schedules contacts directly). GaitManager ships several gait patterns (setWalk, setAmble, setTrot, setPace, setCanter, setGallop, setRotatoryGallop); this script is currently configured for setWalk, but swapping in any of the others produces the same forward motion with a different footfall pattern, worth trying if you want to see how SSQP handles a substantially different contact sequence with no other changes to the problem.

Solve time: 3.6 s (8 iterations, HPIPM)

Formulation: ForwardDynamics

items.title: Go2 Frog
items.text:
The Go2 bounding forward 2 meters with a frog-like, feet-together gait, rather than the alternating-diagonal footfall pattern of a walk or trot. Produced by go2_frog.py, which (unlike go2_gaits.py) schedules every single- and multi-foot contact phase by hand as explicit stage ranges. It's a good example of just how expressive per-stage contact scheduling is: nothing about the constraint API assumes a "gait" in the periodic-footfall sense at all, an arbitrary, asymmetric, non-repeating sequence of which feet touch the ground when is just as representable as a standard one.

Solve time: 1.2 s (14 iterations, HPIPM)

Formulation: ReducedInverseDynamics

items.title: Go2 Multi-Jump
items.text:
The Go2 performing five jumps in place (the same start and end position), also seen on the Home page. Produced by go2_multi_jump.py, which extends the single-jump pattern from Go2 Jump to a predefined sequence of flight windows (JUMP_STEPS), landing on a different combination of feet in each of the four gaps between them (LAND_SEQ: back feet, then right feet, then left feet, then front feet), rather than returning to a full four-foot stance every time.

Solve time: 2.2 s (17 iterations, HPIPM)

Formulation: ReducedInverseDynamics

items.title: G1 Jump
items.text:
The Unitree G1 humanoid jumping vertically in place, torso held level and upright throughout. Produced by g1_jump.py, structurally similar to Go2 Jump (a flight window with contacts dropped, symmetric before and after) but on a humanoid: each of G1's feet is modeled as four independent corner contact points rather than a single point contact per foot, as a flat foot actually needs to resist tipping, not just slipping or lifting off, giving the solver 8 simultaneous contact constraints to schedule per stance stage instead of Go2's 4.

Solve time: 3.4 s (17 iterations, HPIPM)

Formulation: ReducedInverseDynamics

items.title: G1 Walk
items.text:
The Unitree G1 humanoid walking 3 meters forward. Produced by g1_walk.py, which, unlike G1 Jump's simultaneous stance on all 8 corner contact points, alternates strictly between single-leg support: one foot swings for a fixed number of stages while the other stays planted, then they switch, with short standing phases (all contacts active) only at the very start and end. Each foot's four corner contacts are also brought on and off gradually rather than all at once, one toe/heel pair engaging a stage before the other, closer to a real heel-to-toe rolling contact than an instantaneous flat-footed stomp. A hand-tuned per-joint regularization weight also damps the hip-yaw joints specifically, keeping the walk heading straight instead of shuffling sideways.

Solve time: 3.4 s (22 iterations, HPIPM)

Formulation: ReducedInverseDynamics

items.title: Panda Circle
items.text:
A Franka Panda end effector tracing a circle in task space via frame-pose tracking costs, constrained (with --constrain, the default) to stay within a square window inscribed in that circle: watch the path flatten against the square's edges near the circle's corners rather than following it exactly, the constraint visibly winning out over the tracking cost there. This is the trajectory produced by panda_circle.py, covered in detail (including the unconstrained comparison) in Panda Circle (Trajectory Generation); the same motion also appears as a live, closed-loop MPC example in Panda Circle (MPC).

Solve time: 0.2 s (6 iterations, HPIPM)

Formulation: InverseDynamics

items.title: Costs, Constraints & Dynamics
items.text:
Costs, dynamics and constraints are all stagewise functions: they evaluate at a single stage's \((\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u})\) and provide the derivatives SSQP needs to quadratize the cost and linearize the dynamics/constraints at each iteration. StageCost, StageDynamics and StageConstraints all extend a common Function interface (evaluate, output_size, names), then add their own gradient/Hessian requirements.

You can implement any of these from scratch in Python (as in the Quickstart) or C++, or use one of the predefined implementations that ship with SSQP, listed below and fully documented in the Python API reference.

items.title: Inputs and outputs in C++
items.text:
In Python, every method returns its outputs. In C++, they are written into arguments instead, so that the solver can reuse its storage between calls:

  • The inputs are ConstVecXRef (Eigen::Ref<const VecX>), so blocks of larger vectors are passed without copies.
  • evaluate(x, u, out), gradient(x, u, dX, dU), the cost hessian_*, the hessprod_*, constraint right_minus and dynamics state_right_plus/state_right_minus set their outputs, resizing them as needed. A cost's evaluate writes a vector of size 1.
  • evaluate_into, right_minus_into, state_right_plus_into and state_right_minus_into write into an output that is already sized, such as a block of a larger vector. add_gradient, add_hessian_* and add_hessprod_* add to outputs that are already sized.

A custom function only needs the first set: the base classes implement the second through it. The predefined functions do the opposite, deriving from PredefinedStageCost/PredefinedStageConstraints, which implement the first set through the second.

items.title: Costs
items.text:
StageCost (\(\ell_k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) \in \mathcal{R}\), so output_size() is always 1) requires:

  • evaluate(x, u): the scalar cost
  • gradient(x, u): \(\nabla_x \ell_k\) and \(\nabla_u \ell_k\)
  • hessian_xx(x, u), hessian_xu(x, u), hessian_uu(x, u): the cost Hessian blocks

Costs can be named, enabled/disabled at runtime (set_enabled/enabled, though a stage always keeps at least one cost, so disabling every cost on a stage has no effect), and multiple costs can be added to the same stage via Model.addCost / Model.addRunningCost.

items.title: Predefined costs
items.text:
ssqpy.model.costs (ssqp::model::stagewise in C++) ships a library of squared-error costs for common OCP objectives, all built on Pinocchio kinematics for XML-based models:

SquaredJointAngleCost, SquaredJointVelocityCost, SquaredControlCost, SquaredIDTorqueCost, SquaredForceCost, SquaredConfigurationErrorCost, FloatingBaseSquaredTranslationErrorCost, FloatingBaseSquaredRotationErrorCost, FloatingBaseSquaredPoseErrorCost, FloatingBaseSquaredVelocityErrorCost, FrameSquaredTranslationErrorCost, FrameSquaredTerrainHeightErrorCost, FrameSquaredRotationErrorCost, FrameSquaredPoseErrorCost, FrameSquaredVelocityErrorCost, CenterOfMassTrackingCost, FramesInverseSquaredDistanceCost.

See ssqpy.model.costs for constructor arguments and details for each.

Predefined costs and constraints refer to the model they are built with rather than copying it, so they always see its current forces and terrain. In C++, the model must outlive them, and a Model cannot be copied. In Python, each one keeps its model alive.

items.title: Dynamics
items.text:
StageDynamics (\(\boldsymbol{f}_k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) \in \mathcal{R}^{n_x}\)) requires:

  • state_size(), control_size(): dimensions of \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{u}\)
  • evaluate(x, u): the next state
  • gradient(x, u): \(\nabla_x \boldsymbol{f}_k\), \(\nabla_u \boldsymbol{f}_k\)
  • hessprod_xx, hessprod_xu, hessprod_uu: vector-Hessian products against the Lagrange multiplier \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}_k\) (used instead of raw Hessians, since \(n_x\) can be large)

Dynamics also define the manifold structure of the state through state_right_plus/state_right_minus (and state_diff_size, when the tangent space differs in size from the state itself). For a Euclidean state these default to plain vector addition/subtraction; for states that include e.g. a floating-base orientation (a Lie group element), they implement the appropriate manifold operators. Predefined, XML-based dynamics already handle this correctly for the selected SolverMode and Integration.

items.title: Manifold-valued states
items.text:
Not every model's state lives in a flat Euclidean space \(\mathcal{R}^{n_x}\). A floating-base robot's orientation, for example, is an element of the Lie group \(SO(3)\) (or its full pose, \(SE(3)\)), not a vector: adding two orientations, or taking their plain difference, isn't a well-defined operation. Rather than requiring \(\boldsymbol{x} \in \mathcal{R}^{n_x}\), SSQP treats a dynamics function's domain as an arbitrary composite manifold: a state can combine one or more manifold-valued segments with one or more ordinary Euclidean segments, and every place SSQP would otherwise use vector addition/subtraction instead goes through two operators:

  • \(\boldsymbol{x} \oplus \boldsymbol{dx}\) (state_right_plus): retracts a tangent-space update \(\boldsymbol{dx}\) onto the manifold at \(\boldsymbol{x}\), producing a new state.
  • \(\boldsymbol{x}_1 \ominus \boldsymbol{x}_2\) (state_right_minus): the tangent-space displacement between two states, i.e. their local, chart-consistent difference.

For a purely Euclidean state, these reduce to plain vector addition/subtraction, and state_diff_size() (the tangent space dimension \(n_{dx}\)) defaults to state_size() (\(n_x\)). For a manifold-valued segment, \(n_{dx}\) can differ from \(n_x\): a quaternion-parameterized \(SO(3)\) orientation, for instance, contributes 4 parameters to \(n_x\) but only 3 degrees of freedom to \(n_{dx}\). SSQP linearizes, integrates and reports convergence norms in the tangent space, never in the raw parameterization, so the gradients/Hessians returned by gradient/hessprod_* are always sized against state_diff_size() (\(n_{dx} \times n_{dx}\) or \(n_{dx} \times n_u\)), not state_size().

XML-based (Pinocchio-backed) models handle all of this automatically: a free_flyer=True model's floating-base pose is represented and integrated as its native \(SE(3)\)/quaternion manifold element, and the predefined costs/constraints that touch floating-base or frame poses (e.g. FloatingBaseSquaredPoseErrorCost, FrameTranslationBound) use the corresponding Lie-group log/exp maps internally, consistent with the selected Integration scheme. Custom dynamics only need to implement state_right_plus/state_right_minus (and state_diff_size, if it differs from state_size) to opt into the same treatment for their own manifold-valued states.

items.title: Constraints
items.text:
StageConstraints (\(\boldsymbol{c}_k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) \geq \boldsymbol{0}\), or bounded via lower_bound()/upper_bound()) mirrors StageDynamics' derivative interface (gradient and hessprod_xx, hessprod_xu, hessprod_uu against a multiplier \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\)) for an arbitrary output size, and adds:

  • lower_bound() / upper_bound(): per-element bounds (defaults to \([0, \infty)\), i.e. an inequality \(\geq 0\); pass equal bounds for an equality constraint)
  • required_forces() / force_frame(i): for constraints that involve external contact forces (see Contacts and forces in Model)
  • state_only_rows() (optional): the rows of the difference vector that depend only on \(\boldsymbol{x}\). The initial state fixes them at stage 0, so SSQP leaves them out there instead of letting a violated one make the QP infeasible
  • box_rows() (optional): the rows whose gradient is always \(+1\) on a single state or control entry, as BoxRow(row, index, is_control), which HPIPM handles as simple bounds instead of general constraints

In C++, state_only_rows and box_rows overwrite a std::vector passed to them instead of returning one.

items.title: Predefined constraints
items.text:
ssqpy.model.constraints provides: JointAngleConstraint, JointVelocityConstraint, JointControlConstraint, FloatingBaseTranslationBound, FloatingBaseRotationBound, FloatingBasePoseBound, FloatingBaseLinearVelocityBound, FloatingBaseAngularVelocityBound, FrameTranslationBound, FrameTerrainHeightBound, FrameRotationBound, FramePoseBound, FrameLinearVelocityBound, FrameAngularVelocityBound, CenterOfMassBound. The C++ library additionally defines ContactConstraint directly, which Model.addContactConstraint constructs and wires up for you (friction cone + non-penetration against the model's terrain + no-slip zero velocity, which no_slip=False turns off).

See ssqpy.model.constraints for constructor arguments and details for each.

items.title: Reference frames
items.text:
Predefined costs and constraints on a position or a velocity take a reference_frame, either as a constructor argument or through set_reference_frame. It selects the axes that a cost's error, weights and desired value, or a constraint's bounds, are expressed along. Only the axes change: positions keep the world origin. A world vector \(\boldsymbol{v}\) is expressed along axes with rotation \(R\) (whose columns are the axes in world coordinates) as \(R^\top \boldsymbol{v}\).

Option Axes ReferenceFrame.World The world axes ReferenceFrame.Local The axes of the frame the cost or constraint acts on, moving with it ReferenceFrame.Base The axes of the model's floating base, moving with it. On floating base terms this is the same as Local ReferenceFrame(rotation) Fixed axes given by a rotation matrix. A 3x3 array converts to these implicitly ReferenceFrame.yaw(angle) Fixed axes rotated about the world \(z\) axis ReferenceFrame.normal(normal, yaw=0.0) Fixed axes with \(z\) along a surface normal and \(x\) along the horizontal direction at angle yaw from the world \(x\) axis, projected onto the surface

In C++, the same options are ReferenceFrame::World, ReferenceFrame::Local, ReferenceFrame::Base, ReferenceFrame(rotation), ReferenceFrame::yaw(angle) and ReferenceFrame::normal(normal, yaw), in ssqp::model::stagewise::predefined.

Each term supports the options that make sense for it. Positions, a frame's linear velocity bound and its velocity cost default to the world axes, while floating base velocities, which the state holds in the base frame, and a frame's angular velocity bound default to Local:

Term Options Default FrameTranslationBound, FrameSquaredTranslationErrorCost World, Fixed, Local, Base World FloatingBaseTranslationBound, FloatingBaseSquaredTranslationErrorCost World, Fixed, Local (= Base) World FloatingBaseLinearVelocityBound, FloatingBaseAngularVelocityBound, FloatingBaseSquaredVelocityErrorCost Local (= Base, the base frame), World, Fixed Local FrameLinearVelocityBound, FrameSquaredVelocityErrorCost World, Local, Fixed, Base World FrameAngularVelocityBound Local, World, Fixed, Base Local CenterOfMassBound, CenterOfMassTrackingCost, FramesInverseSquaredDistanceCost World, Fixed, Base World

Rotation and pose costs and bounds are not in the list: they already measure their error along their reference's axes, so choosing the reference rotation chooses the axes. For FramesInverseSquaredDistanceCost, the reference frame sets the axes the distance scale applies along.

Passing an option a term does not support raises ValueError (std::invalid_argument in C++), as does Base on a model without a floating base, or a rotation that is not orthonormal with determinant 1.

items.title: Bound centers
items.text:
The position bounds (FrameTranslationBound, FloatingBaseTranslationBound and CenterOfMassBound) also take a center \(\boldsymbol{c}\), through the constructor or set_center, which moves the bounds' origin whatever the reference frame:

\[ \boldsymbol{b}_l \leq R^\top (\boldsymbol{p} - \boldsymbol{c}) \leq \boldsymbol{b}_u \]

For example, a box around a foothold, aligned with the robot's yaw and updated at each MPC step:

import numpy as np
from ssqpy.model import ReferenceFrame, constraints, costs

box = constraints.FrameTranslationBound(
    model,
    "FL_foot",
    lb=np.array([-0.05, -0.03, -np.inf]),
    ub=np.array([0.05, 0.03, np.inf]),
    reference_frame=ReferenceFrame.yaw(robot_yaw),
    center=foothold,
)

# Later, for a new plan
box.set_reference_frame(ReferenceFrame.yaw(new_robot_yaw))
box.set_center(new_foothold)

Similarly, a commanded base velocity given in world axes can be tracked directly, rather than converted to the base frame first:

costs.FloatingBaseSquaredVelocityErrorCost(
    model, v_command, weight, reference_frame=ReferenceFrame.World
)

items.title: Moving axes
items.text: Local and Base axes depend on the state, so the derivatives of these terms include how the axes turn with the frame or the base. On a bound, this gives the solver a second way to satisfy it: turning the frame or the base instead of moving the point. With Base axes on a foot box, for example, the plan may yaw or pitch the body to fit the foot inside. That is the intended behaviour for bounds meant relative to the body. When it is not, use fixed axes, such as ReferenceFrame.yaw with the planned yaw of each stage.

items.title: Innate (XML-derived) constraints
items.text: When a model is built from a URDF/MJCF file, joint position, velocity and torque limits declared in the XML are added automatically as constraints unless ignore_innate_constraints=True is passed to the Model constructor. finalize's custom_lower_position_bounds, custom_upper_position_bounds, custom_velocity_bounds and custom_torque_bounds arguments override the XML-derived values in place.

items.title: Model
items.text:
A Model (ssqpy.model.Model in Python, ssqp::model::Model in C++) is a prerequisite for solving an OCP with SSQP. It bundles, over an optimization horizon \(H\):

  • a cost function for each stage, \(\ell_k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u})\),
  • dynamics functions for each stage, \(\boldsymbol{f}_k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u})\), and
  • constraint functions for each stage, \(\boldsymbol{c}_k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u})\) (optional; a stage may have none).

All stage cost and dynamics functions must be defined; constraints may be left empty.

items.title: Horizon, states and controls
items.text:
A model optimizes over \(H\) steps while treating the initial state \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) as fixed (only the initial controls can be altered). This means there are \(H\) total controls (\(\boldsymbol{u}_0\) to \(\boldsymbol{u}_{H-1}\)) and \(H + 1\) total states (\(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) to \(\boldsymbol{x}_H\)). At the terminal stage \(H\) there are no controls, so stagewise functions must be written to ignore \(\boldsymbol{u}\) at that stage. Predefined functions already account for this.

\(\boldsymbol{x}\) need not be a Euclidean vector: SSQP also supports states that include manifold-valued components, such as a floating-base orientation. See Manifold-valued states in Costs, Constraints & Dynamics.

model = ssqpy.model.Model(horizon, dt)

items.title: Defining a model
items.text:
A model can be defined in two ways, which can also be mixed:

  1. Custom function objects: subclass StageCost, StageDynamics and (optionally) StageConstraints and pass instances to model.finalize(...), as in the Quickstart. This is required for systems that are not described by a robot XML file (e.g. simplified/reduced models).
  2. XML description files: pass urdf_path or mjcf_path to the constructor to load a robot description via Pinocchio. This gives access to robot algorithms (forward/inverse dynamics, kinematics, Jacobians) that the predefined costs and constraints use internally, and lets you use Model.addContactConstraint for contact-implicit stages.

When a model is constructed from an XML file, it is not immediately usable for optimization: call finalize() to assign costs/dynamics/constraints (explicitly, or letting the model build its own robot dynamics) before solving. model.finalized reports whether this has happened.

items.title: Built-in presets
items.text:
A handful of common robots are baked into the ssqp binary as URDF presets, so they can be used without pointing urdf_path at a file on disk. Pass from_preset instead:

model = ssqpy.model.Model(horizon, dt, from_preset=ssqpy.model.Preset.Go2)

Available presets: Go2, A1, Panda, G1, Talos, DoublePendulum (ssqpy.model.Preset.NONE is the default, meaning no preset). Each preset fixes its own urdf_path and free_flyer, so from_preset is mutually exclusive with urdf_path, mjcf_path and free_flyer; passing both raises an error.

items.title: Constructor arguments
items.text:
Model(horizon: int, dt: float, **kwargs)
Keyword argument Description urdf_path / mjcf_path Path to a URDF or MJCF file describing the robot free_flyer Whether the model has a floating base (only relevant when loaded from XML) from_preset A built-in URDF preset to build the model from, instead of urdf_path solver_mode The SolverMode formulation to optimize in integration The Integration scheme used to propagate state ignore_innate_constraints Whether to ignore joint/velocity/torque limits declared in the XML actuated_joints Restrict actuation to a subset of joint indices

items.title: finalize arguments
items.text: model.finalize(**kwargs) accepts, among others: costs / stage_cost / terminal_cost, dynamics, constraints, custom_lower_position_bounds / custom_upper_position_bounds / custom_velocity_bounds / custom_torque_bounds (override XML-derived innate constraint bounds), and init_states / init_controls (initial guesses). See the API reference for the complete, up-to-date list.

items.title: Solver mode
items.text:
SolverMode selects the NLP formulation used for the dynamics equality constraint:

  • Kinematics: no system dynamics; controls are velocities and the state is the system configuration.
  • ForwardDynamics: the state is configuration + velocity; controls are torques applied via forward dynamics.
  • InverseDynamics: the state is configuration + velocity; controls are accelerations, with torques (needed to produce them) constrained to stay within effort limits. This simplifies the LQR formulation and can be more robust than ForwardDynamics.
  • ReducedInverseDynamics: like InverseDynamics, but an unactuated floating base and/or joint subset is enforced implicitly through state propagation rather than via equality constraints.

items.title: Integration scheme
items.text:
Integration selects how velocity and configuration are propagated between stages:

  • ExplicitEuler: \(\boldsymbol{x}_{n+1} = \boldsymbol{x}_n + \boldsymbol{v}_n dt\), \(\boldsymbol{v}_{n+1} = \boldsymbol{v}_n + \boldsymbol{a}_n dt\)
  • SemiImplicitEuler (default): \(\boldsymbol{x}_{n+1} = \boldsymbol{x}_n + \boldsymbol{v}_{n+1} dt\), \(\boldsymbol{v}_{n+1} = \boldsymbol{v}_n + \boldsymbol{a}_n dt\)

items.title: Contacts and forces
items.text:
For XML-based models, Model.addForce(k, frame) declares an external force at a frame for a stage, and Model.addContactConstraint(k, frame, mu=0.6, max_normal_force=inf, eq_tol=0.0, no_slip=True) is a convenience that both adds a contact constraint (friction cone, non-penetration and, unless no_slip=False, a zero linear velocity bound on the frame) and the associated force in one call; this is the mechanism used by legged-robot examples (e.g. Go2, G1) to model foot contacts against the terrain.

See the Python API reference for the full Model method list.

items.title: MPC
items.text:
ssqpy.solvers.MPC (ssqp::solvers::MPC in C++) is a thin helper around ssqp for real-time, receding-horizon control: it repeatedly re-solves the OCP for the system's current state with a small iteration budget, applies the first control of the resulting trajectory, and warm-starts the next solve from the previous solution plus fresh state feedback.

mpc = ssqpy.solvers.MPC(
    model,
    sqp_iters=5,
    qp_iters=50,
    keep_convergence_data=False,
)

mpc.reinitialize(initial_state)

while running:
    state = read_state_from_system()
    x, u = mpc.step(state)
    apply_controls(u.stage(0))

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
MPC.Params (or keyword arguments to the constructor) cap the iteration budget independently of whatever ssqpParams/admmParams/hpipmParams/piqpParams are passed alongside them; the MPC-level sqp_iters and qp_iters are what actually bound the per-step solve time:

  • sqp_iters: maximum SSQP iterations per MPC step (default keeps this low, e.g. 5–10, since MPC relies on warm-starting rather than solving to full convergence every step)
  • qp_iters: maximum QP solver iterations per SSQP iteration
  • keep_convergence_data: whether to retain per-step ssqpConvergenceData, retrievable via mpc.getConvergenceData(), for logging/analysis

items.title: Warm-starting
items.text:
• reinitialize(state): reset the warm start to a given state with zero controls.
  • reinitialize(states, controls): reset the warm start to full state/control trajectories.
  • step(state): the typical receding-horizon call, using state as feedback for stage 0, and the previous solution (shifted) as the warm start for the rest of the horizon.
  • step(states, controls): warm-start explicitly with the given trajectories instead of the previous solution.
  • step(): advance using the current internal guess as-is.

Every step variant returns the full (x, u) FlatVec trajectories; in a control loop you typically only apply u.stage(0) before the next step call.

See examples/mujoco_mpc and examples/real_mpc for complete simulated and real-system MPC loops.

items.title: Parameter Search
items.text: ssqp::param_search (ssqpy.solvers.search in Python) provides online parameter identification for dynamics that expose tunable parameters (e.g. friction, mass, or other physical coefficients embedded in a custom StageDynamics), plus a small utility for searching over SSQP hyperparameters.

items.title: Dynamics parameter search
items.text:
Both searchers take (state, control, resulting next-state) data points and use Armijo line search to update a dynamics model's internal parameters so its predictions better match observed transitions. This is useful for adapting a model online or from offline rollout data.

from ssqpy.solvers import search

searcher = search.DynamicsParamGradientDescent(dynamics, min_data_size=100)

updated = searcher.addData(x_prev, u, x_actual)  # returns whether parameters changed
