  • DynamicsParamGradientDescent: accumulates data points and performs a gradient-descent update once at least min_data_size points have been collected (setMinimumDataSize to change this later).
  • DynamicsParamGaussNewton: maintains a sliding window of window_size data points and performs a Gauss-Newton update against them. setWindowSize(window_size, prune_last=False) resizes the window; when shrinking, prune_last=True drops the most recent points, while the default instead prunes the most similar points, keeping the window's data diverse.

Both share addData(x, u, x_next) and clearData(), and both take armijo_beta/armijo_c1 to control the Armijo line search used for the parameter update step.

items.title: Hyperparameter search
items.text:
HyperParamSearch searches over a set of candidate ssqpParams across a set of Model problems to find the configuration that performs best:

hp_search = search.HyperParamSearch(candidate_params_list, model_list)
best_params = hp_search.search()

or build it up incrementally with addHyperparams(params) / addProblem(model) before calling search().

items.title: QP Solvers
items.text:
At each SSQP iteration, quadratizing the cost and linearizing the dynamics/constraints produces a Quadratic Program with the same stagewise (banded) structure as the original OCP. QPSolver (ssqp::solvers::QPSolver) is the abstract interface all QP backends implement:

virtual void        reset()                  = 0;
virtual void        increaseRegularization() = 0;
virtual SolverState solve(Solution &sol)     = 0;
virtual uint        iterations() const       = 0;

Select the backend via ssqpParams.qp_solver_type (QPSolverType.ADMM, QPSolverType.HPIPM or QPSolverType.PIQP); see The SSQP Solver.

items.title: QP formulation
items.text:
At each SSQP iterate \((\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u})\), with multiplier estimates \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\) (dynamics) and \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) (constraints), the QP solvers find the update \((\Delta\boldsymbol{x}, \Delta\boldsymbol{u})\) that solves

\[ \begin{aligned} \min_{\Delta\boldsymbol{x}, \Delta\boldsymbol{u}} \;& \sum_{k=0}^{H-1} \left( \tfrac{1}{2} \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_k^\top \boldsymbol{Q}^{xx}_k \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_k + \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_k^\top \boldsymbol{Q}^{xu}_k \Delta\boldsymbol{u}_k + \tfrac{1}{2} \Delta\boldsymbol{u}_k^\top \boldsymbol{Q}^{uu}_k \Delta\boldsymbol{u}_k + \boldsymbol{q}^{x\top}_k \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_k + \boldsymbol{q}^{u\top}_k \Delta\boldsymbol{u}_k \right) \\ & + \tfrac{1}{2} \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_H^\top \boldsymbol{Q}^{xx}_H \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_H + \boldsymbol{q}^{x\top}_H \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_H \\ \text{s.t.} \;& \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_0 = \boldsymbol{0} \\ & \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_{k+1} = \boldsymbol{A}_k \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_k + \boldsymbol{B}_k \Delta\boldsymbol{u}_k + \boldsymbol{\gamma}_k, \quad 0 \leq k < H \\ & \boldsymbol{c}^l_k \leq \boldsymbol{D}_k \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_k + \boldsymbol{E}_k \Delta\boldsymbol{u}_k \leq \boldsymbol{c}^u_k, \quad 0 \leq k < H \\ & \boldsymbol{c}^l_H \leq \boldsymbol{D}_H \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_H \leq \boldsymbol{c}^u_H \end{aligned} \]

The data comes from the stagewise functions of the model, all evaluated at the current iterate:

Symbol Meaning \(\boldsymbol{q}^x_k\), \(\boldsymbol{q}^u_k\) Cost gradients, \(\nabla_x \ell_k\) and \(\nabla_u \ell_k\) \(\boldsymbol{Q}^{xx}_k\), \(\boldsymbol{Q}^{xu}_k\), \(\boldsymbol{Q}^{uu}_k\) Hessian of the Lagrangian: the cost Hessian blocks plus the hessprod_* terms of the dynamics (against \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}_k\)) and the constraints (against \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\)) \(\boldsymbol{A}_k\), \(\boldsymbol{B}_k\) Dynamics Jacobians with respect to \(\boldsymbol{x}_k\) and \(\boldsymbol{u}_k\) \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_k\) Dynamics gap, \(\boldsymbol{f}_k(\boldsymbol{x}_k, \boldsymbol{u}_k) \ominus \boldsymbol{x}_{k+1}\) \(\boldsymbol{D}_k\), \(\boldsymbol{E}_k\) Constraint Jacobians with respect to \(\boldsymbol{x}_k\) and \(\boldsymbol{u}_k\) \(\boldsymbol{c}^l_k\), \(\boldsymbol{c}^u_k\) Remaining room to the constraint bounds, here \(\boldsymbol{c}^l_k \ominus \boldsymbol{c}_k(\boldsymbol{x}_k, \boldsymbol{u}_k)\) and \(\boldsymbol{c}^u_k \ominus \boldsymbol{c}_k(\boldsymbol{x}_k, \boldsymbol{u}_k)\)

The terminal stage has no controls. Stages without constraints have empty \(\boldsymbol{D}_k\), \(\boldsymbol{E}_k\), and equality constraints have equal \(\boldsymbol{c}^l_k\) and \(\boldsymbol{c}^u_k\). Since the initial state is fixed, \(\Delta\boldsymbol{x}_0\) is zero. For a manifold-valued state, all of these quantities live in the tangent space, so \(\Delta\boldsymbol{x}_k \in \mathcal{R}^{n_{dx}}\) (see Manifold-valued states). Besides \(\Delta\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\Delta\boldsymbol{u}\), the solver returns the multipliers \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) of the QP's dynamics and constraints, which become the next iterate's estimates.

items.title: ADMM
items.text:
admm_qp is SSQP's own Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers implementation. It requires no extra dependencies (unlike HPIPM and PIQP, see below) and is the default. Key parameters (admmParams, or admm_-prefixed keyword arguments):

  • init_rho, alpha (over-relaxation), sigma (proximal regularization)
  • Adaptive \(\rho\) update: rho_update, rho_min/rho_max, adaptive_rho_tolerance, rho_update_iter_freq
  • Termination: max_iter, abs_tolerance/abs_tolerance_final, rel_tolerance/rel_tolerance_final (tolerance_update_steps anneals both linearly, as with the outer SSQP tolerances)
  • primal_infs_tolerance: every rho_update_iter_freq iterations, ADMM checks whether the change in its dual variable \(y\) certifies that no trajectory satisfying the linearized dynamics can meet the constraint bounds. If so, it returns PrimalInfeasible (see stop_on_qp_infeasibility in Termination). Use -1.0 to disable the check
  • warm_start: warm-start with the unconstrained solution (disable when using InverseDynamics mode)
  • reset_rho / reset_y: whether to reset ADMM's \(\rho\) and \(y\) between successive SSQP formulations (disabling either can cause oscillations)

items.title: HPIPM
items.text:
hpipm_qp wraps HPIPM (via BLASFEO), an interior-point QP solver. It requires building SSQP with -DWITH_HPIPM=ON (see Installation). Key parameters (hpipmParams, or hpipm_-prefixed keyword arguments):

  • mode (HPIPMMode: Robust, Speed, Balance): trades off robustness against speed
  • max_iter, alpha_min, mu0 (initial barrier parameter)
  • tol_stat, tol_eq, tol_ineq, tol_comp: stationarity/equality/inequality/complementarity tolerances
  • reg_prim: primal regularization
  • warm_start, prediction_correction, square_root_riccati, split_step

items.title: PIQP
items.text:
piqp_qp wraps PIQP, a proximal interior-point QP solver, using its multistage KKT solver, which exploits the stagewise structure of the QP. The multistage solver needs BLASFEO, which is shared with HPIPM when both are enabled. It requires building SSQP with -DSSQP_WITH_PIQP=ON, which is the default (see Installation). Key parameters (piqpParams, or piqp_-prefixed keyword arguments):

  • max_iter
  • eps_abs, eps_rel: absolute and relative tolerances
  • rho_init, delta_init: initial primal and dual proximal regularization
  • reg_prim: primal regularization added to the Hessian diagonal, increased when the line search fails. It defaults to 1e-4, far above HPIPM's, because PIQP solves the QP accurately enough that directions with little or no curvature (e.g. lightly weighted contact forces) otherwise produce very large steps that slow SSQP down
  • parallel, num_threads: use PIQP's parallel multistage solver, which splits the horizon into segments that are factorized on separate threads, with num_threads threads (0 uses the OpenMP default, all logical cores). This requires building with -DSSQP_PIQP_OPENMP=ON, and setting parallel otherwise raises an error. With parallel off, the serial solver runs on a single thread either way

The parallel solver mainly pays off for long horizons: on a 301-stage Go2 trajectory it roughly halves the QP solve time with 8 threads, while the setup on the first solve stays sequential. Use about as many threads as the CPU has performance cores, since more are usually slower. As PIQP's documentation recommends, binding the threads to cores (OMP_PLACES=cores OMP_PROC_BIND=close) also helps.

PIQP differs from the other backends in a few ways:

  • It does not provide a feedback gain, so MPC.feedbackGain raises an error with it
  • It reports PrimalInfeasible for some infeasible QPs, but may also stall on one and stop at max_iter
  • Its setup runs on the first solve after the QP solver is created. An MPC creates a new one whenever the problem dimensions change, e.g. when contact constraints are toggled, so each such step pays this cost again

items.title: LQR
items.text:
ssqp::solvers::lqr is a Riccati-recursion based solver used internally to warm-start/solve the unconstrained (equality-only) structure of the QP efficiently, exposing both a structural solve (output_structure, producing gain matrices \(P, K\)) and a full unconstrained solve. It is not exposed as a standalone QPSolverType; instead it backs the ADMM solver's per-iteration linear solves.

See the API reference for ssqpParams, admmParams, hpipmParams and piqpParams in full.

items.title: The SSQP Solver
items.text:
ssqpy.solvers.ssqp (ssqp::solvers::ssqp in C++) drives the outer SQP loop described on the Home page: starting from an initial guess for \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{u}\) (provided via Model.finalize(init_states=..., init_controls=...), or zero), it repeats, until convergence:

  1. Quadratize the cost and linearize the dynamics/constraints at the current guess (cost gradients/Hessians, dynamics/constraint Jacobians) to build a Quadratic Program (QP) that exploits the stagewise (banded) structure of the OCP.
  2. Solve the QP with one of the QP solvers to get an update direction.
  3. Line search to pick a step size along that direction (see below).
  4. Check termination criteria on the updated guess; stop, or go back to 1.
solver = ssqpy.solvers.ssqp(model)  # or ssqpy.solvers.ssqp(model, **kwargs)
state, x, u = solver.solve()

params/keyword arguments accepted by the constructor are defined by ssqpParams (see the API reference for the exhaustive, current list); the most commonly tuned are summarized below.

items.title: Formulation
items.text:
SSQP solves the OCP from the Home page,

\[ \begin{aligned} \min_{\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}} \;& J(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) = \sum_{k=0}^{H-1} \ell_k(\boldsymbol{x}_k, \boldsymbol{u}_k) + \ell_H(\boldsymbol{x}_H) \\ \text{s.t.} \;& \boldsymbol{x}_{k+1} = \boldsymbol{f}_k(\boldsymbol{x}_k, \boldsymbol{u}_k), \quad 0 \leq k < H \\ & \boldsymbol{c}^l_k \leq \boldsymbol{c}_k(\boldsymbol{x}_k, \boldsymbol{u}_k) \leq \boldsymbol{c}^u_k, \quad 0 \leq k < H \\ & \boldsymbol{c}^l_H \leq \boldsymbol{c}_H(\boldsymbol{x}_H) \leq \boldsymbol{c}^u_H \end{aligned} \]

where \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) is fixed and \(\boldsymbol{c}^l_k\), \(\boldsymbol{c}^u_k\) are the constraint bounds. Given the current guess \((\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u})\) and multiplier estimates \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\), \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) of the dynamics and constraints, each iteration solves a QP in the update \((\Delta\boldsymbol{x}, \Delta\boldsymbol{u})\), where \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_k = \boldsymbol{f}_k(\boldsymbol{x}_k, \boldsymbol{u}_k) \ominus \boldsymbol{x}_{k+1}\) is the current dynamics gap:

\[ \begin{aligned} \min_{\Delta\boldsymbol{x}, \Delta\boldsymbol{u}} \;& \sum_{k=0}^{H-1} \tfrac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_k \\ \Delta\boldsymbol{u}_k \end{bmatrix}^\top \boldsymbol{Q}_k \begin{bmatrix} \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_k \\ \Delta\boldsymbol{u}_k \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} \boldsymbol{q}^x_k \\ \boldsymbol{q}^u_k \end{bmatrix}^\top \begin{bmatrix} \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_k \\ \Delta\boldsymbol{u}_k \end{bmatrix} + \tfrac{1}{2} \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_H^\top \boldsymbol{Q}_H \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_H + \boldsymbol{q}^{x\top}_H \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_H \\ \text{s.t.} \;& \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_0 = \boldsymbol{0}, \quad \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_{k+1} = \boldsymbol{A}_k \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_k + \boldsymbol{B}_k \Delta\boldsymbol{u}_k + \boldsymbol{\gamma}_k, \\ & \boldsymbol{c}^l_k \ominus \boldsymbol{c}_k \leq \boldsymbol{D}_k \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_k + \boldsymbol{E}_k \Delta\boldsymbol{u}_k \leq \boldsymbol{c}^u_k \ominus \boldsymbol{c}_k \end{aligned} \]

with \(\boldsymbol{A}_k, \boldsymbol{B}_k\) and \(\boldsymbol{D}_k, \boldsymbol{E}_k\) the dynamics and constraint Jacobians, \(\boldsymbol{q}_k\) the cost gradients and \(\boldsymbol{Q}_k\) the Hessian of the Lagrangian (the cost Hessian plus the hessprod_* terms of the dynamics and constraints against \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}_k\) and \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\)). The terminal stage has no controls, and its constraints use the Jacobian \(\boldsymbol{D}_H\) alone. See QP Solvers for the full form the QP solvers receive.

The QP also returns new multipliers \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\). After the line search picks a step size \(\alpha \in (0, 1]\) (below), the guess is updated through the manifold operator \(\oplus\) (plain addition for Euclidean states):

\[ \boldsymbol{x}_k \leftarrow \boldsymbol{x}_k \oplus \alpha \Delta\boldsymbol{x}_k, \qquad \boldsymbol{u}_k \leftarrow \boldsymbol{u}_k + \alpha \Delta\boldsymbol{u}_k \]

items.title: Termination
items.text:
• max_iter: hard cap on SSQP iterations.
  • tolerance (and optionally tolerance_final / tolerance_update_steps, to anneal it linearly over the first N steps): convergence tolerance on the Lagrangian's Jacobian norms w.r.t. \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{u}\).
  • constraint_tolerance: separate satisfaction tolerance for constraints, if set positive.
  • stop_after_constraint_satisfaction: stop as soon as constraints are satisfied, regardless of Lagrangian norms.
  • loose_success (with loose_success_tolerance, loose_success_stale_iters): an early-exit heuristic that stops if the cost Jacobian norm hasn't improved by more than loose_success_tolerance for loose_success_stale_iters consecutive iterations.
  • stop_on_qp_infeasibility (default on): stop with PrimalInfeasible as soon as the QP solver reports an infeasible QP, returning the current guess. When off, ADMM skips the infeasibility check and runs as it would without it. Only ADMM detects infeasibility.

The result reports a SolverState (Success, LooseSuccess, ConstraintSuccess, PrimalInfeasible, MaxIterReached, Ongoing, …) and detailed ssqpConvergenceData, covering per-iteration timing, step size, norms, cost and violation, retrievable via solver.getConvergenceData().

items.title: Line search
items.text:
The line search measures a trial point \((\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u})\) with three quantities: the total cost \(J(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u})\) from above, the dynamics gap

\[ \Gamma(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) = \sum_{k=0}^{H-1} \left\lVert \boldsymbol{f}_k(\boldsymbol{x}_k, \boldsymbol{u}_k) \ominus \boldsymbol{x}_{k+1} \right\rVert_\infty \]

and the constraint violation

\[ C(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) = \sum_{k=0}^{H} \left\lVert \max\left(\boldsymbol{c}^l_k \ominus \boldsymbol{c}_k,\; \boldsymbol{c}_k \ominus \boldsymbol{c}^u_k,\; \boldsymbol{0}\right) \right\rVert_\infty \]

Starting at \(\alpha = 1\), SSQP evaluates the trial point \(\boldsymbol{x}^+ = \boldsymbol{x} \oplus \alpha \Delta\boldsymbol{x}\), \(\boldsymbol{u}^+ = \boldsymbol{u} + \alpha \Delta\boldsymbol{u}\). While the trial point is rejected, it divides \(\alpha\) by inv_alpha_scale_factor and tries again, until \(\alpha\) drops below min_alpha. The acceptance test depends on the method (line_search_method):

  • Filter (default): a filter line search. Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be the last filter_size accepted \((J, \Gamma, C)\) triples, and \((J_0, \Gamma_0, C_0)\) those of the current guess. The trial point is rejected if it is dominated by any filter entry, i.e. if for some \((J_i, \Gamma_i, C_i) \in \mathcal{F}\)

    \[ J^+ > J_i \;\wedge\; \Gamma^+ > \Gamma_i \;\wedge\; C^+ > C_i \]

    and it is otherwise accepted only if it improves on at least one measure of the current guess:

    \[ J^+ < J_0 \;\vee\; \Gamma^+ < \Gamma_0 \;\vee\; C^+ < C_0 \]

    The accepted triple is then pushed to the filter. No simultaneous improvement on all three measures is required. * Merit: a merit-function line search. The merit function weights the three measures with \(\mu_\Gamma\) (merit_mu_gamma) and \(\mu_C\) (merit_mu_c),

    \[ M(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) = J + \mu_\Gamma \Gamma + \mu_C C \]

    and the trial point is accepted if it satisfies the Armijo sufficient-decrease condition, with \(\beta\) = merit_armijo_beta,

    \[ M(\boldsymbol{x}^+, \boldsymbol{u}^+) < M(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) + \beta \, \alpha \, \nabla M(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u})^\top \begin{bmatrix} \Delta\boldsymbol{x} \\ \Delta\boldsymbol{u} \end{bmatrix} \]

    where \(\nabla M\) uses a smooth (softmax) approximation of the \(\infty\)-norms in \(\Gamma\) and \(C\).

If the line search fails to find an acceptable step even at min_alpha, SSQP by default increases QP regularization and retries; set accept_worse_update to accept the min_alpha step anyway, or skip_regularization to raise an exception immediately instead of regularizing.

items.title: Choosing a QP solver
items.text: qp_solver_type selects between the three QP solvers (ADMM, HPIPM or PIQP); admm_params/hpipm_*/piqp_* keyword arguments (prefixed admm_/hpipm_/piqp_ when passed to the ssqp constructor) configure the selected one.

items.title: Saving and loading trajectories
items.text: solver.write(filepath) writes the current solution to a JSON file; ssqpy.solvers.loadTrajectory(filepath) reads one back as a pair of FlatVec state/control trajectories, useful for warm-starting later runs or for the visualizer example.

items.title: Terrain
items.text:
Terrain (ssqpy.model.terrain, ssqp::model::terrain) describes the ground that a model's contacts act against. Every Model has an associated terrain (Model.terrain), defaulting to FlatTerrain at \(z = 0\).

class Terrain:
    def at(self, x: float, y: float) -> TerrainPoint: ...
    def distance(self, x: float, y: float, z: float) -> float: ...

at(x, y) returns a TerrainPoint: the terrain height, surface normal, two tangent directions, the slope (dhdx, dhdy) and the height second derivatives (d2hdx2, d2hdxdy, d2hdy2) at that point. distance(x, y, z) gives the (default: vertical) distance from a 3D point to the terrain surface. These are used by contact-related constraints (e.g. Model.addContactConstraint) to enforce non-penetration and to build the local contact frame for the friction cone.

The contact constraint differentiates the contact frame with respect to position using the height derivatives, so the frame must follow the convention of TerrainPoint.from_height(height, dhdx, dhdy, d2hdx2, d2hdxdy, d2hdy2):

\[ \boldsymbol{n} = \frac{(-h_x,\, -h_y,\, 1)}{\lVert (-h_x,\, -h_y,\, 1) \rVert}, \qquad \boldsymbol{t}_1 = \frac{(1,\, 0,\, h_x)}{\lVert (1,\, 0,\, h_x) \rVert}, \qquad \boldsymbol{t}_2 = \boldsymbol{n} \times \boldsymbol{t}_1 \]

where \(h_x\) and \(h_y\) are dhdx and dhdy. Always build points with it.

items.title: Predefined terrains
items.text:
terrain = ssqpy.model.terrain.FlatTerrain(base_height=0.0)
terrain = ssqpy.model.terrain.SlopeTerrain(slope_x, slope_y=0.0, base_height=0.0)
terrain = ssqpy.model.terrain.StepTerrain(
    x_start, step_height, step_length=1.0, num_steps=1, base_height=0.0
)
terrain = ssqpy.model.terrain.HeightmapTerrain(heights, resolution, x0=0.0, y0=0.0)

StepTerrain is piecewise flat. The height rises by step_height at x_start and again every step_length along x, for num_steps steps, and stays at the top afterwards. With the default single step, step_length has no effect.

HeightmapTerrain interpolates a uniform grid, where heights[i, j] is the height at \((x_0 + i \cdot \text{resolution},\, y_0 + j \cdot \text{resolution})\), with a bicubic Catmull-Rom spline. The surface passes through every grid height and has continuous slope. Outside the grid it extends flat from the closest edge value. terrain.set_heights(heights, x0=0.0, y0=0.0) replaces the grid and its origin, keeping the resolution, so a model can follow a map that moves with the robot. Models using the terrain see the new heights from their next evaluation. Call it between solves, never while a solver is running (MPC.step releases the GIL, so another thread could).

Pass a terrain to a model with Model(..., terrain=terrain).

solver.write(...) stores a description of the terrain under properties.terrain in the output file, with a type (flat, slope, step or heightmap) and its parameters. visualizer/visualize.py reads it and draws the terrain around the trajectory. Custom terrains are stored as {"type": "custom"} and are not drawn. Files without a terrain are drawn as flat ground at \(z = 0\).

items.title: Custom terrain
items.text: Subclass Terrain and implement at (required) and, optionally, distance (a default implementation is provided). Python subclasses are called from the solver loop for every contact at every stage, so heavy terrains are better implemented in C++.

items.title: C++ API Reference
items.text:
SSQP is written in C++17; the ssqpy Python module documented in the Python API Reference is a near 1:1 nanobind wrapping of the library described here. The library can be used directly from C++ without the Python bindings at all: link against the ssqp CMake target (see Installation) and include the relevant headers under include/.

This reference is generated from the headers' own comments at doc build time, with one page per namespace, so it can't drift out of sync with the source. It does not enumerate every predefined cost/constraint constructor argument, since those mirror the Python bindings closely; consult the corresponding predefined header or the Python reference for exact parameters.

items.title: Namespaces
items.text:
All library code lives under ssqp::, mirroring the Python package layout:

  • ssqp: core types (VecX, MatX, FlatVec, …), log levels and their helpers
  • ssqp::model: Model, Container, Dimensions
  • ssqp::model::presets: URDFs baked into the binary at build time, looked up by Model::Structure::from_preset
  • ssqp::model::stagewise: StageCost, StageDynamics, StageConstraints, Function
  • ssqp::model::stagewise::factory: stage functions made from functors
  • ssqp::model::stagewise::predefined: ReferenceFrame, with the predefined costs and constraints in their own namespaces
  • ssqp::model::terrain: Terrain, with the predefined terrains in their own namespace
  • ssqp::solvers: ssqp, MPC, QPSolver, admm_qp, hpipm_qp, piqp_qp, lqr
  • ssqp::step: the filter and merit line search implementations
  • ssqp::param_search: hyperparameter search, with dynamics parameter search in dynamics_params

items.title: Building against the C++ library
items.text: ssqp is built as a static library by CMake. Other CMake projects link the ssqp::ssqp target, either from an installed package found with find_package(ssqp) or by adding this repository with FetchContent or add_subdirectory; the target propagates its include directories, compile definitions and the static libraries it depends on. See Using the C++ library for both, and CMake options, particularly SSQP_WITH_HPIPM and SSQP_WITH_PIQP if you need the HPIPM or PIQP QP solvers.

items.title: ssqp
items.text:
#include <solvers/ssqp.hpp>

SSQP class Defines an SSQP problem solver based on a given SSQP model and the desired parameters.

SSQP is a Structure-exploiting Sequential Quadratic Programming solver. The solver starts with an initial guess (either provided, or zero) for the states (x) and controls (u) of an optimization problem over a time horizon H.

At each step, SSQP constructs a Quadratic Program at the current SSQP guess with a quadratic cost function and linearized constraints. This is done using the SSQP model, a model of the system being optimized which provides the necessary methods to linearize at each guess, like gradients and hessians.

The solver then utilizes a QP solver to produce a solution to the constructed QP, which can act as an update step for the current SSQP guess. Based on this solution, a line search method is used to update the current guess.

Termination criteria are then checked for the new SSQP guess. The process is repeated until convergence is reached.

items.title: Guess
items.text:
#include <solvers/ssqp.hpp>

Guess struct Stores data related to an SSQP guess.

This includes the solution vectors \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{u}\), as well as the lagrange multipliers \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\) for equality and \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) for inequality constraints

items.title: QPStage
items.text:
#include <types.hpp>

Holds data for non-terminal stages of the below QP Note that all matrix or vector sizes refer to tangent space.

items.title: QPData
items.text:
#include <types.hpp>

Defines a QP of the following form, to be solved using ADMM.

\[ \Large egin{equation} egin{split} &\min_{ oldsymbol{x}, oldsymbol{u}} \sum_{k=0}^{H-1} ( rac{1}{2} \Bigl[ egin{smallmatrix} oldsymbol{x}_k \ oldsymbol{u}_k\end{smallmatrix}\Bigr]^ op \Bigl[ egin{smallmatrix}Q_{xx} \ Q_{xu} \ Q_{ux} \ Q_{uu}\end{smallmatrix}\Bigr] \Bigl[ egin{smallmatrix} oldsymbol{x}_k \ oldsymbol{u}_k\end{smallmatrix}\Bigr] + \Bigl[ egin{smallmatrix} oldsymbol{q}_k \ oldsymbol{r}_k\end{smallmatrix}\Bigr]^ op \Bigl[ egin{smallmatrix} oldsymbol{x}_k \ oldsymbol{u}_k\end{smallmatrix}\Bigr] ) + rac{1}{2} oldsymbol{x}_H^ op Q_H oldsymbol{x}_H + oldsymbol{x}_H^ op q_H \ &+ \sum_{k=0}^{H-1} ( rac{ ho}{2} orm{D_k oldsymbol{x}_k + E_k oldsymbol{u}_k - oldsymbol{z}_k^j + ho^{-1} oldsymbol{y}_k^j}_2^2 ) + rac{ ho}{2} orm{D_H oldsymbol{x}_H - oldsymbol{z}_H^j + ho^{-1} oldsymbol{y}_H^j}_2^2 \ &+ \sum_{k=0}^{H} ( rac{\sigma}{2} orm{ oldsymbol{x}_k - oldsymbol{x}_k^j}_2^2 ) + \sum_{k=0}^{H-1} ( rac{\sigma}{2} orm{ oldsymbol{u}_k - oldsymbol{u}_k^j}_2^2 ) \ & ext{s.t.} oldsymbol{x}_{k+1} = A_k oldsymbol{x}_k + B_k oldsymbol{u}_k + \gamma_k \end{split} \end{equation} \]

Terms with (^j) are constant parts of the current ADMM guess

items.title: SolverMode enum
items.text:
enum SolverMode

Solver Mode The mode the solver uses for the system formulation, corresponding to the equality constraint of the NLP This can either be full dynamics, or a kinematics formulation Options:

  • Kinematics: The solver optimizes in a kinematic mode. This means there are no system dynamics. Instead, the generated controls correspond to velocities, while the state corresponds to the system configuration.
  • ForwardDynamics: The solver optimizes with a forward dynamics approach. The state corresponds to a stacked vector of the system configuration and velocity. The generated controls correspond to torques which, when applied over time to the system, generate the output trajectory.
  • InverseDynamics: The solver optimizes with an inverse dynamics approach. The state corresponds to a stacked vector of the system configuration and velocity. The generated controls correspond to accelerations. This simplifies the LQR formulation and can sometimes lead to more robust solutions. Inverse dynamics is used as a constraint, ensuring the torques producing the generated acceleration controls are within the required effort limits.
  • ReducedInverseDynamics: This mode is similar to the Inverse dynamics mode. In this mode, the floating base (if present) and/or some subset of the model's joints are unactuated. While regular Inverse mode enforces this via equality constraints, this mode instead enforces this implicitly through state propagation.
Value Description Kinematics = 0 ForwardDynamics = 1 InverseDynamics = 2 ReducedInverseDynamics = 3

items.title: Model
items.text:
#include <model/Model.hpp>

Defines an SSQP model An SSQP model object is a prerequisite to performing optimization using SSQP The model contains the following:

  • An optimization horizon, \(H\)
  • A cost function for each stage of the horizon, \(\ell_k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) \in \mathcal{R}\), \(0 \leq k \leq H\)
  • Dynamics functions for each stage of the horizon, \(\boldsymbol{f}_k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) \in \mathcal{R}^n\), \(0 \leq k \leq H\)
  • Constraint functions for each stage of the horizon, \(\boldsymbol{c}_k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) \in \mathcal{R}^c\), \(0 \leq k \leq H\)

Of the above, all stage cost and dynamics functions must be defined, but constraints may be left empty.

Note that models optimize for \(H\) total steps while considering the initial state to be constant, whereas the initial controls can be altered. This means that there are \(H\) total controls ( \(\boldsymbol{u}_0\) to \(\boldsymbol{u}_{H-1}\)) and \(H + 1\) total states ( \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) to \(\boldsymbol{x}_H\)), with \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) being constant. At the terminal stage (stage \(H\)), there are no controls and, as such, stagewise functions must be appropriately defined to ignore them. Predefined functions all have constructors to account for this.

Models may be defined either by passing custom function implementations, or by using XML description files. Some constructors allow for defining a model using an XML file, but without passing the required cost functions. This is done to allow access to robot-related algorithms such as forward dynamics, which may be used to define model costs. Note that, if such constructors are used, the finalize method must be called before attempting to use the model for optimization. The user is responsible for either manually assigning all required costs, or passing them to the finalize method.

items.title: Structure
items.text:
#include <model/Model.hpp>

Model Structure struct

Defines the structure of the SSQP model

A Structure object can be passed to the Model constructor to initialize a model with a structure only, without necessarily finalizing the model

Parameters:

  • urdf_path: Path to URDF describing robot (may be left empty if other description is used)
  • mjcf_path: Path to MJCF describing robot (may be left empty if other description is used)
  • free_flyer: Whether the model has a floating base (only relevant if initialized through XML)
  • from_preset: A URDF preset to build the model from (default Preset::None); mutually exclusive with urdf_path, mjcf_path and free_flyer
  • terrain: The ground terrain (default flat at z=0)
  • solver_mode: The solver mode to use (default ForwardDynamics)
  • integration: The integration scheme to use (default Semi-Implicit Euler)
  • ignore_innate_constraints: Whether to ignore innate constraints from the XML (i.e joint position, velocity and torque limits)
  • actuated_joints: Indices of the actuated joints (default empty -> all joints actuated)

items.title: Config
items.text:
#include <model/Model.hpp>

Model Config struct

Defines the configuration of the SSQP model

A Config object needs to be passed when finalizing the model This can either be done by directly finalizing via the constructor, or by using the finalize method later on

Parameters:

  • costs: (size \(H\)) Vector of stage costs (added to existing costs)
  • stage_cost: Stage cost for all non-terminal stages (added to existing costs)
  • terminal_cost: Stage cost for terminal stage
  • constraints: (empty / size \(H + 1\)) Vector of stage constraints
  • dynamics: (empty -> XML dynamics / size 1 -> same dynamics for every stage / size \(H + 1\)) Vector of stage dynamics
  • custom_lower_position_bounds: Lower position bounds to use in place of the values read from the XML; default XML values are used if left empty; has no effect if innate constraints are ignored
  • custom_upper_position_bounds: Upper position bounds to use in place of the values read from the XML; default XML values are used if left empty; has no effect if innate constraints are ignored
  • custom_velocity_bounds: Velocity bounds to use in place of the values read from the XML; default XML values are used if left empty; has no effect if innate constraints are ignored
  • custom_torque_bounds: Torque bounds to use in place of the values read from the XML; default XML values are used if left empty; has no effect if innate constraints are ignored
  • init_states: (empty / size \(1\) / size \(H + 1\)) Vector of initial states (empty -> \(\boldsymbol{0}\) initial states / size \(1\) -> same initial state for every stage / size \(H + 1\) -> given sizes per stage)
  • init_controls: (empty / size \(1\) / size \(H\)) Vector of initial controls (empty -> \(\boldsymbol{0}\) initial controls / size \(1\) -> same initial controls for every stage / size \(H\) -> given controls per stage)

items.title: StageScope
items.text:
#include <model/Model.hpp>

StageScope class

Kinematics and dynamics queries keep their results in caches, so that queries at the same point share a single computation Each stage has its own caches, so a stage's results are kept even with other stages' queries in between, and default caches serve queries outside of stages

While a StageScope exists, queries use stage k's caches, and the previously used caches are restored when it is destroyed

Results never depend on which cache is used, since each cache keeps the point its results are for; the scope only decides which results are kept for reuse Has no effect on models not loaded from an XML file

items.title: getActuatedTorqueVector
items.text:
VecX getActuatedTorqueVector(
    ConstVecXRef x,
    ConstVecXRef u,
    const std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Force>> &forces = {},
    const std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Force>> &wrenches = {}
) const

Returns the actuated-joint torque vector implied by the inverse dynamics computation for the given state and controls, accounting for the given forces.

For InverseDynamics mode, this is the RNEA torque computed directly from the (full) acceleration control. For ReducedInverseDynamics mode, the full acceleration vector is reconstructed first (see getFullAccelerationVector), and only the actuated joints' torque is returned, since by construction the unactuated joints' torque is always zero

Input:

  • x: The model state
  • u: The model controls
  • forces: The linear forces the force part of u refers to, in order (see forces)
  • wrenches: The wrenches the force part of u refers to, after the linear forces (see wrenches)

Note: XML-based function Note: Assumes the model is in InverseDynamics or ReducedInverseDynamics mode

Operator definitions for states Defines operators between states and state differences If state is a euclidian vector, these operators reduce to simple addition/subtraction If state is a lie group element, these operators perform conversions between elements of the group (manifold) and tangent space elements The state can also be composite, i.e made up of one or more manifolds and one or more euclidian vectors, in which case operators act segment-wise.

Defines right plus operator between state vector and tangent space vector Inputs: State vector \(\boldsymbol{x}\) (size \(n_x\)), state difference vector \(\boldsymbol{dx}\) (size \(n_{dx}\)) Output: State \(\boldsymbol{y}\) (size \(n_x\)) Default behavior: \(\boldsymbol{x} + \boldsymbol{dx}\)

items.title: state_right_plus virtual
items.text:
virtual void state_right_plus(ConstVecXRef x, ConstVecXRef dx, VecX &out) const override

Operator definitions for states Defines operators between states and state differences If state is a euclidian vector, these operators reduce to simple addition/subtraction If state is a lie group element, these operators perform conversions between elements of the group (manifold) and tangent space elements The state can also be composite, i.e made up of one or more manifolds and one or more euclidian vectors, in which case operators act segment-wise.

Defines right plus operator between state vector and tangent space vector Inputs: State vector \(\boldsymbol{x}\) (size \(n_x\)), state difference vector \(\boldsymbol{dx}\) (size \(n_{dx}\)) Output: State \(\boldsymbol{y}\) (size \(n_x\)) Default behavior: \(\boldsymbol{x} + \boldsymbol{dx}\)

Defines right minus operator between states Inputs: Composite states \(\boldsymbol{x}\), \(\boldsymbol{y}\) (vectors/lie group elements, size \(n_x\)) Output: State difference vector \(\boldsymbol{dx}\) (size \(n_{dx}\)) Default behavior: \(\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{y}\).

items.title: ReferenceFrame
items.text:
#include <types.hpp>

Reference frame of a predefined cost or constraint Selects the axes that a cost's error, weights and desired value, or a constraint's bounds, are expressed along.

Only the axes change: positions keep the world origin, unless a bound's center moves it Options:

  • World: The world axes
  • Local: The axes of the frame the cost or constraint acts on, moving with it
  • Fixed: Constant axes given by a rotation matrix \(R\), whose columns are the axes in world coordinates. A vector \(\boldsymbol{v}\) in world coordinates is then expressed as \(R^\top \boldsymbol{v}\)
  • Base: The axes of the model's floating base, moving with it. On floating base costs and constraints, this is the same as Local Each cost or constraint documents the options it supports, and throws std::invalid_argument when given another

items.title: ContactConstraint
items.text:
Bases: ssqp::model::stagewise::predefined::constraints::PredefinedStageConstraints

#include <model/stagewise/predefined/Constraints.hpp>

Predefined contact constraint for a given frame Creates a set of constraints that amount to a contact force constraint for a frame This consists of the following 4-point linearized friction cone constraints:

  • \(f_n \gt 0\)
  • \(|f_1| \leq \mu f_n\)
  • \(|f_2| \leq \mu f_n\) As well as the following constraint on the 3D position of the frame the contact is on:
  • \(p_z = h_z\) And, unless no_slip is false, the following no-slip constraint on the linear velocity of the frame:
  • \(\boldsymbol{v}_f = \boldsymbol{0}\) where:
  • \(f_n\) is the normal of the contact force ( \(f_z\))
  • \(f_1\) is the first component of the tangential contact force ( \(f_x\))
  • \(f_2\) is the second component of the tangential contact force ( \(f_y\))
  • \(\mu\) is the static friction coefficient at the contact
  • \(p_z\) is the \(z-\)component of the translation of the frame the contact is on
  • \(h_z\) is the height of the terrain at point \((p_x, p_y)\)
  • \(\boldsymbol{v}_f\) is the linear velocity of the frame the contact is on Note that when manually adding this contact constraint to a model, an external force must be added to the model and the appropriate methods must be called to correctly assign that force to this constraint. To avoid this, simply use the Model's addConstraints function, instantiated with the template type ContactConstraint. In that case, adding and assigning of the force will be handled automatically.

#include <model/stagewise/predefined/Costs.hpp>

Predefined squared joint angle cost.

Defines the cost term \(\ell(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) = \frac{1}{2} \lVert \boldsymbol{w} \odot \boldsymbol{x}_{ang} \rVert_2^2\)

where:

  • \(\boldsymbol{x}_{ang}\) is the angular (position) part of the state Note that this will ignore the first 7 elements if the model has a floating base
  • \(\boldsymbol{w}\) is the weight on the angular term

Assumes:

  • The model joint configuration is the first part of the state vector (size model.nq()), appearing after the floating base (if present)

items.title: SquaredIDTorqueCost
items.text:
Bases: ssqp::model::stagewise::predefined::costs::PredefinedStageCost

#include <model/stagewise/predefined/Costs.hpp>

Predefined squared inverse dynamics torque cost.

Defines the cost term \(\ell(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) = \frac{1}{2} \lVert \boldsymbol{w} \odot \boldsymbol{\tau} \rVert_2^2\) where:

  • \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) is the actuated-joint torque caused by the controls (see Model::getActuatedTorqueVector)
  • \(\boldsymbol{w}\) is the weight on the torque term

Note that this cost assumes inverse dynamics is being used (i.e. treats controls as accelerations)

Assumes:

  • The model is in Inverse Dynamics or Reduced Inverse Dynamics mode, such that the state is made up of configuration and velocity and the controls are made up of accelerations (including base, for Inverse Dynamics; actuated joints only, for Reduced Inverse Dynamics) and potential forces

The torque accounts for the forces of the stage the cost is added to, which the model passes in when it's finalized. A single instance can only be added to several stages if they all have the same forces, so construct one instance per stage otherwise

#include <model/stagewise/predefined/Costs.hpp>

Predefined squared floating base translation error cost.

Defines the cost term \(\ell(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) = \frac{1}{2} \lVert \boldsymbol{w} \odot R^\top (\boldsymbol{t}_f - \boldsymbol{t}_d)\rVert_2^2\)

where:

  • \(\boldsymbol{t}_f\) is the floating base translation (in \(\mathcal{R}^3\))
  • \(\boldsymbol{t}_d\) is the desired translation of the floating base (in \(\mathcal{R}^3\))
  • \(\boldsymbol{w}\) is the weight on the translation error
  • \(R\) is the rotation of the reference frame the error is expressed in (World, Fixed, Local or Base, identity for World, with Local and Base both the base's axes)

Assumes:

  • The model joint configuration is the first part of the state vector (size model.nq())
  • The floating base translation is extracted from the base pose of the model state representation

  • \(d_d\) is the desired height of the frame above the terrain
  • \(w\) is the weight on the height error

Assumes:

#include <model/stagewise/predefined/Costs.hpp>

Defines the cost term \(\ell(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) = \frac{1}{2} \lVert \boldsymbol{w} \odot (\boldsymbol{v}_f - \boldsymbol{v}_d)\rVert_2^2\)

#include <model/stagewise/predefined/Costs.hpp>

Predefined frames squared inverse distance cost.

Defines the cost term \(\ell(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) = \sum_{i < j} \frac{w}{2 \lVert \boldsymbol{\sigma} \odot R^\top (\boldsymbol{t}_i - \boldsymbol{t}_j)\rVert_2^2}\)

where:

  • \(\boldsymbol{t}_i\) is the frame translation for frame \(i\) of the model (in \(\mathcal{R}^3\))
  • \(w\) is the weight on the translation error
  • \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\) is the distance scale, a per-axis vector (in \(\mathcal{R}^3\)) determining the scaling factor for each axis; the factors work in an inverse manner, i.e. larger values place less importance on an axis, while smaller ones place more
  • \(R\) is the rotation of the reference frame whose axes the distance scale applies along (World, Fixed or Base, identity for World)

Assumes:

  • The model joint configuration is the first part of the state vector (size model.nq())

items.title: Go2 Jump
items.text: examples/trajgen/python/go2/go2_jump.py generates a jumping trajectory for the Go2 quadruped: a stance phase, a flight phase with all four feet off the ground, and a landing back into a specified footprint. Where the previous examples used a single, unchanging set of costs and constraints across the whole horizon, a jump needs the problem itself to change over time: which constraints even apply (a foot mid-air obviously can't be held in a friction cone) depends on which stage you're looking at. This is the first example built around contact scheduling, per-stage enabling and disabling of contact constraints, and it also demonstrates the object-based (as opposed to keyword-argument) style of configuring solver parameters. It builds directly on Panda Circle.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
examples/trajgen/python/go2/go2_jump.py
import ssqpy
import ssqpy.model.costs as costs
import ssqpy.model.constraints as constraints
import numpy as np
import argparse
from math import pi

"""
Go2 Jump example
Performs a simple jump with the Go2 robot
"""

# Model Parameters
HORIZON = 150
dt = 0.01



def parse_args():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="Go2 jump trajectory generation"
    )

    parser.add_argument(
        "--start-step",
        type=int,
        default=60,
        help="Step at which the robot leaves the ground",
    )

    parser.add_argument(
        "--end-step",
        type=int,
        default=90,
        help="Step at which the robot lands",
    )

    parser.add_argument(
        "-o",
        "--output",
        default="../../data/go2_jump.json",
        help="Path of the output JSON file",
    )

    parser.add_argument(
        "-q",
        "--qp-solver",
        choices=["admm", "hpipm", "piqp"],
        default="hpipm",
        help="QP solver used at each SSQP iteration",
    )

    return parser.parse_args()


args = parse_args()

START_STEP = args.start_step
END_STEP = args.end_step

# Weights
A_WGT = 1e-3
V_WGT = 1e-2
U_WGT = 1e-4
F_WGT = 1e-3
C_WGT = 1e-3

MAX_NORMAL_FORCE = 100

# Create an SSQP model for the Go2
model = ssqpy.model.Model(
    HORIZON,

ReducedInverseDynamics solver mode is used, with the Go2 preset (which fixes free_flyer=True for you) since the Go2's base isn't bolted to anything: it's a free-floating rigid body (position + orientation on \(SE(3)\), another instance of the manifold-valued states SSQP handles) whose motion is determined entirely by the forces the legs exert on the ground, not by any actuator directly driving the base. ReducedInverseDynamics (rather than the plain InverseDynamics used for the fully actuated Panda arm) accounts for exactly this: the base's 6 degrees of freedom are unactuated, so they're enforced through the dynamics rather than treated as free control inputs.

START_STEP/END_STEP mark the flight window (stages 60–89 of a 150-stage horizon) during which no foot is in contact with the ground. MAX_NORMAL_FORCE caps how hard each foot is allowed to push, which matters once contact forces become part of the optimization below.

items.title: Initial state and a static-equilibrium initial guess
items.text:
examples/trajgen/python/go2/go2_jump.py
    from_preset=ssqpy.model.Preset.Go2,
    solver_mode=ssqpy.model.SolverMode.ReducedInverseDynamics,
)

nq = model.getnq()
nv = model.getnv()
nu = model.getnu()

# Initial and final positions
base_pos = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.3879793820122])
base_config = np.array([0.0, pi / 6, -pi / 3] * 4)

# Initial configuration
init = np.zeros(nq + nv)
init[:3] = base_pos

base_config is a standing crouch pose, repeated for all four legs (each leg's three joints get the same hip/thigh/calf angles, since the robot starts symmetric). init_control is not zero: each foot's vertical contact force is initialized to roughly a quarter of the robot's weight (\(3.75 \times 9.81\ \text{N}\)), i.e. a static standing equilibrium, a much better initial guess for the stance stages than zero. This matters more here than in the earlier examples: a jump is a highly dynamic, contact-rich motion, and starting the solver's guess for the forces at "the robot is already balanced on all four feet" rather than "no forces at all" avoids wasting early iterations just discovering that a standing robot needs to push against the ground to not fall over.

items.title: Costs and reusable constraint objects
items.text:
examples/trajgen/python/go2/go2_jump.py

init_control = np.zeros(nu + 12)
init_control[-10] = 3.75 * 9.81
init_control[-7] = 3.75 * 9.81
init_control[-4] = 3.75 * 9.81
init_control[-1] = 3.75 * 9.81

joint_angle_cost = costs.SquaredJointAngleCost(model, A_WGT)
joint_vel_cost = costs.SquaredJointVelocityCost(model, V_WGT)
control_cost = costs.SquaredControlCost(model, U_WGT)
force_cost = costs.SquaredForceCost(model, F_WGT)
config_cost = costs.SquaredConfigurationErrorCost(model, base_config, C_WGT)

fl_foot_pos_bound = constraints.FrameTranslationBound(
    model,
    "FL_foot",
    np.array((-np.inf, 0.1, -0.01)),
    np.array((np.inf, np.inf, np.inf)),
)

fr_foot_pos_bound = constraints.FrameTranslationBound(
    model,
    "FR_foot",
    np.array((-np.inf, -np.inf, -0.01)),
    np.array((np.inf, -0.1, np.inf)),
)

rl_foot_pos_bound = constraints.FrameTranslationBound(
    model,
    "RL_foot",
    np.array((-np.inf, 0.1, -0.01)),
    np.array((np.inf, np.inf, np.inf)),
)

rr_foot_pos_bound = constraints.FrameTranslationBound(
    model,
    "RR_foot",
    np.array((-np.inf, -np.inf, -0.01)),
    np.array((np.inf, -0.1, np.inf)),
)

Regularization costs (joint angle, velocity, control, force, and a configuration-tracking cost pulling toward the crouch pose) are created once, to be reused across stages, exactly as in the earlier examples. What's new here is that per-foot position bounds are also created upfront, before the per-stage loop, because the same constraint objects will be attached to every stage:

  • The position bounds keep each foot within its own quadrant of the body frame (preventing legs from crossing, e.g. FL_foot's y-coordinate is bounded to \(y \geq 0.1\), keeping it on the robot's left side throughout).
  • head_constraint keeps the head above a minimum ground clearance throughout, stance and flight alike, so the jump doesn't solve itself by having the robot faceplant.

items.title: The per-stage loop: stance, flight, stance
items.text:
examples/trajgen/python/go2/go2_jump.py

    "Head_lower",

    np.array((np.inf, np.inf, np.inf)),
)

init_controls = []

for k in range(HORIZON):
    # Add regularization costs
    model.addCost(k, joint_angle_cost)
    model.addCost(k, joint_vel_cost)
    model.addCost(k, control_cost)
    model.addCost(k, force_cost)
    model.addCost(k, config_cost)

    model.addConstraints(k, fl_foot_pos_bound)
    model.addConstraints(k, fr_foot_pos_bound)
    model.addConstraints(k, rl_foot_pos_bound)
    model.addConstraints(k, rr_foot_pos_bound)

    model.addConstraints(k, head_constraint)

    if k < START_STEP or k >= END_STEP:
        t1 = model.addContactConstraint(
            k, "FL_foot", max_normal_force=MAX_NORMAL_FORCE, eq_tol=0.01
        )
        t1.set_enabled(False)

        t2 = model.addContactConstraint(
            k, "FR_foot", max_normal_force=MAX_NORMAL_FORCE, eq_tol=0.01
        )
        # t2.set_enabled(False)

        t3 = model.addContactConstraint(
            k, "RL_foot", max_normal_force=MAX_NORMAL_FORCE, eq_tol=0.01
        )
        # t3.set_enabled(False)

        t4 = model.addContactConstraint(

Every stage gets the regularization costs and the position/head bounds unconditionally; those don't depend on whether the robot is airborne. The contact scheduling itself happens in the if k < START_STEP or k >= END_STEP branch, i.e. outside the flight window: for each foot, Model.addContactConstraint adds both a ContactConstraint (friction cone, so the foot can only push, not pull, and only within a friction-limited cone of directions, plus non-penetration, so the foot can't go through the ground, plus a no-slip zero-velocity bound, so a planted foot can't slide along it) and the matching ground-reaction force in one call. These are exactly the constraints that make "standing" or "walking" possible: without a friction cone, a solved trajectory could have feet pushing sideways with unlimited force; without non-penetration, a foot could dip below the terrain to reduce cost elsewhere; without the no-slip bound, a stance foot could skate across the ground.

Inside the flight window (the branch that continues past this block), no contact constraints are added at all: no friction cone, no non-penetration, no zero-velocity bound, for any foot. With nothing tying the feet to the ground, the dynamics reduce to free-falling under gravity for those stages, exactly as a jump should be; the solver isn't told "be airborne", it simply has no way to keep the feet in contact during that window, so the physics does the rest.

Note that this particular script explicitly disables FL's contact constraint (including its no-slip bound) even during the "stance" branch (t1.set_enabled(False)) while leaving FR/RL/RR enabled, a reminder that contacts are toggled independently per foot per stage, not just per phase: nothing in the API requires all four feet to share the same schedule, which is what makes asymmetric gaits (a limp, a three-legged stance, a diagonal trot) representable with the same building blocks. set_enabled(False) also demonstrates the other way to keep a constraint out of the problem for a given stage: instead of only calling addConstraints when a constraint should apply (as done for the other three feet, conditionally, by virtue of being inside the if branch at all), a constraint can be added unconditionally and toggled on/off afterward, which is convenient when a constraint's applicability depends on something more complex than a single stage-index check.

At the terminal stage, a zero base-velocity constraint asks the robot to be at rest, and each foot gets a FrameTranslationBound with equal lower and upper bounds, an equality constraint (see Constraints in Costs, Constraints & Dynamics) pinning each foot to an exact landing position, symmetric front-to-back and left-to-right around the base. Without this, the solver has no reason to prefer landing back in a stable, symmetric stance over any other configuration that happens to be feasible at stage H; pinning the feet gives the last portion of the trajectory (after END_STEP, back inside the stance branch) something concrete to converge back onto.

items.title: Solving, with object-based parameter configuration
items.text:
examples/trajgen/python/go2/go2_jump.py

        np.array((-0.1934, -0.142, -0.00002682)),

# Finalize the model with our state and controls
model.finalize(init_states=init)

# SSQP model parameters
ssqp_params = ssqpy.solvers.ssqpParams()
ssqp_params.loose_success = True
ssqp_params.tolerance = 1e-2
ssqp_params.qp_solver_type = getattr(
    ssqpy.solvers.QPSolverType, args.qp_solver.upper()
)

admm_params = ssqpy.solvers.admmParams()
admm_params.abs_tolerance = 1e-3
admm_params.rel_tolerance = 1e-3
admm_params.max_iter = 25
admm_params.reset_rho = False
admm_params.reset_y = False
admm_params.warm_start = False
ssqp_params.admmParams = admm_params

hpipm_params = ssqpy.solvers.hpipmParams()
hpipm_params.max_iter = 25
hpipm_params.split_step = True
hpipm_params.prediction_correction = True
hpipm_params.tol_stat = 1e-3
hpipm_params.tol_comp = 1e-3
hpipm_params.tol_eq = 1e-3
hpipm_params.tol_ineq = 1e-3

Rather than passing admm_/hpipm_-prefixed keyword arguments (as in Pendubot), this example constructs ssqpParams, admmParams and hpipmParams objects directly and assigns fields on them before passing the top-level ssqp_params to the solver; this is equivalent, just a different style, useful when parameters are computed or reused across multiple solver instances. ssqp_params.loose_success = True is worth calling out specifically: for a problem this constrained and dynamic, waiting for the strict Lagrangian-norm tolerance to be met on every single term can take far longer than reaching a solution that's already good enough for the jump to look and behave correctly; loose success lets SSQP stop once progress has stalled rather than keep grinding on diminishing returns.

Run it (from examples/trajgen/python/go2/, with the environment set up per Installation):

python go2_jump.py

The script prints the final solver state and writes ../../data/go2_jump.json. This is the example most worth visualizing to actually understand: load the result with the visualizer example and watch the base crouch, launch, tuck through flight, and land, with FL's foot behaving differently from the other three throughout stance if you left the set_enabled(False) call in place.

items.title: Things to try
items.text:
• Comment out t1.set_enabled(False) so all four feet share the same stance/flight schedule, and compare the landing symmetry against the default (asymmetric FL) version.
  • Shrink the flight window (bring --start-step and --end-step closer together) for a shorter hop, or widen it for a higher one, and see how far MAX_NORMAL_FORCE and the joint/velocity regularization weights can be pushed before the solver stops converging.
  • Change the terminal foot-position targets to land in a different footprint (e.g. narrower or wider stance) than the one the robot started in.
  • Try setting admm_params.reset_rho/admm_params.reset_y back to their defaults (True) instead of the False used here, and compare convergence; these control whether ADMM's internal state carries over between the different QP formulations solved across SSQP iterations.

items.title: Go2 Walking (MPC)
items.text:
examples/mujoco_mpc/go2/go2_walking.py walks a Unitree Go2 quadruped around in a live MuJoCo simulation, with a trot driven by a gamepad: the sticks command a forward, sideways and turning velocity, and further buttons change the base height, tilt and step height, or make the robot jump in place. Everything is planned by a single whole-body MPC that solves for joint accelerations and contact forces, and the torques that come out of it are applied to the simulator directly.

It combines two earlier examples. From Go2 Jump it takes the Go2 model, the ReducedInverseDynamics solver mode and the idea of scheduling contacts per stage, but where the jump fixed its schedule once, here it is regenerated at every plan stage from the joystick. From Panda Circle (MPC) it takes the receding-horizon loop and the pattern of keeping the costs in lists, so that each step can point them at a different target. What is new is the part in the middle: the code that turns "go forward at 0.4 m/s" into a base trajectory, a set of footholds and swing paths, and finally a setting for each cost and constraint of the model.

The model itself knows nothing about gaits. This is worth keeping in mind while reading the script: the SSQP model is built once, as a list of generic costs and contact constraints, and everything that makes it walk is in how they are updated.

items.title: Timing
items.text:
examples/mujoco_mpc/go2/go2_walking.py
        description="Go2 walking MPC in MuJoCo using SSQP"
    )

    parser.add_argument(
        "-q",
        "--qp-solver",
        choices=["admm", "hpipm", "piqp"],
        default="hpipm",
        help="QP solver used at each SSQP iteration",
    )

    return parser.parse_args()

There are two clocks. MuJoCo runs at dt = 2 ms. The MPC has 20 stages of mpc_dt = 24 ms, so it plans 0.48 s ahead. They are related by STAGE_EVERY, the 12 simulation steps in one plan stage, and mpc_dt is required to be a multiple of dt for this to be a whole number. The script keeps a counter stage that advances once per plan stage, not once per simulation step, and the whole planner is written in stages: the gait period, the jump phases and the base references are all counted in them.

The MPC is also solved once per stage, which is every 24 ms of simulation time. Solving every simulation step would be 12 times more work for little gain, since the plan only has a new first stage every mpc_dt anyway. The simulation is synced with the controller, so if a solve takes longer than 24 ms of real time, the simulation simply runs slower than real time.

items.title: Weights
items.text:
examples/mujoco_mpc/go2/go2_walking.py
ssqpy.setSilentMode()
np.set_printoptions(suppress=True)


dt = 0.002
mpc_H = 20
# Keep mpc_dt a multiple of dt, so that plan stages line up with sim steps
mpc_dt = 0.024

# stage indexes the plan (mpc_dt per step), so only advance it once per
# planning step, not every simulation step
STAGE_EVERY = round(mpc_dt / dt)

# Print and sync the viewer once per plan stage, so that each measured window
# holds exactly one MPC solve

T_WGT and R_WGT weigh position and rotation tracking, the base's and the feet's. C_WGT is a weak pull of the joints toward a nominal standing configuration, V_WGT penalizes joint velocity, and U_WGT and F_WGT penalize the control and the contact forces. The meaning of the control depends on the dynamics mode: in forward dynamics it is a joint torque, but in ReducedInverseDynamics it is a joint acceleration, which has very different units, so the weight is different for each (with U_WGT much smaller for accelerations). Changing the mode in this script without checking the weights would silently retune the controller.

items.title: Building the model
items.text:
examples/mujoco_mpc/go2/go2_walking.py
JUMP_LAND_STAGES = 12
# Base height at takeoff and touchdown
JUMP_TAKEOFF_HEIGHT = 0.36
# Weight holding the legs in their takeoff configuration while in the air,
# where the feet and the base's path can no longer be steered
JUMP_CONFIG_WGT = 1.0
GRAVITY = 9.81

JUMP_SPEED = GRAVITY * JUMP_FLIGHT_STAGES * mpc_dt / 2
JUMP_CROUCH_HEIGHT = (
    JUMP_TAKEOFF_HEIGHT - JUMP_SPEED * JUMP_PUSH_STAGES * mpc_dt / 2
)
JUMP_LAND_HEIGHT = (
    JUMP_TAKEOFF_HEIGHT - JUMP_SPEED * JUMP_LAND_STAGES * mpc_dt / 2
)

THIGH_LENGTH = 0.213
# Distance from the knee to the foot frame
CALF_LENGTH = 0.23648

model = ssqpy.model.Model(
    mpc_H,
    mpc_dt,
    mjcf_path="../../assets/mjcf/go2/go2.xml",
    free_flyer=True,
    solver_mode=dynamics_mode,
)

nq = model.getnq()
nv = model.getnv()
nu = model.getnu()

The model is built from the robot's MJCF file with free_flyer=True (the Go2 Jump example uses the Go2 preset instead). MuJoCo simulates the same robot description, in a scene file that adds the floor and obstacles. The initial configuration places the base at BASE_HEIGHT of 0.34 m and sets every leg with leg_config, the closed-form hip, thigh and calf angles that put the foot straight below the hip at that height (a two-link inverse kinematics problem, using the thigh and calf lengths). The base quaternion is the identity, so the robot starts facing along \(+x\), away from the obstacles in the scene.

examples/mujoco_mpc/go2/go2_walking.py

    calf = -np.arccos(
        (height**2 - THIGH_LENGTH**2 - CALF_LENGTH**2)
        / (2 * THIGH_LENGTH * CALF_LENGTH)
    )
    thigh = np.arcsin(-CALF_LENGTH * np.sin(calf) / height)
    return np.array([0.0, thigh, calf])


base_pos = np.array([0.0, 0.0, BASE_HEIGHT])

base_config = np.tile(leg_config(BASE_HEIGHT), 4)

# Initial configuration
init_state = np.zeros(37)
init_state[:3] = base_pos
init_state[6] = 1.0
init_state[7:19] = base_config


foot_names = ["FL_foot", "FR_foot", "RL_foot", "RR_foot"]

# Trot pairs, swinging in alternate gait periods
SWING_PAIRS = [["FL_foot", "RR_foot"], ["FR_foot", "RL_foot"]]

# The base starts facing along the world x axis, away from the scene's
# obstacles
R = np.eye(3)

# Foot positions relative to the base, on the ground

Two sets of geometry are computed from the initial pose with forward kinematics. foot_offsets is each foot's position relative to the base, flattened to the ground, which is where the foot would stand when the robot is upright; the planner uses it as the foot's nominal position under the base. hip_offsets and HIP_LENGTH give the hip geometry that the leg inverse kinematics (leg_ik, further down in the script) needs, since the Go2's thigh is offset sideways from the hip joint.

items.title: The gait
items.text:
A trot moves diagonal pairs of feet together. SWING_PAIRS lists the two pairs, and they take turns: in even gait periods FL and RR swing while FR and RL stand, and in odd periods the roles swap. GAIT_PERIOD is 10 stages (0.24 s), so every foot swings for 0.24 s and then stands for 0.24 s, always with two feet on the ground.

examples/mujoco_mpc/go2/go2_walking.py
    )


def predict_poses(pose, count):
    predicted = [pose]
    for _ in range(count):
        x, y, yaw = predicted[-1]

foothold(name, period) answers where a foot should land at the end of its swing in a given period. The answer is the spot that puts the foot at its nominal position under the base when the base passes over it in the middle of the following stance, using the base poses predicted from the current velocity command (poses, below). A robot that wants to go forward will therefore put its feet ahead of where they are, proportionally to the command, and one that wants to turn will land its feet on an arc. For periods that are already over (pose_stage has moved past them), the foothold is where the foot actually landed, kept in landed.

examples/mujoco_mpc/go2/go2_walking.py
    blend = 0.5 * (1 - np.cos(np.pi * phase))
    return (1 - blend) * JUMP_LAND_HEIGHT + blend * base_height


def jump_foothold(name):
    # Where the foot stands through the jump, which is where its last swing
    # before the jump lands
    period = jump_start // GAIT_PERIOD - 1
    if name not in SWING_PAIRS[period % 2]:
        period -= 1
    return foothold(name, period)


def in_flight(k):
    # Whether all feet are in the air at stage k
    j = jump_stage(k)
    flight = JUMP_CROUCH_STAGES + JUMP_PUSH_STAGES
    return j is not None and flight <= j < flight + JUMP_FLIGHT_STAGES

foot_reference(name, k) is what the model needs: given a foot and a plan stage \(k\) (which may be anywhere in the future), the position the foot should be at and whether it is swinging. A foot that is not in the swing pair for that period stays at the foothold of its last swing. A swinging foot interpolates from its previous foothold to the next with a cosine blend, which gives it zero velocity at both ends so that it lifts off and touches down without sliding, and a raised-sine bump of step_height on top of that clears the ground in the middle of the swing.

items.title: The reference trajectory
items.text:
examples/mujoco_mpc/go2/go2_walking.py
    # Base orientation relative to the walking direction
    return rotation_z(yaw) @ rotation_y(-pitch) @ rotation_x(roll)


def stance_config(height, pitch, roll, yaw):
    # Joint angles keeping each foot on its nominal spot on the ground, with
    # the base at the given height and orientation
    R = base_rotation(pitch, roll, yaw)
    base = np.array([0.0, 0.0, height])
    return np.hstack(
        [
            leg_ik(
                R.T @ (foot_offsets[name] - base) - hip_offsets[name],
                1 if foot_offsets[name][1] > 0 else -1,
            )

predict_poses extends the base's pose \((x, y, \text{yaw})\) forward for count stages by integrating the current velocity command, as if it were held constant. The command is in the base frame, so each step rotates it by the yaw. These poses are used both as the base's reference, and, through foothold, to decide where the feet land. The planner looks mpc_H + 3 * GAIT_PERIOD stages ahead rather than just mpc_H, since a foot swinging at the end of the horizon needs the base pose from the stance after its swing to know where to land.

items.title: Costs and constraints
items.text:
examples/mujoco_mpc/go2/go2_walking.py
    # Returns the foot's reference position at stage k and whether it swings
    if jump_stage(k) is not None:
        return jump_foothold(name), in_flight(k)

    period, phase = divmod(k, GAIT_PERIOD)
    phase /= GAIT_PERIOD

    if name not in SWING_PAIRS[period % 2]:
        return foothold(name, period - 1), False

    # Ease in and out of the swing, so that the foot lifts off and touches
    # down without sliding
    blend = 0.5 * (1 - np.cos(np.pi * phase))
    p = (1 - blend) * foothold(name, period - 2) + blend * foothold(
        name, period
    )
    p[2] += step_height * np.sin(np.pi * phase) ** 2
    return p, True


config_cost = ssqpy.model.costs.SquaredConfigurationErrorCost(
    model, init_state[7:nq], C_WGT
)
v_cost = ssqpy.model.costs.SquaredJointVelocityCost(model, V_WGT)
u_cost = ssqpy.model.costs.SquaredControlCost(model, U_WGT)
f_cost = ssqpy.model.costs.SquaredForceCost(model, F_WGT)

base_costs = []
flight_costs = []
foot_funcs = {name: [] for name in foot_names}

for k in range(mpc_H):
    model.addCost(k, config_cost)
    model.addCost(k, v_cost)
    model.addCost(k, u_cost)
    model.addCost(k, f_cost)

    base_costs.append(
        ssqpy.model.costs.FrameSquaredPoseErrorCost(
            model, "base_link", base_pos, R, T_WGT, R_WGT
        )
    )
    model.addCost(k, base_costs[-1])

    flight_costs.append(
        ssqpy.model.costs.SquaredConfigurationErrorCost(
            model,
            stance_config(JUMP_TAKEOFF_HEIGHT, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0),
            JUMP_CONFIG_WGT,

The shared costs (config_cost, v_cost, u_cost, f_cost) are single objects added to every stage, since they do not change from stage to stage. The remaining ones are created per stage and kept in lists, so that update_model can later retarget the one for stage idx independently:

  • base_costs[idx] is a FrameSquaredPoseErrorCost on base_link, tracking the commanded base pose.
  • foot_funcs[name][idx] holds, for each foot, a FrameSquaredTranslationErrorCost and the foot's contact constraint. The contact constraint has a friction coefficient of 0.6, a 150 N normal force limit, and no_slip=False, so that stance feet are not forced to a zero velocity.
  • flight_costs[idx] is a configuration cost that is only used for the jump.

Every foot has both a contact constraint and a tracking cost at every stage; which of them is actually active depends on whether the foot is swinging, and is decided at run time (below). This is the contact scheduling from Go2 Jump, done with set_enabled on constraints and costs that already exist, rather than by choosing which ones to add.

items.title: Reading the joystick
items.text:
examples/mujoco_mpc/go2/go2_walking.py
    global jump_start, jump_button_held

    # Forget the jump once it is over
    if (
        jump_start is not None
        and current_stage >= jump_start + JUMP_PERIODS * GAIT_PERIOD
    ):
        jump_start = None

    # Schedule a jump on each new press of the jump button
    held = JUMP_BUTTON in joystick.buttons
    if (
        held
        and not jump_button_held
        and jump_start is None
        and np.max(np.abs(v_cmd)) < JUMP_MAX_VEL
    ):
        jump_start = (current_stage // GAIT_PERIOD + 1) * GAIT_PERIOD
    jump_button_held = held

    target = np.array(
        joystick.read(MAX_VEL_FRONT, MAX_VEL_BACK, MAX_VEL_SIDE, MAX_VEL_YAW)
    )
    if jump_start is not None:
        target[:] = 0.0
    max_change = np.array([MAX_ACC, MAX_ACC, MAX_YAW_ACC]) * mpc_dt
    v_cmd[:] += np.clip(target - v_cmd, -max_change, max_change)

    base_height = np.clip(
        base_height - joystick.dpad_y * HEIGHT_RATE * mpc_dt,
        MIN_BASE_HEIGHT,
        MAX_BASE_HEIGHT,
    )

    step_height = np.clip(
        step_height + joystick.dpad_x * STEP_HEIGHT_RATE * mpc_dt,
        MIN_STEP_HEIGHT,
        MAX_STEP_HEIGHT,
    )

    tilt = (PITCH_UP_BUTTON in joystick.buttons) - (
        PITCH_DOWN_BUTTON in joystick.buttons
    )

update_command is called once per stage and turns the gamepad state into the quantities the planner uses. The stick command is first read, scaled to the maximum speeds MAX_VEL_FRONT, MAX_VEL_SIDE and so on, and then v_cmd moves toward it by at most MAX_ACC * mpc_dt per stage, so the robot cannot be asked to accelerate faster than it can follow. The remaining inputs are rate-limited in the same way, each one a value with a range and a rate: the D-pad moves base_height and step_height, and pairs of buttons set base_pitch, base_roll and base_yaw to a limit while held, and back to zero when released.

Input Effect Sticks Forward, sideways and yaw velocity command D-pad up and down Base height D-pad left and right Step height BTN_Z, BTN_TR Pitch the base up or down BTN_NORTH, BTN_EAST Roll the base to the left or right BTN_WEST, BTN_TL Turn the front to the left or right, with the feet staying in place BTN_C Jump in place, when the command is near rest

The names are evdev codes, which map to different physical buttons on different gamepads.

items.title: Retargeting the horizon every stage
items.text:
examples/mujoco_mpc/go2/go2_walking.py
        tilt * MAX_BASE_PITCH - base_pitch, -max_change, max_change
    )

    tilt = (ROLL_RIGHT_BUTTON in joystick.buttons) - (
        ROLL_LEFT_BUTTON in joystick.buttons
    )
    max_change = ROLL_RATE * mpc_dt
    base_roll += np.clip(
        tilt * MAX_BASE_ROLL - base_roll, -max_change, max_change
    )

    turn = (YAW_LEFT_BUTTON in joystick.buttons) - (
        YAW_RIGHT_BUTTON in joystick.buttons
    )
    max_change = YAW_RATE * mpc_dt
    base_yaw += np.clip(
        turn * MAX_BASE_YAW - base_yaw, -max_change, max_change
    )


def update_model(current_stage):
    global pose_stage, poses

    # Feet finishing their swing keep the foothold they were aiming for
    period = current_stage // GAIT_PERIOD
    if current_stage > 0 and current_stage % GAIT_PERIOD == 0:
        for name in SWING_PAIRS[(period - 1) % 2]:
            landed[name] = foothold(name, period - 1)

    # Look far enough ahead for the footholds of every swing in the horizon
    poses = predict_poses(
        poses[current_stage - pose_stage], mpc_H + 3 * GAIT_PERIOD
    )
    pose_stage = current_stage

    config_cost.set_desired_configuration(
        stance_config(base_height, base_pitch, base_roll, base_yaw)
    )

    for idx in range(mpc_H):
        k = current_stage + idx
        x, y, yaw = poses[idx]

        j = jump_stage(k)
        height = base_height if j is None else jump_base_height(j)
        base_costs[idx].set_desired_translation(np.array([x, y, height]))

update_model is what makes the robot walk, and is called once per plan stage, after the joystick is read. It does five things:

  1. Records landed feet. On the first stage of each new gait period, the pair that just finished swinging has landed at its target foothold, and landed is updated, so from now on the foot references use where the feet are, not where they were planned to land.
  2. Rebuilds the base poses, starting from the pose the plan has reached, with the latest command.
  3. Sets the nominal configuration. config_cost is pointed at stance_config(...), the leg angles that keep every foot on its nominal spot with the base at the commanded height and orientation. This is how the D-pad and the tilt buttons work: they do not command anything directly, they change what "standing" means.
  4. Sets the base cost of every stage to the pose for that stage and the tilt commands. The stage \(k\) of the model corresponds to the absolute stage current_stage + idx of the gait, which is what foot_reference takes.
  5. Sets each foot. Swinging feet have their contact constraint disabled and their cost tracking the swing path. Stance feet have the contact constraint enabled and a cost holding them at their foothold. As the comment in the code says, the constraint only bounds the foot's height, so the cost is also what stops stance feet sliding.

Note that the schedule is entirely periodic: at every stage the same function is evaluated at a different \(k\), and the window slides along, with a foot's contact turning off as its swing enters the horizon and on again as it leaves it. This is why no part of the model ever needs to be rebuilt after model.finalize.

items.title: The jump
items.text:
examples/mujoco_mpc/go2/go2_walking.py
    return predicted


def foothold(name, period):
    # Where the foot lands at the end of its swing in the given period, placed
    # so that the base passes over the foot's nominal position mid-stance
    if (period + 1) * GAIT_PERIOD <= pose_stage:
        return landed[name]
    x, y, yaw = poses[int((period + 1.5) * GAIT_PERIOD) - pose_stage]
    return np.array([x, y, 0.0]) + rotation_z(yaw) @ foot_offsets[name]


def jump_stage(k):
    # Stage k's index within the jump, or None outside of it
    if jump_start is None:
        return None
    j = k - jump_start
    return j if 0 <= j < JUMP_PERIODS * GAIT_PERIOD else None


def jump_base_height(j):
    # Base reference height at stage j of the jump
    push = JUMP_CROUCH_STAGES
    flight = push + JUMP_PUSH_STAGES

Pressing the jump button when the command is near rest schedules a jump in place, starting at the next gait period. It reuses the machinery above rather than adding a new one. During the jump (jump_stage(k) is not None):

  • The base height reference follows jump_base_height: a crouch, a push-off with constant acceleration up to the takeoff speed, a ballistic flight, a landing that decelerates, and a recovery back to the normal height. The takeoff speed JUMP_SPEED is set from the flight time, so that the base lands at the height it left. The velocity command is held at zero throughout.
  • All four feet stand at the same footholds, those of their last swing before the jump (jump_foothold).
  • In flight (in_flight(k)), every foot is marked as swinging, so all contact constraints and foot costs are disabled. The base's translation weight is zeroed too, since its path can no longer be steered once the feet are off the ground, and a flight_costs configuration cost is enabled instead to hold the legs in their takeoff pose.

This is the same stance, flight, stance structure as Go2 Jump, but built from the pieces that already exist for walking, and decided at every stage instead of once.

items.title: Solver parameters
items.text:
examples/mujoco_mpc/go2/go2_walking.py
