            foot_pos, swinging = foot_reference(name, k)
            foot_cost, foot_constraint = foot_funcs[name][idx]

            # Swinging feet track their swing trajectory, while stance feet
            # stay in contact. The contact constraint only bounds the foot's
            # height, so the tracking cost also keeps stance feet from sliding
            foot_constraint.set_enabled(not swinging)
            foot_cost.set_enabled(not flight)
            foot_cost.set_desired_translation(foot_pos)


update_model(0)

model.addCost(mpc_H, v_cost)

model.finalize(init_states=[init_state])

HPIPM is the QP solver, with tolerances of \(10^{-4}\). The MPC wrapper is given just two SQP iterations, since the problem is warm started from the previous stage's solution (see Warm-starting). The admm_params are set in the script but unused, as long as the QP solver type is HPIPM.

items.title: The simulation loop
items.text:
examples/mujoco_mpc/go2/go2_walking.py
# Start the viewer maximized
glfw.init()
glfw.window_hint(glfw.MAXIMIZED, glfw.TRUE)
with mujoco.viewer.launch_passive(mjmodel, mjdata) as viewer:
    while viewer.is_running():
        display = step % DISPLAY_EVERY == 0

        """
        if display:
            print(f"\rSimulation time: {mjdata.time:.2f}s")

            if step > 0:
                loop_rate = DISPLAY_EVERY / (time() - display_time)
                print(
                    f"\rLoop frequency: {loop_rate:.2f}Hz\t"
                    f"MPC frequency: {(loop_rate / STAGE_EVERY):.2f}Hz"
                )

            display_time = time()
        """

        state = mujoco_to_ssqp_state(np.hstack((mjdata.qpos, mjdata.qvel)))
        state = clip_joints_to_limits(state, mjmodel)

        # Solve once per plan stage and hold the stage's torques in between,
        # as the planner assumes
        if step % STAGE_EVERY == 0:
            try:
                x, u = mpc.step(state)
                xk = ssqp_to_mujoco_state(x.stage(1))

                if dynamics_mode == ssqpy.model.SolverMode.ForwardDynamics:
                    uk = ssqp_to_mujoco_control(u.stage(0))
                elif (
                    dynamics_mode
                    == ssqpy.model.SolverMode.ReducedInverseDynamics
                ):
                    uk = ssqp_to_mujoco_control(
                        np.hstack(
                            (
                                np.zeros(6),
                                model.getActuatedTorqueVector(
                                    state, u.stage(0), model.getForces(0)

Every simulation step, the state is read from MuJoCo and converted (quaternion order, base velocity frame and joint ordering, by utils_go2_mujoco.py) and clipped to the joint limits that the model enforces, because MuJoCo's joint limits are soft. Then:

  • Every STAGE_EVERY steps, mpc.step(state) solves. From the result it keeps the next stage's state xk, as a joint target, and the torques that the first stage's accelerations and forces need at the current measured state, from model.getActuatedTorqueVector. In forward dynamics mode, the control is the torque already. If the solver fails with a regularization error, the loop exits.
  • Every step, the command applied is those torques, held until the next solve, plus a small joint PD term (Kp = 0.01) toward the next stage's joint position and velocity, which corrects drift between solves. The [6:18] slice drops the base entries, which are not actuated, and ssqp_to_mujoco_ctrl_kin reorders the legs for MuJoCo's actuators.
  • Every STAGE_EVERY steps, after the command is set, stage advances and update_command and update_model run, so the next solve sees the retargeted horizon. They run before mj_step, in the same iteration.

The torques are therefore computed once per solve, from the state at that moment, and held for the 12 simulation steps of the stage. This matches the planner's assumption that the controls are constant over a stage.

items.title: Running it
items.text:
From examples/mujoco_mpc/go2/, with a gamepad connected, the environment set up per Installation and MuJoCo's own virtual environment per Examples:

python go2_walking.py

The MuJoCo viewer opens maximized and the robot stands. Use the sticks to walk, and the other controls to change the posture. The script does not wait to match real time, so the simulation runs as fast as the solves allow, and printing the frequency is available in the commented block at the top of the loop. The inputs package is needed to read the gamepad.

items.title: Things to try
items.text:
• Change GAIT_PERIOD to make the trot faster or slower, and see how the speeds that work change with it.
  • Raise STEP_HEIGHT, or the base height, and check how the robot handles it.
  • Lower mpc_H, and notice that the footholds near the end of the horizon, and so the response to a command change, get less accurate.
  • Set Kp to zero to see how much the small PD term between solves contributes.
  • Change dynamics_mode to ForwardDynamics and retune U_WGT and F_WGT: the weights are different for the two modes for a reason.
  • Press the jump button while walking: it is ignored unless the velocity command is below JUMP_MAX_VEL.

items.title: Panda Circle (MPC)
items.text: examples/mujoco_mpc/panda/panda_circle.py runs the same circular end-effector motion as Panda Circle (Trajectory Generation), but as closed-loop MPC against a live MuJoCo simulation instead of one offline solve. The earlier examples all follow the same shape: build a model for the whole problem once, solve it once, done. This one is different in kind, not just degree: SSQP only ever sees and solves a short window of the motion, MuJoCo (not SSQP) is the source of truth for what the robot's state actually is at each moment, and the two are wired together in a loop that re-solves every simulated timestep. It's the example to read once trajectory generation makes sense and you want to see the receding-horizon pattern end to end: a short MPC horizon chasing a long target trajectory, retargeted every step.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
examples/mujoco_mpc/panda/panda_circle.py
import mujoco
import mujoco.viewer
import glfw
import ssqpy
import numpy as np
import argparse
from math import pi, sin, cos, sqrt
from time import time, sleep


def parse_args():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="Panda circle tracking MPC in MuJoCo using SSQP"
    )

    parser.add_argument(
        "-p",
        "--plot",
        action=argparse.BooleanOptionalAction,
        default=False,
        help="Whether to run a single circle and plot the tracking error \
            and trajectory afterwards",
    )

    parser.add_argument(
        "-i",
        "--inverse-mode",
        action=argparse.BooleanOptionalAction,
        default=False,
        help="Whether to use the inverse dynamics formulation instead of \
            the forward dynamics one",
    )

    parser.add_argument(
        "-c",
        "--constrain",
        action=argparse.BooleanOptionalAction,
        default=True,
        help="Whether to constrain the end effector to a square inscribed \
            in the circle",
    )

    parser.add_argument(
        "-q",
        "--qp-solver",
        choices=["admm", "hpipm", "piqp"],
        default="hpipm",
        help="QP solver used at each SSQP iteration",
    )

    return parser.parse_args()


args = parse_args()

PLOT = args.plot
INVERSE_MODE = args.inverse_mode
CONSTRAIN = args.constrain

ssqpy.setSilentMode()

if PLOT:
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

H = 400
dt = 0.01
mpc_H = 10
mpc_dt = 0.05

T_WGT = 10.0
R_WGT = 1.0
V_WGT = 1e-1
U_WGT = 5e-3
C_WGT = 0.18

cx = 0.3
cy = 0
cz = 0.26
cr = 0.22

Two different horizons are in play here, and the distinction matters: H/dt (400 steps at 0.01s) describe the full circular trajectory the end effector should eventually trace over four seconds, exactly as in the trajectory-generation version, while mpc_H/mpc_dt (10 steps at 0.05s) describe the much shorter horizon the MPC model actually optimizes over at every control step. Note that mpc_dt is coarser than dt: the MPC model's internal discretization doesn't have to match the simulator's, or the rate at which controls are actually applied; it only has to be fine enough to represent the dynamics reasonably over its own, much shorter window. See Parameters in MPC for why this budget is kept small: an MPC step has to complete fast enough to keep up with real time, so 10 stages at 5x the simulation timestep is a deliberate trade of horizon length for solve speed, not an oversight.

The script takes three command line flags, which are turned into the PLOT, INVERSE_MODE and CONSTRAIN variables used below. --inverse-mode switches the internal SSQP model between ForwardDynamics (the default here, unlike the trajectory-generation example's InverseDynamics) and InverseDynamics; when it is given, the control applied to MuJoCo is computed by running the resulting acceleration back through model.inverseDynamics to recover torques (see the simulation loop, below). This example defaults to ForwardDynamics so mpc.step(...) output can be sent to MuJoCo directly, without that extra conversion step, at the cost of the smoother QP linearity InverseDynamics would otherwise buy you (see Panda Circle); with a short, frequently re-solved MPC horizon, the two modes are worth comparing directly rather than assuming one is always better. --constrain (on by default, turned off with --no-constrain) adds the box constraint, and --plot (off by default) is covered after the simulation loop.

Note also that the internal model is built from SSQP's Panda preset (which embeds the Panda's URDF) while MuJoCo, further down, loads a separate MJCF (../../assets/mjcf/panda/panda.xml). This mirrors a real deployment: the model SSQP optimizes against and the "real" system it's controlling are two different descriptions of the same robot, not necessarily even the same file format, and MuJoCo's simulated physics plays the role a real robot's sensors and actuators would.

items.title: The target trajectory
items.text:
examples/mujoco_mpc/panda/panda_circle.py
φ0 = 0

# Square inscribed in the circle, used as the end effector bounds
square_side_hlf = cr / sqrt(2)
constraint_hlines = [cz - square_side_hlf, cz + square_side_hlf]
constraint_vlines = [cy - square_side_hlf, cy + square_side_hlf]


traj = []

Identical in spirit to the trajectory-generation example: a full circle, precomputed as H + 1 points, though this time it outlives the MPC model's own horizon, which only ever sees a 10-stage window of it at a time. This is the trajectory MPC is chasing; the MPC model itself, built next, has no idea the full circle exists.

items.title: Building the (short-horizon) model
items.text:
examples/mujoco_mpc/panda/panda_circle.py
    φk = φ0 + ω * k * dt
    traj.append(np.array([cx, cy + cr * sin(φk), cz + cr * cos(φk)]))

# Desired end effector orientation, pointing down
Rd = np.eye(3)
Rd[1, 1] = -1
Rd[2, 2] = -1

model = ssqpy.model.Model(
    mpc_H,
    mpc_dt,
    from_preset=ssqpy.model.Preset.Panda,
    solver_mode=(
        ssqpy.model.SolverMode.InverseDynamics
        if INVERSE_MODE
        else ssqpy.model.SolverMode.ForwardDynamics
    ),
)

nq = model.getnq()
nv = model.getnv()
nu = model.getnu()

init_state = np.zeros(nq + nv)
init_state[:nq] = [
    0.0013,
    -0.9115,
    -0.0010,
    -2.6316,
    -0.0008,
    1.7431,
    0.7862,
    0.0,
    0.0,
]

pose_costs = []

lb = np.array((-np.inf, constraint_vlines[0], constraint_hlines[0]))
ub = np.array((np.inf, constraint_vlines[1], constraint_hlines[1]))
box_constraint = ssqpy.model.constraints.FrameTranslationBound(
    model, "panda_ee", lb, ub
)

config_cost = ssqpy.model.costs.SquaredConfigurationErrorCost(
    model, init_state[:nq], C_WGT
)
v_cost = ssqpy.model.costs.SquaredJointVelocityCost(model, V_WGT)
u_cost = ssqpy.model.costs.SquaredControlCost(model, U_WGT)

for k in range(mpc_H):
    pose_costs.append(
        ssqpy.model.costs.FrameSquaredPoseErrorCost(
            model, "panda_ee", traj[k], Rd, T_WGT, R_WGT
        )
    )

    model.addCost(k, v_cost)
    model.addCost(k, u_cost)
    model.addCost(k, config_cost)
    model.addCost(k, pose_costs[-1])

    if CONSTRAIN:
        model.addConstraints(k, box_constraint)

pose_costs.append(
    ssqpy.model.costs.FrameSquaredPoseErrorCost(
        model, "panda_ee", traj[mpc_H], Rd, T_WGT, R_WGT

The model itself has mpc_H stages, not H: as far as this Model object is concerned, the "problem" is only ever 10 stages long, and it has no built-in notion of a 400-stage circle at all. A pose-tracking cost is created per MPC stage and kept in the pose_costs list; this is what makes retargeting possible (see below), since a cost that only knows its target at construction time couldn't be pointed at a different part of the circle later. A box constraint again keeps the end effector inside a square window, same as the trajectory-generation version.

One addition not present in the offline version is config_cost, a SquaredConfigurationErrorCost pulling gently (C_WGT is small relative to the tracking weight) toward the arm's starting configuration, added at every stage alongside the pose-tracking cost. The Panda's 7-joint arm has one more degree of freedom than the 6-dimensional pose (3 for position, 3 for orientation) the cost tracks, so multiple joint configurations can produce the same end-effector pose; left unconstrained, that extra freedom is free for the solver to drift through arbitrarily from one MPC step to the next, since the pose cost alone doesn't penalize it. config_cost resolves this, and, incidentally, holds the two gripper finger joints near their starting position too, since it applies to the full configuration, by mildly preferring joint configurations close to the nominal start pose: a standard way to keep a redundant-arm controller's joint motion well-behaved over a long closed-loop run instead of just its end-effector position.

items.title: Retargeting the horizon every step
items.text:
examples/mujoco_mpc/panda/panda_circle.py
model.addCost(mpc_H, v_cost)
model.addCost(mpc_H, pose_costs[-1])

Since the MPC model only has stages for the next mpc_H steps, but the target trajectory traj describes a full 400-step circle, update_pose_costs slides the window: given the current real-time stage, it pushes the correct upcoming target point into each stage's pose cost via set_desired_translation, a mutator exposed on FrameSquaredPoseErrorCost for exactly this purpose (predefined costs' target values aren't fixed at construction time). This is called once per simulation step, after mpc.step, so the model is always tracking the correct absolute segment of the circle regardless of how short its own horizon is; without this call, the MPC model would keep re-solving the same fixed 10-stage arc it was built with, forever, instead of progressing around the circle.

items.title: MPC and solver parameters
items.text:
examples/mujoco_mpc/panda/panda_circle.py
# Shift the desired poses forward along the (looping) trajectory
def update_pose_costs(current_stage):
    for k in range(current_stage, current_stage + mpc_H):
        pose_costs[k - current_stage].set_desired_translation(traj[k % H])


ssqp_params = ssqpy.solvers.ssqpParams()
ssqp_params.tolerance = 1e-2

ssqpy.solvers.MPC wraps the model with its own iteration budget (sqp_iters=4, qp_iters=100), deliberately low, since this now has to run once per real-time control step rather than once, offline (see Parameters in MPC). Four SSQP iterations is not enough to fully converge a fresh problem from a poor guess; it's enough to make good progress from a guess that's already close to correct, which is exactly what MPC provides at every step after the first, since consecutive re-solves only need to adjust a trajectory that was already nearly right one timestep ago (see Warm-starting in MPC).

items.title: The simulation loop
items.text:
examples/mujoco_mpc/panda/panda_circle.py
    ssqpy.solvers.QPSolverType, args.qp_solver.upper()
)

mpc = ssqpy.solvers.MPC(model, ssqp_params, sqp_iters=4, qp_iters=100)

mjmodel = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_path("../../assets/mjcf/panda/panda.xml")
mjdata = mujoco.MjData(mjmodel)

mjdata.qpos = init_state[:9]

elapsed = 0
steps = 0
total_steps = int(1 / dt)

stage = 0

state_data = None
if PLOT:
    state_data = []

# Start the viewer maximized
glfw.init()
glfw.window_hint(glfw.MAXIMIZED, glfw.TRUE)
with mujoco.viewer.launch_passive(mjmodel, mjdata) as viewer:
    while viewer.is_running():
        frame_start = time()

        state = np.hstack((mjdata.qpos, mjdata.qvel))

        if PLOT:
            state_data.append(
                model.forwardKinematics(mjdata.qpos, "panda_ee")[0]
            )

            if stage == H:
                break

        pre = time()
        # MuJoCo has 8 actuators (7 arm joints and one finger), the model has 9 DoF
        if INVERSE_MODE:
            mjdata.ctrl = model.inverseDynamics(
                mjdata.qpos, mjdata.qvel, mpc.step(state)[1].stage(0)
            )[:8]
        else:
            mjdata.ctrl = mpc.step(state)[1].stage(0)[:8]
        elapsed += time() - pre
        steps += 1

        if steps == total_steps:
            print(f"\rControl frequency: {(1 / (elapsed*dt)):.2f}Hz\t", end="")
            elapsed = 0
            steps = 0

        mujoco.mj_step(mjmodel, mjdata)

Each iteration: read the current MuJoCo state (qpos/qvel), which is treated as ground truth and fed to SSQP as \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\), call mpc.step(state) to get updated (x, u) trajectories, and apply u.stage(0), the first stage's control only, to the simulator (either directly as torques, or through model.inverseDynamics if --inverse-mode is given). This is exactly the receding-horizon pattern described in MPC: only the very first control of a freshly (re-)solved trajectory is ever actually used, and everything the solve computed for the remaining 9 stages is discarded and recomputed from the new state next step, rather than played back open loop. mujoco.mj_step then advances the physics under that control, stage is incremented, update_pose_costs retargets the horizon for the next call, and the loop sleeps to hold real time; the control-frequency counter printed to the terminal is a direct measure of whether the MPC solve is actually keeping up with dt.

Run it (from examples/mujoco_mpc/panda/, with the environment set up per Installation and MuJoCo's own virtual environment, per Examples):

python panda_circle.py

A MuJoCo viewer window opens and the Panda arm should trace the circle live, correcting continuously as the simulation runs; the terminal prints the achieved control frequency. With --plot, the loop exits after one full lap (stage == H) and the same tracking-error/trajectory plots as the offline example appear for comparison; by default, that check is skipped entirely (it's nested inside the if PLOT block), so the simulation instead keeps looping the circle indefinitely, since update_pose_costs wraps the stage index with % H, until you close the viewer window yourself. A control frequency well below \(1/dt = 100\text{Hz}\) is a sign that each MPC solve is taking too long relative to the simulation timestep; that's exactly the failure mode the low sqp_iters/qp_iters budget above is there to avoid.

items.title: Things to try
items.text:
• Run with and without --inverse-mode and compare tracking quality and the printed control frequency; inverse dynamics adds a conversion step per control application but may converge in fewer SSQP iterations per solve.
  • Increase mpc_H (and/or decrease mpc_dt) to see the tracking improve as the MPC model looks further ahead, at the cost of a slower per-step solve and a lower achieved control frequency.
  • Lower sqp_iters/qp_iters while keeping the box constraint on (the default) to see constraint satisfaction degrade gracefully while tracking defaults to following just the cost, or raise them to see how much headroom there is before the control frequency starts dropping.
  • Set C_WGT to 0 to remove the redundancy-resolving configuration cost, run a few laps, and watch the arm's posture drift over time even though the end-effector path stays correct.

items.title: Panda Circle (Trajectory Generation)
items.text: examples/trajgen/python/panda/panda_circle.py generates a trajectory that drives a Franka Panda arm's end effector around a circle on the yz-plane, optionally constrained to stay within a square window inscribed in that circle. Where Pendubot tracked a fixed target configuration, this example tracks a moving target pose in task space: at every stage, the cost doesn't care what the joint angles are, only where the end effector ends up and how it's oriented, which is a much more common way to specify a manipulation task. It's the best next step after Pendubot: frame-relative pose tracking, a real (non-XML-derived) box constraint, and InverseDynamics mode.

items.title: Setup and the target trajectory
items.text:
examples/trajgen/python/panda/panda_circle.py
import ssqpy
import numpy as np
import argparse
from math import pi, sin, cos

"""
Panda Circle example
Perform a circular motion with the Panda's end effector on the yz-plane
Optionally, constrain the movement within a rectangle inside the circle
"""


def parse_args():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="Panda end effector circle trajectory generation"
    )

    parser.add_argument(
        "-p",
        "--plot",
        action=argparse.BooleanOptionalAction,
        default=True,
        help="Whether to plot error and trajectory",
    )

    parser.add_argument(
        "-c",
        "--constrain",
        action=argparse.BooleanOptionalAction,
        default=True,
        help="Whether to add a box constraint within the circle for the end \
            effector",
    )

    parser.add_argument(
        "-o",
        "--output",
        default="../../data/panda_circle.json",
        help="Path of the output JSON file",
    )

    parser.add_argument(
        "-q",
        "--qp-solver",
        choices=["admm", "hpipm", "piqp"],
        default="admm",
        help="QP solver used at each SSQP iteration",
    )

    return parser.parse_args()


args = parse_args()

PLOT = args.plot
CONSTRAIN = args.constrain

if PLOT:
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

H = 400
dt = 0.01

# Weights
T_WGT = 3.0
R_WGT = 1.0
V_WGT = 3e-3
U_WGT = 3e-3

# Horizontal and vertical line coordinates for constraints
constraint_hlines = [0.1, 0.41]
constraint_vlines = [-0.15, 0.15]

# Circle properties
cx = 0.3
cy = 0
cz = 0.26
cr = 0.22

DISTANCE = 2 * pi
ω = DISTANCE / (H * dt)
φ0 = 0

# Trajectory
traj = []

# Keep x-coordinate constant

The circular path is precomputed as a plain Python list of 3D points, one per stage, parameterized by angular velocity \(\omega\) so the end effector completes exactly one full circle over the horizon (\(H = 400\) stages at \(dt = 0.01\text{s}\), i.e. four seconds). This is the target the cost will track, not a constraint: nothing stops the solver from cutting corners if doing so is cheaper, which matters once --constrain clips the circle into a square later on. Rd is the desired end-effector orientation (constant throughout, on the yz-plane the arm reaches "forward" with a fixed wrist rotation), expressed as a rotation matrix rather than e.g. Euler angles, since that's what the frame-pose costs expect and it avoids the singularities/ambiguities of angle-based representations.

The two command line flags, --plot and --constrain (both on by default, and turned off with --no-plot and --no-constrain), are the two things worth toggling first if you want to see this example do something different before reading further: --plot shows the tracking error and the resulting trajectory after solving; --constrain decides whether the box constraint (below) is actually applied.

items.title: Building the model
items.text:
examples/trajgen/python/panda/panda_circle.py
for k in range(H + 1):
    φk = φ0 + ω * k * dt
    traj.append(np.array([cx, cy + cr * sin(φk), cz + cr * cos(φk)]))

Rd = np.eye(3)
Rd[1, 1] = -1
Rd[2, 2] = -1

# Create an SSQP model with H and dt, from the URDF at the below path
model = ssqpy.model.Model(
    H,
    dt,
    from_preset=ssqpy.model.Preset.Panda,
    solver_mode=ssqpy.model.SolverMode.InverseDynamics,
)

nq = model.getnq()
nv = model.getnv()
nu = model.getnu()

# Use the following initial state
# This will act as:
#  1) An initial state for the system at the first time step (x0); this cannot
#     be changed by the solver
#  2) An initial guess for every time step xk; this will be changed by the
#     solver to minimize the cost and satisfy the constraints
# If we wanted to help the solver converge faster, we could also choose to
# provide a more accurate initial guess
init_state = np.zeros(nq + nv)
init_state[:nq] = [
    0.0013,
    -0.9115,

This model uses InverseDynamics solver mode, so controls are joint accelerations rather than torques, which the example's comments note can simplify convergence for this kind of task: accelerations enter the dynamics linearly, so the QP the solver builds at each iteration is a better local approximation of the true problem than it would be with torques, where the mapping to acceleration is nonlinear in the joint configuration.

init_state is a single, fixed arm configuration (not the resting/neutral one) chosen to already be reasonably close to the circle. As the comment in the source explains, this array does double duty: it's the fixed initial state \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) (the arm has to actually start there), and the initial guess used to seed every other stage before the solver improves on it. A better initial guess generally means fewer SSQP iterations to converge; picking one near the expected solution, as here, is a common and effective way to help a local solver like SSQP. See finalize arguments in Model.

items.title: A real constraint: keeping the end effector inside a box
items.text:
examples/trajgen/python/panda/panda_circle.py
    -2.6316,
    -0.0008,
    1.7431,
    0.7862,
    0.0,
    0.0,
]

# Create a box constraint for the position of the end effector
# This will constrain the position within `vlines[0]` <= p[1] <= `vlines[1]` in the

FrameTranslationBound is a predefined constraint bounding a frame's position component-wise; -np.inf/np.inf leaves the x-coordinate free (the plane the circle lives on is already fixed by the cost, so the constraint only needs to act on y/z) while the y/z coordinates are boxed in around the circle. Since the box is inscribed inside the circle, this constraint is genuinely active: whenever the tracked point on the circle falls outside the box (near the four "corners" of the circle relative to the square), the solver has to trade off cost against constraint satisfaction, and the resulting path visibly flattens against the box edges instead of following the circle exactly. This is a good example to compare --constrain against --no-constrain and look at the --plot output for; with it off, the trajectory follows the circle everywhere, since nothing stops it from doing so.

The constraint object is created once and reused across every stage it's added to, since constraints don't need to be re-instantiated per stage unless their bounds actually differ.

items.title: Per-stage costs and constraints
items.text:
examples/trajgen/python/panda/panda_circle.py
# Note: here, we only create the constraint; for it to be applied to some stage
# of the horizon, we actually have to add it to the model
lb = np.array((-np.inf, constraint_vlines[0], constraint_hlines[0]))
ub = np.array((np.inf, constraint_vlines[1], constraint_hlines[1]))
box_constraint = ssqpy.model.constraints.FrameTranslationBound(
    model, "panda_ee", lb, ub
)

for k in range(H):
    # Add a squared pose error cost for the end effector (`"panda_ee"` frame) to
    # follow the generated trajectory, while keeping its orientation at `Rd`
    # We use weights `P_WGT` and `R_WGT` for the translation and rotation
    # respectively
    model.addCost(
        k,
        ssqpy.model.costs.FrameSquaredPoseErrorCost(
            model, "panda_ee", traj[k], Rd, T_WGT, R_WGT
        ),
    )

    # Add regularization costs for joint velocity (v) and control (u)
    model.addCost(k, ssqpy.model.costs.SquaredJointVelocityCost(model, V_WGT))
    model.addCost(k, ssqpy.model.costs.SquaredControlCost(model, U_WGT))

    if CONSTRAIN:
        # Add the previously created box constraint to stage k
        model.addConstraints(k, box_constraint)

# Add the same pose error for the terminal stage
model.addCost(
    H,
    ssqpy.model.costs.FrameSquaredPoseErrorCost(
        model, "panda_ee", traj[H], Rd, T_WGT, R_WGT
    ),
)

FrameSquaredPoseErrorCost is added at every stage with that stage's own target point from traj and the fixed orientation Rd, weighted separately for translation (T_WGT) and rotation (R_WGT); translation is weighted three times as heavily here, so the solver prioritizes tracing the circle's shape over holding the wrist exactly level, though both matter. Velocity and control regularization are added too, at every stage, for the same reason as in Pendubot: without them, the solver has no reason to prefer a smooth, low-effort trajectory among the many that satisfy the pose cost equally well. The box constraint is added too, if --constrain is set.

Note the terminal stage (H) only gets the velocity regularization, not the control one, since there are no controls at the terminal stage (see Horizon, states and controls in Model); it does still get its own pose-tracking cost, added separately just below this block, so the very last point on the circle is tracked too.

items.title: Solving
items.text:
examples/trajgen/python/panda/panda_circle.py
# There are no controls (u) at the terminal stage, so we cannot add a control
# regularization cost; thus, we only add the joint velocity regularization cost
model.addCost(H, ssqpy.model.costs.SquaredJointVelocityCost(model, V_WGT))

if CONSTRAIN:
    # Add box constraint to terminal stage as well
    model.addConstraints(H, box_constraint)

# Finalize the model
# This will generate the final model, ready for use by SSQP for optimization
# By passing a single configuration as an init_state, this configuration will
# be applied to all stages (including as an initial stage)
model.finalize(init_states=init_state)

# Initialize an SSQP solver object with the created model
# Parameters are passed as keyword arguments
# ADMM-specific parameters start with "admm_"
solver = ssqpy.solvers.ssqp(
    model,
    loose_success=False,
    tolerance=1e-2,
    # line_search_method=ssqpy.solvers.LineSearchMethod.Merit,
    admm_abs_tolerance=1e-3,
    admm_rel_tolerance=1e-3,
    admm_adaptive_rho_tolerance=10,
    # admm_rho_update_iter_freq=10,
    # admm_max_iter=1000,
    qp_solver_type=getattr(
        ssqpy.solvers.QPSolverType, args.qp_solver.upper()
    ),
    hpipm_max_iter=250,

The solver parameters here are mostly tightened tolerances (admm_abs_tolerance/admm_rel_tolerance) rather than a different QP backend; this is a much less pathological problem than Pendubot's swing-up (there's no local-minimum trap to route around), so the default ADMM solver, given a reasonably good initial guess, is enough. After solving, model.forwardKinematics(q, "panda_ee") is used (in the plotting code that follows, not shown here) to recover the actual end-effector path from the solved joint trajectory, for comparison against the target traj, using the same Pinocchio-backed algorithm used internally by the frame-based costs and constraints; this is exactly how you'd check tracking accuracy for any frame-based task, not just in plotting code.

Run it (from examples/trajgen/python/panda/, with the environment set up per Installation):

python panda_circle.py

With --plot (the default), two figures appear after solving: end-effector tracking error over the horizon on the left (small and roughly constant with --no-constrain, spiking near the box edges with --constrain), and the traced-out trajectory against the target circle on the right, with the box drawn in when constrained. The solver also prints its final SolverState to the terminal; Success (or LooseSuccess) is what you should see for the default configuration.

items.title: Things to try
items.text:
• Toggle --constrain and compare both plots: the tracking-error spikes and the flattened corners in the trajectory plot are a direct, visual consequence of the constraint being active.
  • Loosen or tighten the box (constraint_hlines/constraint_vlines) and watch how much of the circle gets clipped.
  • Try solver_mode=ForwardDynamics instead of InverseDynamics (you'll need to drop the hpipm_max_iter override or retune it) and compare convergence; this is a good way to build intuition for when the choice of solver mode actually matters in practice.
  • Replace init_state with the zero/neutral configuration (drop init_states=init_state from model.finalize) and see how much slower or less reliable convergence becomes from a worse initial guess.

items.title: Pendubot Swing-Up
items.text:
A pendubot is a double pendulum actuated only at the shoulder joint; the elbow is free-swinging. Because there's no direct control over the second link, the only way to bring it up is to swing the whole system through its nonlinear dynamics and let the coupling between the two links do the work; no simple feedback law does this, which is why it's a natural OCP: pick a cost that rewards being upright, hand SSQP the horizon, and let it discover a trajectory that gets there.

examples/trajgen/python/double_pendulum/pendubot.py generates a trajectory that swings the pendubot up from hanging and holds it stationary pointing against gravity. It's a good first "real" example after the Quickstart: an XML-based model, predefined costs, and a scheduling trick that's worth understanding before moving to constrained examples.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
examples/trajgen/python/double_pendulum/pendubot.py
import ssqpy
import numpy as np
import argparse

"""
Pendubot example
Using the pendubot (double pendulum with only the shoulder joint actuated),
move and remain at a vertical position in the opposite direction of gravity
"""


def parse_args():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="Pendubot trajectory generation"
    )

    parser.add_argument(
        "-o",
        "--output",
        default="../../data/pendubot.json",
        help="Path of the output JSON file",
    )

    parser.add_argument(
        "-q",
        "--qp-solver",
        choices=["admm", "hpipm", "piqp"],
        default="hpipm",
        help="QP solver used at each SSQP iteration",
    )

    return parser.parse_args()


args = parse_args()

H = 200

The model is loaded straight from a URDF, so no custom dynamics are needed; see Defining a model in Model. pendubot_cont.urdf declares both joints as continuous (unbounded revolute joints, as opposed to a joint with hard angle limits), which Pinocchio represents on the circle manifold \(S^1\) as a \((\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\) pair rather than a raw angle. That's why nq is 4 for a 2-link system, one \((\cos, \sin)\) pair per joint, and it's a concrete instance of the manifold-valued states SSQP supports: SSQP optimizes over the joints' tangent (angular-velocity) space while keeping every intermediate guess a valid point on the circle.

DESIRED_CONFIG = (-1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0) decodes to shoulder angle \(\pi\) (from \((\cos, \sin) = (-1, 0)\)) and elbow angle \(0\) (from \((1, 0)\)), i.e. both links extended straight up, opposing gravity. No init_state is passed to model.finalize, so SSQP falls back to its own manifold-aware neutral configuration, which sets each continuous joint's \(\cos\) component to \(1\) (angle \(0\)) rather than leaving the state at literal zero (which wouldn't even be a valid point on the circle). Angle \(0\) for both joints is exactly "hanging straight down", so the solver's initial guess for every stage is the pendubot at rest, and the whole trajectory has to be discovered from there.

items.title: Building the model
items.text:
examples/trajgen/python/double_pendulum/pendubot.py
V_WGT = 1e-2
U_WGT = 1e-3
C_WGT = 5.0

DESIRED_CONFIG = np.array((-1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0))
# DESIRED_CONFIG = np.array((np.pi, 0.0))

model = ssqpy.model.Model(
    H,
    dt,

ForwardDynamics is the default solver mode, where controls are joint torques: the most direct formulation, and a reasonable default when there's no particular reason to prefer accelerations (as in Panda Circle) or a reduced floating-base formulation (as in Go2 Jump).

items.title: Costs, and why the tracking cost turns on late
items.text:
examples/trajgen/python/double_pendulum/pendubot.py
    # actuated_joints=[0],
    solver_mode=ssqpy.model.SolverMode.ForwardDynamics,
)

nq = model.getnq()
nv = model.getnv()
nu = model.getnu()

vel_cost = ssqpy.model.costs.SquaredJointVelocityCost(model, V_WGT)
u_cost = ssqpy.model.costs.SquaredControlCost(model, U_WGT)
config_cost = ssqpy.model.costs.SquaredConfigurationErrorCost(
    model, DESIRED_CONFIG, C_WGT
)

Three predefined costs are used: SquaredJointVelocityCost and SquaredControlCost are cheap regularization terms added at every stage, keeping the motion and effort small by default (V_WGT/U_WGT are both small, so they barely influence the solution except where nothing else does). SquaredConfigurationErrorCost, the one that actually pulls the pendulum toward DESIRED_CONFIG (weighted much more heavily, C_WGT = 5.0), is only added for k > 150, i.e. only over the last quarter of the horizon (H = 200), and separately set as the terminal_cost so the very last stage is held to it too.

This is a deliberate swing-up trick, and the reason the example is worth reading rather than just running: SSQP is a local method, it improves on whatever guess it's given rather than searching globally, and the initial guess here is the pendulum at rest. If the tracking cost were active from stage 0, gradient descent on a strongly-weighted, highly nonlinear configuration error from a resting start pulls the shoulder the "short way", directly toward the target angle, which for a double pendulum is exactly the motion that doesn't generate the momentum needed to bring the second link up; the solver settles into that local minimum and gets stuck well short of upright. Leaving the early stages free to minimize only velocity/effort gives SSQP's line search room to explore a swinging motion that costs some torque now in exchange for reaching the target cheaply later, and only the later stages commit to actually holding it. This is a general pattern worth keeping in mind for other underactuated or highly nonlinear swing-type problems: a cost that's "obviously correct" as a final objective can actively prevent convergence if applied too early or too uniformly across the horizon.

items.title: Solving
items.text:
examples/trajgen/python/double_pendulum/pendubot.py
    model.addCost(k, vel_cost)
    model.addCost(k, u_cost)

    if k > 150:
        model.addCost(k, config_cost)

model.finalize(terminal_cost=config_cost)

solver = ssqpy.solvers.ssqp(
    model,
    tolerance=1e-2,
    qp_solver_type=getattr(ssqpy.solvers.QPSolverType, args.qp_solver.upper()),
    filter_size=10,
    admm_adaptive_rho_tolerance=25,
    admm_abs_tolerance=1e-3,
    admm_rel_tolerance=1e-4,
    admm_max_iter=500,
    admm_warm_start=False,
)

state, x, u = solver.solve()

print("Solver state:", state)

Solver and QP parameters are passed as keyword arguments: hpipm_/admm_-prefixed ones configure the QP solver actually selected via qp_solver_type; the rest are ignored. This example selects HPIPM explicitly (SSQP defaults to ADMM) and tunes several of its and ADMM's parameters away from their defaults; swing-up is enough more nonlinear than plain regularization that the defaults, tuned for easier problems, may need help. If you're adapting this example for your own underactuated system and convergence stalls or MaxIterReached shows up, these are exactly the parameters worth revisiting first, alongside tolerance and filter_size (see The SSQP Solver). solver.write saves the trajectory for later use, e.g. with the visualizer.

Run it (from examples/trajgen/python/double_pendulum/, with the environment set up per Installation):

python pendubot.py

The script prints only the final solver state, and writes ../../data/pendubot.json. Visualize the result with the visualizer example to see the actual swing-up motion, or load the JSON yourself and plot the shoulder/elbow angles over time to see the "wait, then commit" pattern described above: little motion in the first 150 stages beyond light damping, then a swing into the upright configuration over the last quarter of the horizon.

items.title: Things to try
items.text:
• Move the threshold (k > 150) earlier or later and see how it trades off "the tracking cost has more time to act, so the final approach is gentler" against "the solver has less free room to discover the swing, so it's more likely to get stuck."
  • Set the threshold to k > 0 (tracking active from the very first stage) to reproduce the local-minimum failure described above, and compare the resulting (much worse) trajectory to the default.
  • Increase C_WGT to see the final approach become more aggressive (and possibly jerkier); decrease it to see how loosely the terminal configuration is actually held.
  • Remove the qp_solver_type/hpipm_* overrides to fall back to SSQP's default ADMM solver, and compare convergence (iteration count, SolverState) against the tuned HPIPM configuration used here.

items.title: Installing with pip
items.text:
Prebuilt wheels are available for Linux x86_64 and Python 3.10 or newer:

pip install ssqp

The package provides the ssqpy module. The wheels require a CPU with AVX2 and FMA (Intel Haswell, AMD Excavator or newer). On older CPUs, importing ssqpy fails with an illegal instruction error, so build from source instead, as described below. Building from source is also needed for the C++ library, other platforms, or non-default CMake options.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
SSQP only expects a couple of dependencies to already be present on the system:

  • Eigen3: linear algebra
  • NumPy: only required if SSQP_BUILD_PYTHON is enabled (the default); ssqpy's bindings convert between Eigen and NumPy arrays, so NumPy must be importable in whatever Python interpreter CMake picks up (via find_package(Python); pass -DPython_EXECUTABLE=/path/to/python to cmake to pin a specific one) both when building and when later using ssqpy

Tip

Building Pinocchio (and, if enabled, HPIPM/BLASFEO and PIQP) from source is the default, but SSQP also supports building against prebuilt packages for them instead; see Building against prebuilt dependencies below.

Everything else is fetched and built from source automatically as part of the CMake build, statically linked, and baked into the final artifacts (including the ssqpy shared object), with no system-wide install, package manager, or manual build step required:

  • Boost filesystem/serialization: always linked statically into the final artifacts, and used from the system when a suitable install is found there, falling back automatically otherwise, in one of two ways: if Boost headers are present but not both required static archives, CMake fetches and builds just the filesystem/serialization component sources at the matching, already-installed Boost version; if no system Boost is found at all, CMake fetches and builds a full Boost release instead (the SSQP_BOOST_VERSION CMake option, default 1.86.0, picks which one). None of this applies when building against a prebuilt Pinocchio package (see below), which bundles its own Boost static libs instead.
  • Pinocchio: rigid body dynamics algorithms, along with the dependency chain needed for its URDF parser (urdfdom, urdfdom_headers, console_bridge, tinyxml2)
  • nanobind: Python bindings, fetched automatically if SSQP_BUILD_PYTHON is enabled (the default)
  • BLASFEO and HPIPM: fetched automatically if the SSQP_WITH_HPIPM CMake option is enabled, for the HPIPM-based QP solver (see QP Solvers)
  • PIQP: header-only, fetched automatically if the SSQP_WITH_PIQP CMake option is enabled, for the PIQP-based QP solver (see QP Solvers). Its multistage solver also needs BLASFEO, which is shared with HPIPM when both are enabled and fetched and built for PIQP otherwise
  • nlohmann/json and Tracy: vendored under external/ as git submodules

Make sure to clone submodules along with the repository:

git clone --recurse-submodules git@github.com:upatras-lar/ssqp.git

The dependencies fetched by CMake (see cmake/) require network access during the build. The first build will take noticeably longer than subsequent ones since it has to compile Pinocchio and, if enabled, HPIPM/BLASFEO from source (PIQP itself is header-only); later builds only recompile them if their vendored sources change. The .ci/Dockerfile documents a working system setup (Ubuntu 24.04, Eigen3, Boost) to have in place before running CMake; Boost is included there so CI doesn't pay the fetch-and-build cost on every run, not because it's strictly required (see Dependencies above).

items.title: Building the library
items.text:
From the repository root:

mkdir build && cd build
cmake ..
cmake --build .

Every dependency SSQP builds itself, Boost included, is linked statically, so the ssqpy Python extension only keeps the platform's C/C++ runtime as a shared dependency. With SSQP_BUILD_PYTHON=ON (the default) and readelf available, verify this for a completed build with:

cmake --build . --target verify-static-dependencies

items.title: CMake options
items.text:
Option Default Description SSQP_WITH_HPIPM ON Fetch, build and link against HPIPM and BLASFEO to enable the HPIPM QP solver SSQP_PREBUILT_PINOCCHIO_DIR (empty) Path to a prebuilt Pinocchio package instead of building it from source; see Building against prebuilt dependencies SSQP_PREBUILT_HPIPM_DIR (empty) Path to a prebuilt HPIPM/BLASFEO package instead of building it from source (only relevant if SSQP_WITH_HPIPM=ON) SSQP_WITH_PIQP ON Fetch and link against PIQP (and BLASFEO) to enable the PIQP QP solver SSQP_PIQP_OPENMP OFF Build the PIQP backend with OpenMP, enabling its parallel multistage solver; adds a shared dependency on the OpenMP runtime (only relevant if SSQP_WITH_PIQP=ON) SSQP_PREBUILT_PIQP_DIR (empty) Path to a prebuilt PIQP package instead of fetching it, along with BLASFEO when SSQP_WITH_HPIPM=OFF (only relevant if SSQP_WITH_PIQP=ON) SSQP_BOOST_VERSION 1.86.0 Boost release fetched when no system Boost headers are available (see Dependencies above) SSQP_ENABLE_PROFILING OFF Enable Tracy profiling SSQP_DISABLE_LOGGING OFF Compile out SSQP's logging (see ssqp::set_log_level) SSQP_BUILD_EXAMPLES OFF Build the C++ example executables under examples/trajgen/c++ SSQP_BUILD_TESTS ON Build the unit test suite under tests/; OFF when SSQP is added to another project SSQP_BUILD_PYTHON ON Build the ssqpy Python extension via nanobind; OFF when SSQP is added to another project

Pass options as -D<OPTION>=<VALUE> to cmake, e.g.:

cmake -DSSQP_WITH_HPIPM=ON -DSSQP_BUILD_EXAMPLES=ON ..

items.title: CMake targets
items.text:
Build a specific target instead of everything with cmake --build . --target <target>:

Target Description ssqp The static C++ library; always built ssqpy The ssqpy Python extension module (SSQP_BUILD_PYTHON=ON, the default) run_tests The unit/regression test executable under tests/ (SSQP_BUILD_TESTS=ON, the default) (per-file, e.g. analytical-di) One executable per C++ example under examples/trajgen/c++ (SSQP_BUILD_EXAMPLES=ON); named after the file's path relative to that directory, with / replaced by - install Installs the C++ package (cpp component, see Using the C++ library) and the built ssqpy (python component, see Using the Python bindings) verify-static-dependencies Confirms ssqp/ssqpy link no shared Boost, Pinocchio, URDF, HPIPM, or BLASFEO libraries (SSQP_BUILD_PYTHON=ON and readelf available) package-pinocchio Assembles a redistributable prebuilt Pinocchio package; see Building against prebuilt dependencies below (unavailable when SSQP_PREBUILT_PINOCCHIO_DIR is set) package-hpipm Assembles a redistributable prebuilt HPIPM/BLASFEO package; see Building against prebuilt dependencies below (SSQP_WITH_HPIPM=ON, unavailable when SSQP_PREBUILT_HPIPM_DIR is set) package-piqp Assembles a redistributable prebuilt PIQP package, which also holds BLASFEO when SSQP_WITH_HPIPM=OFF; see Building against prebuilt dependencies below (SSQP_WITH_PIQP=ON, unavailable when SSQP_PREBUILT_PIQP_DIR is set)

items.title: Building against prebuilt dependencies
items.text:
Building Pinocchio (and, if SSQP_WITH_HPIPM is on, HPIPM/BLASFEO) from source is the default, but that isn't always practical, since the target machine may lack network access, or its CPU/toolchain combination may trip up one of their builds. As an alternative, SSQP provides prebuilt packages for Pinocchio, HPIPM/BLASFEO and PIQP that a build can link against directly instead of building them from source.

Point a build at them:

mkdir build && cd build
cmake -DSSQP_WITH_HPIPM=ON \
      -DSSQP_PREBUILT_PINOCCHIO_DIR=/path/to/prebuilt/pinocchio \
      -DSSQP_PREBUILT_HPIPM_DIR=/path/to/prebuilt/hpipm \
      -DSSQP_PREBUILT_PIQP_DIR=/path/to/prebuilt/piqp \
      ..
cmake --build .

This build only compiles ssqp itself, needing no network access and no Pinocchio/urdfdom/HPIPM/BLASFEO compiler toolchain. The Pinocchio package also bundles the Boost headers and static libs it was built against (ssqp's own sources include Pinocchio headers that use Boost types directly, not just precompiled code, so this is needed even though the linking itself is static), so SSQP_PREBUILT_PINOCCHIO_DIR can be used without Boost installed at all either: unlike the default from-source build (see Dependencies above), this mode never has to detect, fetch, or build Boost itself. SSQP_PREBUILT_HPIPM_DIR can be set independently of SSQP_PREBUILT_PINOCCHIO_DIR and vice versa; each falls back to building from source if left unset. The same goes for SSQP_PREBUILT_PIQP_DIR, except that a PIQP package only holds BLASFEO when it was made with SSQP_WITH_HPIPM=OFF. With HPIPM on, PIQP uses the BLASFEO from the HPIPM build or package, so a PIQP package made that way only works for builds that also have HPIPM on.

A prebuilt package is tied to the architecture, compiler, and (for HPIPM/BLASFEO) CPU microarchitecture it was built on. It isn't a portable, run-anywhere artifact, just a way to build once and reuse the result across machines with matching setups.

Note

Instead of using a package we provide, you can also produce your own. On a machine that can build from source matching your target architecture, a build can package what it just built into a redistributable directory: cmake --build . --target package-pinocchio, cmake --build . --target package-hpipm and cmake --build . --target package-piqp produce build/prebuilt/pinocchio/{include,lib}, build/prebuilt/hpipm/{include,lib} and build/prebuilt/piqp respectively. Copy any of these directories to another machine and point SSQP_PREBUILT_PINOCCHIO_DIR/SSQP_PREBUILT_HPIPM_DIR/SSQP_PREBUILT_PIQP_DIR at it, same as above.

items.title: Using the C++ library
items.text: SSQP is a static library, libssqp.a, exposed to CMake as the ssqp::ssqp target. You can install a prebuilt release, install your own build, or build SSQP as part of your project. In every case your code is compiled with SSQP's architecture flag (-march=native for your own builds, see SSQP_MARCH_NATIVE), since Eigen's memory alignment must match between SSQP and the code calling it.

items.title: Installing a release
items.text:
Each GitHub release provides prebuilt packages for Linux x86_64. Like the pip wheels, they are built with -march=x86-64-v3 and need a CPU with AVX2 and FMA, and they include the HPIPM QP solver.

On Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04, download the .deb for your Ubuntu version and install it with apt, which also installs Eigen:

sudo apt install ./libssqp-dev_0.2-1-ubuntu24.04_amd64.deb

Your project then finds it with find_package(ssqp), as shown below.

On other distributions, use the ssqp-v0.2-linux-x86_64.tar.gz archive, which also contains the Python module, the examples and the prebuilt dependency packages. Extract it and pass its directory to your project with -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH, or let CMake download it:

include(FetchContent)
FetchContent_Declare(ssqp
    URL https://github.com/upatras-lar/ssqp/releases/download/v0.2/ssqp-v0.2-linux-x86_64.tar.gz
)
FetchContent_MakeAvailable(ssqp)
find_package(ssqp REQUIRED PATHS ${ssqp_SOURCE_DIR} NO_DEFAULT_PATH)

target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE ssqp::ssqp)

The archive needs Eigen 3.4 on the system.

items.title: Installing your own build
items.text:
Install the library, its headers and a CMake package into a prefix of your choice:

cmake --install build --component cpp --prefix ~/.local

This installs libssqp.a under lib/, the static libraries it links (Pinocchio, its URDF parser, Boost and, with SSQP_WITH_HPIPM=ON, HPIPM/BLASFEO) under lib/ssqp/, the headers under include/ssqp/ and the CMake package under lib/cmake/ssqp/. Your project then finds it with:

find_package(ssqp REQUIRED)
target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE ssqp::ssqp)

Pass -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=~/.local when configuring your project if the prefix isn't one CMake searches by default. The package needs Eigen3 on the system, compatible with the version SSQP was built against, but no Pinocchio, Boost or HPIPM.

items.title: Adding SSQP to a CMake project
items.text:
Alternatively, build SSQP as part of your project with FetchContent (or add_subdirectory on a checkout):

include(FetchContent)
FetchContent_Declare(ssqp
    GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/upatras-lar/ssqp.git
    GIT_TAG v0.2
)
FetchContent_MakeAvailable(ssqp)

target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE ssqp::ssqp)

The CMake options above work the same here, set before FetchContent_MakeAvailable or on the command line. SSQP_BUILD_TESTS and SSQP_BUILD_PYTHON default to OFF in this case. The first build compiles Pinocchio as described in Dependencies, unless SSQP_PREBUILT_PINOCCHIO_DIR points to a prebuilt package.

items.title: Using the Python bindings
items.text:
Once built with SSQP_BUILD_PYTHON=ON (the default), the ssqpy extension module is produced under build/bindings/. There are two ways to make it importable:

Install it into whichever Python interpreter it was built against (the one find_package(Python) picked up at configure time; pass -DPython_EXECUTABLE=/path/to/python to pin a specific one, e.g. a virtualenv's):

cmake --install build --component python

This drops ssqpy (plus its type stubs) directly into that interpreter's site-packages, so import ssqpy works from anywhere, in any script or shell, with no environment setup. This is the same interpreter build already needs NumPy in (see Dependencies above). Installing to a different one than you built against risks an ABI mismatch, since ssqpy is not a portable, version-independent artifact.

Or, without installing, add build/bindings directly to your PYTHONPATH for the current shell only:

export PYTHONPATH="$(pwd)/build/bindings:${PYTHONPATH}"

The examples/ directory provides a setup_env.sh script that does this (and sets up other example-specific environment variables); source it from within examples/ before running any Python example:

cd examples
source setup_env.sh
python trajgen/python/di.py

See Quickstart to write your own script against ssqpy.

items.title: Quickstart
items.text:
This walks through the smallest complete SSQP problem: driving a 1D double integrator to a target position, with custom (non-robot) dynamics and a custom cost. It corresponds to examples/trajgen/python/di.py; the code blocks below are pulled live from that file at doc build time.

Make sure ssqpy is importable first; see Installation.

items.title: 1. Define the dynamics
items.text:
Custom dynamics subclass ssqpy.model.dynamics.StageDynamics and must provide, at minimum, output_size, state_size, control_size, evaluate and gradient (Hessian-vector products are optional, defaulting to zero, and only needed if you want exact second-order information):

examples/trajgen/python/di.py
def parse_args():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="Double integrator trajectory generation"
    )

    parser.add_argument(
        "-q",
        "--qp-solver",
        choices=["admm", "hpipm", "piqp"],
        default="admm",
        help="QP solver used at each SSQP iteration",
    )

    return parser.parse_args()


args = parse_args()

# Horizon and time step
H, dt = 10, 0.1


# Discrete double integrator, with the acceleration as the control
class DoubleIntegrator(ssqpy.model.dynamics.StageDynamics):
    def output_size(self):
        return 2

    def state_size(self):
        return 2

    def control_size(self):
        return 1

    def evaluate(self, x, u):
        p, v = x[:]
        vn = v + u[0] * dt
        pn = p + vn * dt

        return np.array([pn, vn])

The state is \([p, v]\) (position, velocity), the control is a scalar acceleration \(u\), and evaluate implements semi-implicit Euler integration with \(dt = 0.1\).

items.title: 2. Define the cost
items.text:
Custom costs subclass ssqpy.model.costs.StageCost and must provide evaluate, gradient, hessian_xx, hessian_xu and hessian_uu:

examples/trajgen/python/di.py
        dX[0, 0] = 1.0
        dX[0, 1] = dt
        dX[1, 1] = 1.0

        dU = np.zeros((2, 1))
        dU[0, 0] = dt**2
        dU[1, 0] = dt

        return dX, dU

    def hessprod_xx(self, x, u, lambda_):
        return np.zeros((2, 2))

    def hessprod_xu(self, x, u, lambda_):
        return np.zeros((2, 1))

    def hessprod_uu(self, x, u, lambda_):
        return np.zeros((1, 1))


# Drives the position towards 1
class Cost(costs.StageCost):
    def evaluate(self, x, u):
        return 0.5 * (x[0] - 1.0) ** 2

This penalizes deviation of the position \(p\) from a target of \(1.0\), applied both at every running stage and at the terminal stage.

items.title: Python API Reference
items.text:
This section is generated directly from the ssqpy bindings' docstrings (via mkdocstrings), so it always reflects the module as built. It documents the Python surface only; see the C++ API Reference for the corresponding C++ API, and Concepts for a guided, prose explanation of how the pieces fit together.

  • ssqpy: the top-level module, covering log levels
  • ssqpy.model: Model, SolverMode, Integration, Dimensions
  • ssqpy.model.costs: StageCost and predefined costs
  • ssqpy.model.constraints: StageConstraints and predefined constraints
  • ssqpy.model.dynamics: StageDynamics
  • ssqpy.model.terrain: Terrain, FlatTerrain
  • ssqpy.solvers: ssqp, MPC, ssqpParams, admmParams, hpipmParams, piqpParams, FlatVec, convergence data
  • ssqpy.solvers.search: dynamics and hyperparameter search

Note

Custom subclasses (of StageCost, StageDynamics, StageConstraints or Terrain) that you write in Python only need to implement the abstract methods described on each base class's page. See the Concepts pages for the full contract.

items.title: LogLevel
items.text:
Bases: IntEnum

The available log levels Each is used for a different class of output, and is independent of the others

items.title: model
items.text: Submodule containing classes related to the SSQP model, a respresentation of the system used for optimization.

items.title: SolverMode
items.text:
Bases: Enum

Solver Mode The mode the solver uses for the system formulation, corresponding to the equality constraint of the NLP This can either be full dynamics, or a kinematics formulation Options:

  • Kinematics: The solver optimizes in a kinematic mode. This means there are no system dynamics. Instead, the generated controls correspond to velocities, while the state corresponds to the system configuration.
  • ForwardDynamics: The solver optimizes with a forward dynamics approach. The state corresponds to a stacked vector of the system configuration and velocity. The generated controls correspond to torques which, when applied over time to the system, generate the output trajectory.
  • InverseDynamics: The solver optimizes with an inverse dynamics approach. The state corresponds to a stacked vector of the system configuration and velocity. The generated controls correspond to accelerations. This simplifies the LQR formulation and can sometimes lead to more robust solutions. Inverse dynamics is used as a constraint, ensuring the torques producing the generated acceleration controls are within the required effort limits.
  • ReducedInverseDynamics: This mode is similar to the Inverse dynamics mode. In this mode, the floating base (if present) and/or some subset of the model's joints are unactuated. While regular Inverse mode enforces this via equality constraints, this mode instead enforces this implicitly through state propagation.

items.title: Integration
items.text:

The type of integration used for the system dynamics Options:

  • ExplicitEuler: \(\boldsymbol{x}_{n+1}=\boldsymbol{x}_n+\boldsymbol{v}_ndt\) \(\boldsymbol{v}_{n+1}=\boldsymbol{v}_n+\boldsymbol{a}_ndt\)
  • SemiImplicitEuler: \(\boldsymbol{x}_{n+1}=\boldsymbol{x}_n+\boldsymbol{v}_{n+1}dt\) \(\boldsymbol{v}_{n+1}=\boldsymbol{v}_n+\boldsymbol{a}_ndt\)

items.title: Model
items.text:
Model(horizon, dt, **kwargs)

Defines an SSQP model An SSQP model object is a prerequisite to performing optimization using SSQP The model contains the following:

  • An optimization horizon, \(H\)
  • A cost function for each stage of the horizon, \(\ell_k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) \in \mathcal{R}\), \(0 \leq k \leq H\)
  • Dynamics functions for each stage of the horizon, \(\boldsymbol{f}_k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) \in \mathcal{R}^n\), \(0 \leq k \leq H\)
  • Constraint functions for each stage of the horizon, \(\boldsymbol{c}_k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) \in \mathcal{R}^c\), \(0 \leq k \leq H\)

Of the above, all stage cost and dynamics functions must be defined, but constraints may be left empty.

Note that models optimize for \(H\) total steps while considering the initial state to be constant, whereas the initial controls can be altered. This means that there are \(H\) total controls (\(\boldsymbol{u}_0\) to \(\boldsymbol{u}_{H-1}\)) and \(H + 1\) total states (\(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) to \(\boldsymbol{x}_H\)), with \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) being constant. At the terminal stage (stage \(H\)), there are no controls and, as such, stagewise functions must be appropriately defined to ignore them. Predefined functions all have constructors to account for this.

Models may be defined either by passing custom function implementations, or by using XML description files. Some constructors allow for defining a model using an XML file, but without passing the required cost functions. This is done to allow access to robot-related algorithms such as forward dynamics, which may be used to define model costs. Note that, if such constructors are used, the finalize method must be called before attempting to use the model for optimization. The user is responsible for either manually assigning all required costs, or passing them to the finalize method.

Initialize an SSQP Model.

Positional arguments (required): horizon (int): Optimization horizon (excluding initial stage) dt (float): Optimization time step

Keyword arguments (optional): urdf_path (str): Path to URDF file to use for the system dynamics mjcf_path (str): Path to MJCF file to use for the system dynamics free_flyer (bool): Whether the model has a floating base from_preset (ssqpy.model.Preset): Use a preset urdf instead of supplying a path; mutually exclusive withurdf_path, mjcf_path and free_flyer solver_mode (ssqpy.model.SolverMode): The solver mode to solve in integration (ssqpy.model.Integration): The integration method to use ignore_innate_constraints (bool): Whether to ignore XML constraints actuated_joints (list of int): List of joints to apply controls to; if non-empty, all joints whose indices are not included will not be actuated

items.title: finalize

Finalize the model with the provided configuration.

Keyword arguments (optional): costs (list of StageCost): Costs for each optimization stage stage_cost (StageCost): Cost to add to each non-terminal stage terminal_cost (StageCost): Cost for the terminal stage constraints (list of StageConstraints): Constraints for each optimization stage dynamics (list of StageDynamics): Dynamics for each optimization stage custom_lower_position_bounds (np.array of float): Lower position bounds to use in place of the values read from the XML; default XML values are used if left empty; has no effect if innate constraints are ignored custom_upper_position_bounds (np.array of float): Upper position bounds to use in place of the values read from the XML; default XML values are used if left empty; has no effect if innate constraints are ignored custom_velocity_bounds (np.array of float): Velocity bounds to use in place of the values read from the XML; default XML values are used if left empty; has no effect if innate constraints are ignored custom_torque_bounds (np.array of float): Torque bounds to use in place of the values read from the XML; default XML values are used if left empty; has no effect if innate constraints are ignored init_states (np.array or list of np.array): Initial states for each optimization stage; if np.array: initial state to use for every stage init_controls (np.array or list of np.array): Initial controls for each optimization stage; if np.array: initial controls to use for every stage

JointAngleConstraint(model, lb, ub, name='')

Bases: StageConstraints

Predefined joint angle constraint

Creates a constraint on the joint angles of the model

Note: this constraint is separate to any potential innate constraints \(\boldsymbol{q}_l \leq \boldsymbol{q} \leq \boldsymbol{q}_u\)

where:

  • \(\boldsymbol{q}_l\), \(\boldsymbol{q}_u\): Lower and upper configuration vectors
  • \(\boldsymbol{q}\): The model's joint configuration vector

items.title: FloatingBaseTranslationBound
items.text:
FloatingBaseTranslationBound(model, lb, ub, reference_frame=..., center=..., name='')

Bases: StageConstraints

Floating base position bound constraint

Creates a linear bound constraint on the position of the floating base: \(\boldsymbol{b}_l \leq R^\top (p_f - \boldsymbol{c}) \leq \boldsymbol{b}_u\)

where:

  • \(\boldsymbol{b}_l\), \(\boldsymbol{b}_u\): Lower and upper bound vectors on the base position (in \(\mathcal{R}^3\))
  • \(p_f\): Floating base position extracted from the system state
  • \(R\): Rotation of the reference frame the bounds are expressed in (World, Fixed, Local or Base, identity for World, with Local and Base both the base's axes)
  • \(\boldsymbol{c}\): Center the bounds are taken around (in \(\mathcal{R}^3\))

Assumes:

  • The Model contains a floating-base where the base position is the first part of the configuration vector (first 3 elements of size model.nq())

items.title: FloatingBaseRotationBound
items.text:
FloatingBaseRotationBound(model, Rref, lb=..., ub=..., name='')

Bases: StageConstraints

Predefined floating base orientation bound

Creates a nonlinear bound constraint on the orientation of the floating base: \(\boldsymbol{b}_l \leq \log_{SO3}(R_{ref}^\top R_f) \leq \boldsymbol{b}_u\)

where:

  • \(\boldsymbol{b}_l\), \(\boldsymbol{b}_u\): Lower and upper bound vectors on the orientation error (in \(\mathcal{R}^3\))
  • \(R_f\): Floating base rotation matrix
  • \(R_{ref}\): Reference rotation matrix

Assumes:

  • The model joint configuration is the first part of the state vector (size model.nq())
  • The floating base orientation is represented as a rotation matrix in SE(3) and can be extracted from the base pose in the system state

items.title: FloatingBasePoseBound
items.text:
Bases: StageConstraints

Predefined floating base SE(3) pose bound

Creates a nonlinear bound constraint on the full pose (position + orientation) of the floating base: \(\boldsymbol{b}_l \leq \log_{SE3}(T_{ref}^{-1} T_f) \leq \boldsymbol{b}_u\)

where:

  • \(\boldsymbol{b}_l\), \(\boldsymbol{b}_u\): Lower and upper bound vectors on the pose error (in \(\mathcal{R}^6\))
  • \(T_f\): Floating base pose in SE(3)
  • \(T_{ref}\): Reference pose in SE(3)

Assumes:

  • The model joint configuration is the first part of the state vector (size model.nq())
  • The floating base pose is represented as an SE(3) transform and can be extracted from the base state in the system model

items.title: ContactConstraint
items.text:
Bases: StageConstraints

Predefined contact constraint for a given frame Creates a set of constraints that amount to a contact force constraint for a frame This consists of the following 4-point linearized friction cone constraints:

  • \(f_n \gt 0\)
  • \(|f_1| \leq \mu f_n\)
  • \(|f_2| \leq \mu f_n\) As well as the following constraint on the 3D position of the frame the contact is on:
  • \(p_z = h_z\) And, unless no_slip is false, the following no-slip constraint on the linear velocity of the frame:
  • \(\boldsymbol{v}_f = \boldsymbol{0}\) where:
  • \(f_n\) is the normal of the contact force (\(f_z\))
  • \(f_1\) is the first component of the tangential contact force (\(f_x\))
  • \(f_2\) is the second component of the tangential contact force (\(f_y\))
  • \(\mu\) is the static friction coefficient at the contact
  • \(p_z\) is the \(z-\)component of the translation of the frame the contact is on
  • \(h_z\) is the height of the terrain at point \((p_x, p_y)\)
  • \(\boldsymbol{v}_f\) is the linear velocity of the frame the contact is on Note that this constraint cannot be manually added in the Python library, use the Model's addContactConstraint method instead.

items.title: StageCost
items.text: General abstract constraint function for an optimization stage \(k\): \(\ell_k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u})\) Defines the required functions for a stage cost, while providing default implementations for some

Set enabled status for StageCost A stage always keeps at least one cost, so this has no effect if every cost on the stage is disabled

items.title: gradient
items.text:
gradient(x, u)

Get cost Jacobians with respect to \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{u}\), evaluated at given \((\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u})\): \(\nabla_x \ell_k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u})\) and \(\nabla_u \ell_k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u})\) Returns: dx: gradient with respect to \(\boldsymbol{x}\), \(n_{dx} \times 1\) du: gradient with respect to \(\boldsymbol{u}\), \(n_u \times 1\)

items.title: hessian_xx
items.text:
hessian_xx(x, u)

Get cost function hessian matrix with respect to \(\boldsymbol{xx}\), evaluated at given \((\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u})\): \(\nabla_{xx}^2 \ell_k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u})\) Returns: Hxx: Hessian matrix, \(n_{dx} \times n_{dx}\)

items.title: hessian_xu
items.text:
hessian_xu(x, u)

Get cost function hessian matrix with respect to \(\boldsymbol{xu}\), evaluated at given \((\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u})\): \(\nabla_{xu}^2 \ell_k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u})\) Returns: Hxu: Hessian matrix, \(n_{dx} \times n_u\)

items.title: hessian_uu
items.text:
hessian_uu(x, u)

Get cost function hessian matrix with respect to \(\boldsymbol{uu}\), evaluated at given \((\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u})\): \(\nabla_{uu}^2 \ell_k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u})\) Returns: Huu: Hessian matrix, \(n_u \times n_u\)

items.title: SquaredJointAngleCost
items.text:
Bases: StageCost

Predefined squared joint angle cost

Defines the cost term \(\ell(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) = \frac{1}{2} \lVert \boldsymbol{w} \odot \boldsymbol{x}_{ang} \rVert_2^2\)

where:

  • \(\boldsymbol{x}_{ang}\) is the angular (position) part of the state Note that this will ignore the first 7 elements if the model has a floating base
  • \(\boldsymbol{w}\) is the weight on the angular term

Assumes:

  • The model joint configuration is the first part of the state vector (size model.nq()), appearing after the floating base (if present)

items.title: SquaredJointVelocityCost
items.text:
Bases: StageCost

Predefined squared joint velocity cost

Defines the cost term \(\ell(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) = \frac{1}{2} \lVert \boldsymbol{w} \odot \boldsymbol{x}_{vel} \rVert_2^2\)

where:

  • \(\boldsymbol{x}_{vel}\) is the velocity part of the state
  • \(\boldsymbol{w}\) is the weight on the velocity term

Assumes:

  • The model joint velocity is the final part of the state vector (size model.nv())

items.title: SquaredControlCost
items.text:
Bases: StageCost

Predefined squared control cost

Defines the cost term \(\ell(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) = \frac{1}{2} \lVert \boldsymbol{w} \odot \boldsymbol{u}_{ctrl} \rVert_2^2\)

where:

  • \(\boldsymbol{u}_{ctrl}\) is the control part of the controls
  • \(\boldsymbol{w}\) is the weight on the control term

Assumes:

  • The model control is the first part of the control vector (size model.nu())

items.title: SquaredIDTorqueCost
items.text:
Bases: StageCost

Predefined squared inverse dynamics torque cost

Defines the cost term \(\ell(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) = \frac{1}{2} \lVert \boldsymbol{w} \odot \boldsymbol{\tau} \rVert_2^2\)

where:

  • \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) is the actuated-joint torque caused by the controls
  • \(\boldsymbol{w}\) is the weight on the torque term

Note that this cost assumes inverse dynamics is being used (i.e. treats controls as accelerations)

Assumes:

  • The model is in Inverse Dynamics or Reduced Inverse Dynamics mode, such that the state is made up of configuration and velocity and the controls are made up of accelerations (including base, for Inverse Dynamics; actuated joints only, for Reduced Inverse Dynamics) and potential forces

The torque accounts for the forces of the stage the cost is added to, which the model passes in when it's finalized. A single instance can only be added to several stages if they all have the same forces, so construct one instance per stage otherwise

items.title: SquaredForceCost
items.text:
Bases: StageCost

Predefined squared force cost

Defines the cost term \(\ell(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) = \frac{1}{2} \lVert \boldsymbol{w} \odot \boldsymbol{u}_{f} \rVert_2^2\)

where:

  • \(\boldsymbol{u}_{f}\) is the force part of the controls
  • \(\boldsymbol{w}\) is the weight on the force term

Assumes:

  • The model forces make up the second and final part of the control vector, following the control part of size model.nu(), for any remaining elements

items.title: SquaredConfigurationErrorCost
items.text:
Bases: StageCost

Predefined squared configuration error cost

Defines the cost term \(\ell(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) = \frac{1}{2} \lVert \boldsymbol{w} \odot (\boldsymbol{q} - \boldsymbol{q}_d)\rVert_2^2\)

where:

  • \(\boldsymbol{q}\) is the configuration part of the state
  • \(\boldsymbol{q}_d\) is the desired configuration
  • \(\boldsymbol{w}\) is the weight for the configuration error

Assumes:

  • The model joint configuration is the first part of the state vector (size model.nq())

items.title: FloatingBaseSquaredTranslationErrorCost
items.text:
Bases: StageCost

Predefined squared floating base translation error cost

Defines the cost term \(\ell(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) = \frac{1}{2} \lVert \boldsymbol{w} \odot R^\top (\boldsymbol{t}_f - \boldsymbol{t}_d)\rVert_2^2\)

where:

  • \(\boldsymbol{t}_f\) is the floating base translation (in \(\mathcal{R}^3\))
  • \(\boldsymbol{t}_d\) is the desired translation of the floating base (in \(\mathcal{R}^3\))
  • \(\boldsymbol{w}\) is the weight on the translation error
  • \(R\) is the rotation of the reference frame the error is expressed in (World, Fixed, Local or Base, identity for World, with Local and Base both the base's axes)

Assumes:

  • The model joint configuration is the first part of the state vector (size model.nq())
  • The floating base translation is extracted from the base pose of the model state representation

Defines the cost term \(\ell(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) = \frac{1}{2} \lVert \boldsymbol{w} \odot \log_{SO(3)}(R_f^\top R_d)\rVert_2^2\)

where:

  • \(R_f\) is the floating base rotation (in \(\mathit{SO3}\))
  • \(R_d\) is the desired rotation of the floating base (in \(\mathit{SO3}\))
  • \(\boldsymbol{w}\) is the weight on the rotation error

Assumes:

items.title: FloatingBaseSquaredPoseErrorCost

Predefined squared floating base pose error cost

Defines the cost term \(\ell(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) = \frac{1}{2} D^\top W D\)

where:

  • \(D = \log_{SE(3)} T^{-1}T_d\)
  • \(T\) is the floating base pose (in \(\mathit{SE3}\))
  • \(T_d\) is the desired floating base pose (in \(\mathit{SE3}\))
  • \(W\) is a weight matrix, made up of parameters \(w_p\) for translation and \(w_r\) for rotation

Assumes:

  • The model joint configuration is the first part of the state vector (size model.nq())

items.title: FrameSquaredTerrainHeightErrorCost
items.text:
FrameSquaredTerrainHeightErrorCost(model, frame, desired_height, weight, name='')

Bases: StageCost

Predefined squared frame terrain height error cost

Defines the cost term \(\ell(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) = \frac{1}{2} w^2 (p_z - h(p_x, p_y) - d_d)^2\)

where:

  • \(\boldsymbol{p}\) is the frame translation for a given frame of the model (in \(\mathcal{R}^3\))
  • \(h\) is the height of the terrain at the frame's horizontal position, the model's terrain unless the cost is given one of its own
  • \(d_d\) is the desired height of the frame above the terrain
  • \(w\) is the weight on the height error

Assumes:

  • The model joint configuration is the first part of the state vector (size model.nq())

Defines the cost term \(\ell(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) = \frac{1}{2} \lVert \boldsymbol{w} \odot R^\top (\boldsymbol{c} - \boldsymbol{c}_r)\rVert_2^2\)

where:

  • \(\boldsymbol{c}\) is the center of mass for the model (in \(\mathcal{R}^3\))
  • \(\boldsymbol{c}_r\) is the reference point for the center of mass (in \(\mathcal{R}^3\))
  • \(R\) is the rotation of the reference frame the error is expressed in (World, Fixed or Base, identity for World)

items.title: FramesInverseSquaredDistanceCost
items.text:
Bases: StageCost

Predefined frames squared inverse distance cost

Defines the cost term \(\ell(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{u}) = \sum_{i < j} \frac{w}{2 \lVert \boldsymbol{\sigma} \odot R^\top (\boldsymbol{t}_i - \boldsymbol{t}_j)\rVert_2^2}\)

where:

  • \(\boldsymbol{t}_i\) is the frame translation for frame \(i\) of the model (in \(\mathcal{R}^3\))
  • \(w\) is the weight on the translation error
  • \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\) is the distance scale, a per-axis vector (in \(\mathcal{R}^3\)) determining the scaling factor for each axis; the factors work in an inverse manner, i.e. larger values place less importance on an axis, while smaller ones place more
  • \(R\) is the rotation of the reference frame whose axes the distance scale applies along (World, Fixed or Base, identity for World)

Assumes:

  • The model joint configuration is the first part of the state vector (size model.nq())
